UOR-R4

UOR-R4 documentation

Read online (planned; live once the site workflow deploys): https://uor-foundation.github.io/uor-r4/. The earlier Studio web app moves to https://uor-foundation.github.io/uor-r4/studio/.

In one paragraph. This is the map of the UOR-R4 documentation. UOR-R4 is an open research project building a language model that predicts text with geometry and whole-number arithmetic instead of a transformer's large grids of decimal multiplications, so that it can run fast on a laptop or in a browser. It is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete, and no model built under its rules holds a useful conversation yet (where we are). The pages here explain what the project is, where it stands and where it is going in plain words first, then give the evidence for every claim so an expert can check it. What UOR-R4 is

In one paragraph. UOR-R4 is an attempt to build a language model, the kind of program behind chat assistants, that is cheap enough to train and run on an ordinary laptop or inside a web browser. Today's language models are transformers. They spend most of their effort multiplying very large grids of decimal numbers. UOR-R4 bets that a different toolkit can do the same job for far less: rotations of a geometric object, exact whole-number addresses built from primes, small lookup tables, and an exact memory. This page explains that bet in about five minutes. It is a research project and it is pre-alpha. None of its 8 milestones is complete, and no model built under its rules holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS, NOW).

How UOR-R4 predicts the next word. Each step uses only whole numbers. The picture shows the design; it does not show a model that already works well.

Words in bold are defined in the glossary. Claims are labelled proof (follows from definitions or code), measurement (from a recorded run) or hypothesis (an untested idea), as in docs/formal_vocabulary.md.

What a language model does

A language model reads text and guesses what comes next. First a tokenizer cuts the text into numbered pieces called tokens. A token is a word or part of a word. UOR-R4's tokenizer has 4,096 pieces (tokenizer). The model then looks at the pieces so far and predicts the next one. Given "the cat sat on the", a good model puts "mat" near the top of its list. It appends its guess and repeats.

Everything a chat assistant does, answering, summarising, writing code, comes from running this one loop many times. So a model is only as good as its next-piece guesses, and only as fast as one turn of the loop.

What a transformer is, and where its cost goes

A transformer is the design behind almost every modern language model (background: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", 2017, arXiv:1706.03762). One turn of its loop looks like this:

flowchart LR
  t["Token"] --> e["Embedding:<br/>a long list of decimals"]
  e --> a["Attention:<br/>compare with EVERY earlier token<br/>(softmax)"]
  a --> m["Feed-forward:<br/>multiply by large learned grids<br/>(matrix multiplication)"]
  m --> o["Output:<br/>score EVERY word in the vocabulary<br/>(softmax)"]
  o --> n["Next token"]
  m -. "repeat for many layers" .-> a

One turn of a transformer. The three expensive operations are named in brackets.

Three operations carry most of the cost:

  1. Matrix multiplication. Each token is carried as a long list of decimal numbers. Every layer multiplies that list by large learned grids of numbers. Nearly all of the arithmetic is here.
  2. Attention. To decide what matters, the newest token is compared with every earlier token. The work grows with the length of the text, and the model keeps a stored copy of every earlier position.
  3. Softmax. Scores are turned into probabilities with exponentials and a sum over everything, once inside attention and once over the whole vocabulary to choose the next word.

The project bans two of the three outright, softmax-like squashing functions and matrix multiplication, anywhere: training, evaluation, tools and serving (charter, sections 3.2 and 3.3). All-pairs attention is not banned as an idea; it is replaced by bounded reads of a few nearby tokens. The reason, in the owner's words: "my goal with all of these bans is to ban expensive operations" (charter, section 1).

The bet: geometry and exact memory instead

UOR-R4 replaces each expensive part with something cheaper:

Transformer partUOR-R4's replacement
A long list of decimals per tokenA short address: 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers, each block a fixed point on a geometric object
Compare with every earlier tokenA local read (a "read" is the step that looks back at earlier text): look at a few nearby earlier tokens, found by their addresses
Softmax over every wordAdmission: open a few "drawers" (called cells) of words near what was read, then pick the nearest word inside them
Learned grids of decimalsRotations from a fixed, finite set, plus table look-ups
A growing store of every past positionExact memory: write a fact once under an exact name, read it back exactly

The finished model is meant to run with whole numbers only: adds, subtractions, comparisons and table look-ups, with no multiply instruction at all. This rule is called D11 (charter, section 3.6). The lead measure of success is tokens per second on ordinary hardware (charter, section 1).

Whether these replacements can match a transformer's quality is the open question. It is a hypothesis. No measurement so far shows it, and the next page says which parts are built and which are missing: transformer vs geometry.

What "geometry" means here

"Geometry" in this project means a few concrete objects, each chosen because it can be computed exactly with whole numbers. The geometry section has one illustrated chapter for each.

A token's address is built from fixed points. Each of the 4,096 tokens owns 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers. Each block is always one of 16 fixed points of a famous eight-dimensional lattice called E8. Every such point is a signed rearrangement of (2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0): two of the eight places hold 2 or −2 and the rest are zero. There are \(16^4 = 65{,}536\) possible addresses, more than the 4,096 tokens, so every token can have its own (proof, by counting; see the model page). The model does not yet use all 240 points of E8 (E8, H4 and the 600-cell).

Moving means rotating. Changing a block means swapping one fixed point for another, which is a rotation from a finite set. Nothing is rounded, so a rotation can always be undone exactly (quaternions and rotation).

Names come from primes; starting places from zeta phases. Each token can be named exactly by a prime number, and that name never collides with another. Separately, angles taken from the zeros of the Riemann zeta function (a fixed, reproducible set of numbers from mathematics) scatter the tokens' starting addresses. One such construction, PrimeZeta, gives all 4,096 tokens distinct starting addresses (measurement, construction record). The distinctness comes from a cell-balancing step, not from the zeta angles; whether the angles help at all is untested (primes and zeta phases).

Near means few steps apart. Distance between two addresses is the sum of the differences between their numbers, which needs only subtraction and addition. "Nearby earlier tokens" and "the nearest word" both use this distance (the model page).

Learning means trying the legal moves. The current model does not use calculus. To learn, it tries all 16 legal values of one block on the graphics card and keeps a change only if a whole-number score strictly improves (training, discrete learning).

Transformer parts and their geometric replacements

In one paragraph. A transformer is built from a handful of standard parts: a tokenizer, an embedding table, a position signal, attention, feed-forward layers, normalization, an output layer, a loss and an optimizer. UOR-R4 tries to replace each part with a geometric or exact mechanism that avoids softmax and matrix multiplication. This page puts each transformer part beside the project's replacement and says how far that replacement has got. The short version: most parts have a candidate, and several candidates are built and tested. Two parts have no candidate at all: position and normalization. No two replacements have yet been trained together into a model that beats simple word-count tables (audit synthesis, section 1).

Each transformer part beside its replacement. Colour gives the status. The two dashed boxes are the gaps.

Terms are in the glossary. Labels follow docs/formal_vocabulary.md: proof, measurement or hypothesis.

How to read the status

Every mechanism has exactly one of three statuses, set on the mechanism board:

  • ACTIVE: on the current model path, crates/uor-r4-discrete.
  • READY: built and tested, but never trained into a model.
  • PARKED: the forms tried so far failed or broke a rule. The mechanism stays open, and its page lists what would reopen it.

There is no "retired" or "dead" status. A failed run closes one configuration, never a mechanism (charter, section 4.1). Today the board has 10 ACTIVE, 4 READY and 13 PARKED mechanisms.

A passing test shows that code does what it claims. It is not a trained capability, and a test marked NOT_RUN is not a pass.

One status is disputed. The board keeps D11 integer serving as ACTIVE, as its own page says, but the audit would call it READY, because no lawful model has been exported through it yet (mechanism board, contradictions).

The two gaps

Gap 1: position. A transformer adds a signal that says where each token sits in the sequence. No UOR-R4 mechanism is assigned to this job, and no lawful evidence exists for one. The current model keeps the most recent tokens in order at the leaves of a small tree, so order is present in its layout, but nothing is learned about it (the model page). The nearest result is about carrying a running state by quaternion rotation. It beat no rotation by 0.071 and 0.077 nats (a nat is a unit of prediction error; lower is better), but in a model that still used softmax attention, a sigmoid gate and dense layers, with 332,928 fewer parameters in the comparison arm (transport record). So "rotation can carry order" is a hypothesis.

Gap 2: normalization. A transformer rescales its signals between layers so they stay in a workable range. UOR-R4 has no designed mechanism for this. Snapping each block back to one of its fixed lattice points might play that role, but no record says so or tests it (mechanism board). This is also a hypothesis.

What "replaces" does not mean yet

Having a replacement on paper is not the same as having a working model:

  • No replacement has matched its transformer part on quality. Every attention-style read that learned well in the older decimal experiments had help from softmax during training, and the best softmax-free read was rejected (softmax-free read; audit synthesis (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md), section 1).
  • No two parts have been trained together except on the current discrete path. That path has no feed-forward layer and no position mechanism, and it scores below a table of word counts (measurement, K16 outcome).
  • Several other things are not built: using an exact address as the read, any consumer of the object store, an exporter that turns a trained model into a D11 file, and an output step that avoids scanning the whole vocabulary (audit synthesis, section 1).

The project does not compare its models against transformers. It compares them against count tables and earlier geometric models, and grades them with fixed, deterministic checks (charter, sections 3.10 and 4.4).

Where UOR-R4 is today

In one paragraph. UOR-R4 is pre-alpha. None of its 8 milestones is complete, and no model built under its rules holds a conversation (STATUS, NOW). Many of the parts work on their own: a whole-number model path on the graphics card, three ways of reading earlier text, one shared word table, a whole-number engine that runs in a browser, and an exact storage system. But the best model trained so far guesses the next piece of text correctly far less often than two very simple tables of word counts. Nobody yet knows why. This page lists what works, what does not, and the measured numbers, each with its source.

Correct first guesses out of 14,287 test positions. The trained model is far below both count tables, and the new M1 bar sits at the higher table.

Terms are in the glossary. Claims are labelled proof, measurement or hypothesis (docs/formal_vocabulary.md). A passing check shows that code does what it says. It is not a trained capability, and NOT_RUN never means passed.

How the model is scored

The test set is 14,287 positions in 400 held-out documents, called the DEV panel (count tables record). At each position the model makes one guess for the next token. A top-1 score counts how many of those guesses are right.

Two plain tables, built from the same training text the model sees, set the floor:

  • The unigram table always guesses the single most common token. It scores 1,226 (measurement).
  • The next-word table (called T2) looks only at the previous token and guesses the token that most often followed it in training. It scores 6,300 (measurement).

Both come from the count tables record. A model that cannot beat them has not yet learned anything a lookup table cannot do. The project compares against these tables, not against transformers (charter, section 3.10).

These parts are built and pass their checks. None of them is a language result. (A read is the step that looks back at earlier text; reach is how many test positions have the right answer among the candidates the model opens at all.)

What does not work yet

No model holds a conversation (STATUS). The detail:

The best trained model is below both count tables. The last full experiment (called K16) trained two variants of the model, each on two random seeds, for 16,404 batches (K16 outcome; all measurement):

VariantSeedCorrect first guessesReach: positions where the right answer was among the candidates openedCells in use (of 256)
A (nearest-address margin)1652,237209
A24633,167192
R (occupied-cell rank)110112,08920
R223012,46619

Variant A is the one the record selects. Its reach fell below the required 4,894 positions on both seeds. Variant R kept a high reach only by collapsing into 19 or 20 cells, so that each guess was drawn from about 3,400 of the 4,096 tokens, nearly the whole vocabulary; that reach is not real discrimination. The registered verdict was an occupancy collapse (record code OCCUPANCY_COLLAPSE_TRIGGERED), and no run was kept. All four miss the run's own top-1 bar of 1,941 and are far below the next-word table's 6,300. The large gap between seeds (65 against 463) also shows how noisy one run is.

The cause is not established. The first guess was that too few distinct starting vectors were to blame. That is ruled out as the main cause: in variant A, training raised the distinct vectors from 16 to about 275, yet top-1 stayed low (K16 outcome, census section). The candidates still open are:

  • The address key may be too coarse. The key is the distance that orders the drawers. It uses only the first and last block and takes only 5 values (0, 4, 8, 12 or 16) to order up to 256 cells (proof, from the kernel source), so which drawers open is largely decided by their arbitrary numbering (the model page, chief architect's review §3.2). Whether this causes the low score is a hypothesis.
  • The read, the ranking capacity, or the training schedule. One full run sees fewer than half of the training targets: 1,049,856 of 2,425,925 (measurement, audit dossier). These remain hypotheses.

The newest run stopped early. The address-cell run (A8) began with the better reach above, but training eroded it. At its first checkpoint the Relation read held 551 reachable positions, below half its starting 1,351, which triggered the registered stop (the control held 857; measurement, A8 dose). A version that protects the reach is built; its GPU qualification is NOT_RUN (controller record).

No model trained under today's rules has been exported or timed. No exporter turns a trained discrete model into a D11 file (the older float stacks were exported and served in October), and tokens per second for this model have never been measured (lut-serving).

Parts are missing. The current model has no position mechanism, no normalization and no feed-forward layer (transformer vs geometry).

Training is on hold. Each training run needs a reviewed one-page plan and a release typed by the owner personally (charter, section 5).

What about the older models?

Before October, the project trained a decimal-number model called the geometric stack, from 7 million to 214 million parameters. Four 214-million-parameter checkpoints are published on Hugging Face as historical evidence. Their chat versions (which predate today's rules) could rewrite and summarise, while code and arithmetic were wrong (audit dossier, from the model card). That stack used softmax, the SiLU activation (a smooth squashing curve) and matrix multiplication; geometry was about 0.05% of its arithmetic. Served through the integer engine, its best version (19.9 million parameters) reached 0.933 bits per byte and the charted versions 1.20 to 1.24, all missing the old M1 bar of 0.90 (D11 serving record; audit dossier). It breaks today's rules and is PARKED (geometric stack). It shows the project can train a model that writes text. It does not show that the geometric replacements can.

How the project got here

Between 12 and 19 October the owner (project lead Casey Allard) made 19 decisions, several of which rebuilt the model's foundations: no softmax anywhere, no matrix multiplication, GPU-only research compute, whole numbers on the active path. Much of that week went into rebuilding and checking rather than learning. In the week of 12 to 18 October, 34 of 309 records were results; the rest were tooling, plans and reviews, part of it ordered by those decisions. Five training runs on the new discrete path followed, and none produced a kept result (audit synthesis, section 3). The history has the long story.

Where UOR-R4 is going

In one paragraph. The goal is a fast language model that runs on your own laptop or in your browser, holds a conversation with a durable memory, and later reasons and writes code, all on the geometric path with no transformer. The project marks progress with eight milestones, M1 to M8. None is complete yet. On 19 October 2026 the owner set a plain first bar: the model must beat two simple word-count tables, on each of two seeds, through its whole-number export. This page explains the milestones in plain words, the shortest credible path from today to a first simple conversation, and the three products at the end. The path is a plan, not a promise. Every training step still needs the owner's release, and the central question, whether a softmax-free model can learn to rank words well, is unanswered.

The road from today to the products. Stage 0 is where the project stands. Each gate needs an owner release.

Terms are in the glossary. Labels are proof, measurement or hypothesis (docs/formal_vocabulary.md).

The eight milestones in plain words

M6Reasoning and codingWorking reasoning and coding on the same modelNot started#2034

Statuses are from the ROADMAP table, which states each bar in full. A milestone closes only when its bar is met on a saved model.

The new M1 bar

M1 closes when one saved discrete model passes five conditions (charter, section 4.8; D39, item 1):

  • (a) Starting reach. Before training, the right answer is among the candidates the model opens (its "reach") at no fewer than 4,894 of the 14,287 test positions (the gate called G-Pre; the "G-" names are gate codes from D39).
  • (b) Reach kept. That reach survives training, on both seeds (G-Adm).
  • (c) Real spread. More than 16 of the 256 word cells (the "drawers" of words) are in use, plus the further occupancy condition in D39 (G-Occ).
  • (d) Beat the count tables (new, 19 October). Whole-number top-1, measured through the D11 export, beats both the unigram table (1,226 of 14,287) and the next-word table (6,300 of 14,287) on the same test panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported. This replaces the earlier bar of 0.90 bits per byte, which the current model cannot be scored on because its loss gives no probabilities. Bits per byte returns at a later milestone.
  • (e) Fresh transfer. The gain holds on a fresh, sealed test panel registered in advance.

For scale: the best trained model today scores 65 and 463 (measurement, where we are). The gap to 6,300 is large.

The shortest path to a first conversation

The audit of 19 October laid out the shortest credible path as six stages (audit synthesis, section 4). It is a proposal. The stage order follows the owner's fixed sequence in D39 item 4; changing it is the owner's decision.

Stage 0. Run what is already FIT'd. A capacity test (called W2, about $0.91) is FIT-reviewed and queued, awaiting an owner release (NOW, row 6). "Capacity" here means how many different words the addresses can tell apart. W2 decides whether the shortfall comes from the representation (the addresses cannot tell enough words apart) or the learning law (the training method cannot find good addresses). Next comes the rerun of the address-cell model with its reach protected (controller record). Decides: fix the addresses, or move on to Stage 2.

Stage 1. Make the capacity measurable. Replace the coarse address key (today it can take only 5 different values, so it barely separates the drawers) with one that uses the whole vector, and measure it before any training. A wider code is optional and needs new GPU code. Bar: enough distinct vectors that the number of positions still winnable clears the run bar of 1,941, and a starting reach above the address-cell model's 1,351 of 3,847.

Stage 2. Pick the learning law. First a faster discrete method that scores 16 coordinates at once (called BVG-K; its first stage is qualified), at about $12 for two seeds. Only if Stage 0 blames the learning law and BVG-K fails: one decimal-training run in a separate module, at about $5 to $10 plus build work. Decimal numbers are allowed in offline training only; the shipped file stays whole-number (charter, section 3.7). Bar: beat the unigram table, then the admission-matched next-word table (the version W2 produces, not the 6,300 full-panel table), on two seeds.

Stage 3. Add the missing parts. Build a trunk with a feed-forward layer (the Hamilton gate), a recurrence with quaternion rotation, and the Flock and Relation reads. None of these has been trained together, and the only supporting evidence is weak, so this stage is a hypothesis test, not reuse of proven parts. Scale and data are also open: no trained stack has used the 1.39-billion-token chat corpus the project assembled (UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#1660). Bar: beat Stage 2's best by more than the seed-to-seed noise, with a fresh-panel number.

Stage 4. Export and serve. Write the missing exporter that turns a trained model into a D11 file, then measure the export gap and tokens per second on a laptop. Bar: the integer audits stay green, the gap stays within the noise band, and tokens per second is reported for both reading the prompt and writing the reply. This is where M1's bar (d) and M4 are tested.

Stage 5. First simple conversation. Train on fixed example answers produced once by a donor model (not yet generated), as the owner's one-time exception D41 allows: the student sees only the answers, never the donor's probabilities. Ground replies in the exact memory and the object store. Bar: M2's bar, at least 256 of 512 saved questions and at least 40% of fresh ones, graded by fixed deterministic checks.

Binding conditions on every stage. Training is held until the owner releases each reviewed plan, and the owner types each release personally (charter, section 5). M1 can only be closed by a whole-number-trained ("discrete") model, so if Stages 3 and 4 use a trunk (the main body of the network) trained with decimals, the owner must first redefine the milestone. Under D41, the Stage 5 student stays on the discrete path unless the owner decides otherwise (audit synthesis, section 4).

What the audit proposes to stop: rerunning the old starting table (built from a fixed random seed) that gives at most 16 distinct vectors; tuning admission objectives on the 5-value key; and reading much into any run that loses to the two count tables.

After the first conversation

Stages 0 to 5 aim at M1, M4 and M2; M3 is not yet staged. The rest of the road is:

  • M5: measure the real cost on an M1-class laptop: energy per token, memory and tokens per second. An integer path is not an efficiency result until it is measured (charter, section 3.9, "Efficiency is measured").
  • M6: add reasoning and coding to the same model. Exact arithmetic is the visible gap.
  • M7: make the browser worker, the command line and the Rust library give identical tokens.
  • M8: the owner declares an alpha release.

The products at the end

The owner defined three products on 19 October (charter, section 2; products):

ProductWhat it will beWhat exists today
The modelOne whole-number model file, built in crates/uor-r4-discrete and served by crates/uor-r4-integerThe serving engine, tested on a synthetic stand-in. No trained model to put in it
Web clientThe Studio in your browser, running the model on your own device in WebAssemblyThe Studio page and the browser engine, not yet connected. Website deploys are paused
Desktop clientA Tauri app sharing the web interface, running the model natively, with durable memory and offline use on M1-class laptopsA written specification only

Nothing ships until a trained model passes M1 to M8. Running the finished model on your own computer or in your browser is the product, and the rule that research compute must use a GPU does not apply to it (charter, section 3.6).

The biggest unknown

Every read that learned well in the older experiments had help from softmax during training, and the best softmax-free read was rejected (softmax-free read). Whether a lawful read can learn to rank words without it is a hypothesis, and no amount of assembly answers it before Stage 2 runs (open questions).

Frequently asked questions

In one paragraph. These are the questions newcomers and would-be contributors ask most often, answered plainly. The short version: UOR-R4 is a pre-alpha research project that tries to build a fast language model out of geometry instead of a transformer's expensive arithmetic. Parts of it are built and tested. No model it has trained holds a useful conversation yet, and the best one so far predicts the next word worse than a simple table of word counts (STATUS). Words in the answers are defined in the glossary.

Which section of this page to read first.

Claims are labelled proof (follows from definitions or code), measurement (from a recorded run) or hypothesis (untested), as in docs/formal_vocabulary.md. NOT_RUN means a test was planned and never executed. It is not a pass.

The basics

1. What is UOR-R4, in plain words?

It is an open research project that asks one question: can a language model run on an ordinary laptop or in a browser if its core arithmetic is geometry (rotations, exact whole-number addresses built from primes, lookup tables) instead of the huge decimal multiplications inside today's chat AIs? The project is pre-alpha and the answer is not known yet. See what UOR-R4 is and the charter, section 1.

2. Is this a transformer?

No, by design. The charter says the project is "not a transformer" (section 1), bans matrix multiplication (section 3.3) and excludes "a dense model disguised as lookup tables" from serving (section 3.6) (charter). The current model (crates/uor-r4-discrete) reads earlier words with three bounded reads (Route, Flock, Relation) and has no feed-forward block at all. But be careful with the history: the project's older float models (7 million to 214 million parameters) used softmax, matrix multiplication and a SiLU activation (a smooth squashing curve), so they did not follow today's rules (measurement, geometric stack). The comparison page is transformer vs geometry.

3. Does it work yet?

No. Zero of the eight milestones are complete (STATUS). What works is the parts: for example the integer substrate passes 25 of 25 admitted GPU construction controls (measurement, K16 qualification), and the whole-number serving engine runs in a browser and contains no multiply, divide or decimal instruction in 7 of 7 serving functions (measurement, WASM record). Passing a control is not a language result. No two replacements have been trained together into a model that beats the count tables (open questions).

4. How good is the best model so far?

Not good. On 14,287 development rows, the best trained arm (K16-A) got its first guess right 65 and 463 times on its two seeds. A table of overall word counts gets 1,226, and a table that looks up the last word and returns its most common successor gets 6,300 (measurement, K16 outcome, count tables). The model has to beat both tables before the first milestone can close (charter, section 4.8).

5. Why does it lose to a count table? Do you know the cause?

The cause is not established. One early suspect, that too few distinct starting vectors capped the score, was tested and did not explain it: training broke much of the aliasing and the score stayed low (K16 outcome). The open candidates are how well the output step can rank, the read, the address key (it takes only 5 values to order up to 256 cells, a proof from the kernel source in the architect's audit; whether that causes the low score is a hypothesis) and the training schedule (one pass sees under half the training targets). The next test, W2 (FIT-reviewed and queued, awaiting an owner release), decides whether the wall is the representation or the learning law (open questions).

6. Will it reach frontier capability?

That is the goal, in the owner's words "almost frontier level capability" on a laptop (charter, section 1). It is a hypothesis. Nothing measured so far supports or refutes it, and the data and model scale needed are not established. The shortest planned path is in where we're going.

The rules

7. Why no softmax?

The owner's reason is cost, not taste: "to ban expensive operations" (charter, section 1). Softmax turns scores into probabilities with exponentials and a sum over everything, and it hides a dense global normalisation. The charter bans it, and every softmax-like function, in the model, its training, its comparators and any renamed or table form (section 3.2). The price is real: every earlier read that learned a ranking had softmax helping it somewhere in training, and the best softmax-free read was a recorded REJECT, 0.0172 bits per byte worse and 15% slower (measurement, open questions, record). Whether a softmax-free read can learn ranking at all is the project's biggest open question.

8. Why no matrix multiplication?

Matrix multiplication is nearly all of a transformer's arithmetic, so removing it is the point of the project (charter, section 3.3). A geometric feed-forward block, such as the Hamilton gate, is allowed. A dense one is not. One mechanism, spin-native weights, matched a dense model's score but only by running a dense block multiplication, so it is PARKED.

9. Why use GPUs for research but laptops for serving?

They are different jobs. Research compute (training, evaluation, qualification) must run on the GPU, because host runs gave wrong timing and wrong evidence, and spending GPU only where a run can change a decision keeps costs down (charter, section 3.5). The finished model, though, is meant to run on the user's own device: serving the exported integer file on a laptop CPU, in a browser or on Apple silicon is the product, and the GPU-only rule does not apply to it (section 3.6). Scoring an exported model for a milestone still counts as research compute.

10. Why can training use decimals when serving cannot?

Decimals train faster, and only the shipped file has to be integer (charter, section 3.7, from decision D37). Any float-trained candidate must report its export gap, the quality lost when it is snapped to whole numbers, and a gap above the noise band disqualifies it. The current discrete model avoids the question because it is integer from end to end. See serving and export.

11. Why primes, zeta zeros, E8 and quaternions? Do they actually help?

The owner's rule is "use geometry", because the bet is that exact geometry can replace dense arithmetic (charter, section 1). What has been shown is narrow. An injective code is possible by counting (\(16^4 = 65{,}536 \ge 4{,}096\), proof), and the PrimeZeta construction gives all 4,096 tokens distinct vectors (measurement). The address-structured table reached 1,351 of 3,847 targets at zero training, against 127 for the plain PrimeZeta start (measurement). But no run has shown that any geometric choice beats a plain alternative on language. Architectural priority is not measured advantage. See the geometry chapters.

12. Why so much process? What is a FIT sheet?

A pre-registration sheet is a one-page plan written before a run: the bar, the noise, the controls, the seeds, the cost and what each outcome decides. A FIT review is a check by someone other than the author that the test can answer its question. The project added this because early results kept turning out to be measurement artefacts (what the project knows). It also overdid it: in the week of 12 to 18 October only 11% of recorded lab work was a model result (measurement, history). Since 19 October a sheet is required only before GPU training or evaluation and before any run a milestone claim rests on (the rules).

Running it

13. Can I run it?

You can build it and run its checks, but you cannot chat with it, because no model trained under today's rules has been exported to the serving engine. From a clone, with the pinned Rust toolchain, the README's commands are cargo check --locked -p uor-r4-discrete --lib and cargo test --locked -p uor-r4-discrete --lib. These execute no model (README). Training needs CUDA GPUs rented through the project's tools and a personal release by the owner for each run (training).

14. Is there a web or desktop app?

Not one you can use. The web client is meant to be a local model in a browser tab, and the desktop client a Tauri app with durable memory. Today the Studio interface and a WebAssembly build of the engine exist separately, the Studio still imports an older engine, and the desktop app is a specification only (products, web client, desktop client).

15. What about the models on Hugging Face?

Four 214 million parameter checkpoints are public, but they are historical: trained before the no-softmax and no-matrix-multiplication rules, in the float form, and not the served model. Their chat variants rewrite and summarise usably, while code and arithmetic are wrong (data and tokenizer, README).

16. How fast is it? How much does it cost to train?

Tokens per second is the project's lead metric, and it has never been measured for the current model (charter, section 1; lut-serving). For cost, the audit quotes the K16 runs at "1.2 h ($2)", the chief architect's figure (section 7 of the architect audit), that is about 1.2 hours and $2 for all four K16 runs together. Spending is capped at 4 rented pods and $8 an hour across all labs (charter, section 5.4). These are estimates, not invoices.

Contributing

17. How can I contribute?

Start with the one-page plan, NOW.md, then CONTRIBUTING.md. Model work on the first four milestones is gated and owned by the labs. Work that is genuinely open to outsiders includes documentation and claim-wording fixes, reproducing a published negative result, and tooling that does not touch the model path. Post a short comment on the owning issue saying what you will do, work on a short branch, and open a pull request that says References #N. A maintainer runs the project's gates for you (CONTRIBUTING).

18. What are the labs, and who decides?

A lab is any contributor, human or AI, working under the charter. Labs so far include Claude, Codex and DeepSeek, with Kimi in the project-manager seat. The owner, Casey, decides the charter, the constraints, holds, spending, milestone bars and exceptions, and types every run release personally. The project manager sequences work, and labs choose tasks from NOW.md. Subagents review and test but never make critical decisions. See the rules.

19. What do ACTIVE, READY and PARKED mean? Is PARKED dead?

The three statuses describe how far a mechanism has got. ACTIVE is on the current model path, READY is built and tested but not yet trained in, and PARKED means the tested forms failed or broke a rule. PARKED is not dead: owner decision D22 says a negative closes one tested configuration, never a mechanism, and each PARKED page lists what would reopen it. Of 27 mechanisms, 10 are ACTIVE, 4 READY and 13 PARKED. See the mechanism board.

Records

20. Where is the old research?

Nothing was deleted. Dated records from before 18 October moved unchanged into archive/, and a generated catalog lists them: archive/CATALOG.md. The story of what was tried is in how the project got here, the distilled lessons in what the project knows, and one page per research line in the notebooks and lines. The pre-charter rulebook is preserved in archive/integration/DECISIONS-2026-10-19.md.

21. What happened to the 437 of 512 and the 0.877 results I may have seen?

Both are old and narrow. The 437 of 512 replies were later judged to be panel fitting, and they fell to 0 of 128 on opened transfer rows (a genuinely fresh test has not run) (native geometric engine). The 0.877 bits per byte was a float score on one 19.9 million parameter stack that used softmax and matrix multiplication; served through the integer engine it scored 0.933 against a 0.90 bar, and the two numbers were not measured on the same windows (serving and export). Neither is a result of the current model.

22. What is in projects/?

Seven side projects that are related to UOR-R4 but are not on the model's training or serving path, such as the SpiralCore network transport and a Lean proof scaffold. None of them is evidence that the model works. See projects/README.md.

23. Who is behind it, and what is the licence?

The citation file names Casey Allard and the UOR Foundation as authors, and the project is released under the MIT licence (CITATION.cff, LICENSE).

24. How do I know the claims in these pages are honest?

Every number on a page is linked to a repository path, a pull request or an audit file. Each claim is labelled proof, measurement or hypothesis, and the repository runs a claim-wording check (cargo run -q --locked -p uor-r4-claim-wording -- .) that rejects strong proof wording unless the same line links a proof or certificate. If you find a claim that is wrong or unsourced, open an issue; that is a welcome contribution.

Glossary

In one paragraph. UOR-R4 uses a lot of words that come from three places: language models (token, softmax, BPB), geometry (quaternion, E8, icosian) and the project's own rulebook (FIT, KEEP, PARKED). This page defines each one in a sentence or two and links to the page that explains it properly. Words are in alphabetical order. If you meet a code name such as K16 or A8 in a record, look for it here too. The project is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS).

How to read this page

  • A word in bold at the start of an entry is the term. "See" points to the entry that holds the definition.
  • Claims are labelled proof (follows from definitions or code), measurement (from a recorded run) or hypothesis (an untested idea), as in docs/formal_vocabulary.md.
  • Numbers come from the linked page, which cites its own source. NOT_RUN means a test was planned and never executed. It is not a pass.

Jump to: A · B · C · D · E · F · H · I · K · L · M · N · O · P · Q · R · S · T · U · V · W · Z

A

A8. The nickname of the address-structured cells table, the starting table of the current model, and of the training run that began from it. At zero training it let the reader reach 1,351 of 3,847 copy-successor targets, against 127 for the plain PrimeZeta start (measurement). Learning then eroded that gain, and the first training run stopped at its first checkpoint. See address cells.

ACTIVE. A mechanism status: the mechanism is on the current model path. See mechanism status.

Address. A token's place in the model. It is 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers, and each block is one of 16 fixed points of the E8 lattice. Exact token identity is kept separately from this geometric address. (A token's prime address, defined below, is a different thing: its exact name as a prime number.) See the model, end to end.

Admission. The shortlist step before the model picks a word. The 4,096 words sit in 256 cells, and the model opens only the few cells nearest to what its read points at. A word in an unopened cell can never be chosen, so admission caps everything before it (proof, by construction). See admission.

Artifact. A saved model file together with the data, seed, settings and parameters that made it. The charter requires every artifact to bind all of these. See charter, section 3.12.

Attention. The step in which a language model decides which earlier words matter. A transformer compares the newest word with every earlier word. UOR-R4 replaces it with three cheaper reads: Route, Flock and Relation. See transformer vs geometry.

B

Bar. A pass line that is fixed before a run, so the result cannot be bent to fit afterwards. Bars are never narrower than the measured noise. See the rules.

BPB (bits per byte). A score of how well a model predicts text: the average number of bits it needs for each byte. Lower is better. The older milestone bars use it (M4 asks for 0.90 or less). The current discrete model has no probabilities, so it cannot produce BPB, and on 19 October the owner replaced M1's BPB bar with a top-1 comparison. See rank-margin and charter, section 4.8.

BPE (byte-pair encoding). The way the tokenizer builds its pieces. It starts from the 256 single bytes and repeatedly glues the most common neighbouring pair into a new piece. The pinned tokenizer has 4,096 pieces: 3 special ones, 256 bytes and 3,837 merges. See tokenizer and data and tokenizer.

BVG-K (batched verified coordinates). A faster version of the learning step. It scores K table entries in one GPU launch and commits them together only if their joint loss beats the best single move. Scoring was about 16 times faster at K=16 (measurement), but it has never run as a learning law. See training.

C

Carrier. The small integer block the model passes along: 8 whole numbers drawn from a 16-root orbit of E8, moved by 64 exact signed actions. Four carriers make one token's vector. See SpiralCore and architecture.

Cell. One of the 256 drawers that admission opens. A word's cell is the pair of roots of its first and last block, so the grid is 16 by 16 and each cell starts with 16 words (training can move words between cells). See admission.

Charter. The project's short rulebook, adopted by the owner on 19 October 2026. It replaced the older stack of instructions and numbered decisions. Only the owner changes it. See CHARTER.md and the rules in plain language.

Codebook. The table that gives each of the 4,096 tokens its starting vector. In the current model it is built by a fixed recipe, not drawn at random: see PrimeZeta and A8. See data and tokenizer and architecture.

Control. A run identical to the one being tested except for the one thing under test. Controls here must be lawful non-neural baselines, such as count tables. See the rules.

Counterfactual move. One step of learning. The machine picks one table entry and tries all 16 of its legal states (staying put plus 15 rotations), counts the mistakes after each on a batch of 64 examples, and keeps the best only if it strictly beats staying put. There are no gradients. See discrete learning and training.

D

D-entries (D11, D22, D37 and the rest). Numbered owner decisions, from D0 to D41, that used to be the project's rulebook. The charter now holds the rules that still bind, and the decision map says what became of each decision. The ones you will meet most are D11, D22 and D37.

D11. The serving contract: the finished model runs with whole numbers only. It has five rules. Two of them are that the served program uses no floating point and no multiply or divide instruction. See serving and export.

D19 object store. A store that keeps bytes exactly, in a tree of fingerprinted pieces, so repeats are stored once and any range can be checked. It is built and tested (20 integration tests pass in the delivery record, 60 after later work), but no model uses it yet. See object store.

D22. The owner's rule that a negative result closes one tested configuration, never a mechanism. Stopping a mechanism needs the owner. This is why no mechanism has a "retired" status. See the rules and decision map.

D24. The owner's rule of 12 October 2026 that no model compute runs on the CPU: training, evaluation and every research measurement of the model are GPU work. Serving the exported D11 integer artifact on a client device is the product, not research compute (charter 3.6). See the rules.

D37. The owner's rule of 18 October that floating point is legal in offline training. Softmax-like functions and matrix multiplication stay banned, and every float-trained candidate must report its export gap. See training.

DEV panel. The set of 14,287 development rows used to score models while they are being designed. A model's first guess is right on some number of them (see top-1). The "fresh" panel is a separate sealed set, scored once after the design is chosen. See K16 outcome.

Diagnostic stop. A run ended early on purpose, by a stop rule written down beforehand, so the cause can be found. It is not a negative result and not a failure of the mechanism. See research notebooks.

E

E8. A famous lattice in eight dimensions with 240 "root" points. The project builds a pairing of the 120 icosians with a golden-ratio-scaled copy of themselves and gets these 240 roots. The current model uses only a 16-root piece of E8, not all 240. See E8, H4 and the 600-cell.

Embedding. In a transformer, the learned list of decimals that stands for each token. UOR-R4's counterpart is the constructed integer codebook. See PrimeZeta.

Exact memory. The idea of writing a fact once under an exact name (a prime-based address) and reading it back exactly, instead of smearing it across weights. The trained forms tested so far missed their bars, so the mechanism is PARKED. See exact memory.

Export gap. The quality lost when a model trained with decimals is snapped into the whole-number file that ships. It is the served score minus the float score on the same evaluator. A float candidate whose gap exceeds the two-seed noise band is disqualified. Nobody has measured it for a model built under today's rules, because none has been exported. See serving and export.

F

FBS. The project's name for the three-branch tree that holds earlier words in order. The tree is built by SpiralCore and gives the context at most 243 positions (\(3^5\)). See SpiralCore and SpiralCore/FBS projection.

FIT (TEST FITNESS: FIT). The verdict of a review, by someone other than the author, that a pre-registered test is fit to answer its question. A fresh-context subagent counts as a non-author. A FIT releases nothing by itself: the owner still has to release the run. See the rules and training.

Float. Decimal (floating-point) arithmetic. Allowed in offline training under D37, never in the served model. See serving and export.

Flock read. An attention replacement modelled on a starling flock. The model picks about seven of the nearest earlier positions, rotates what each knows into its own point of view, and moves toward their consensus. Nothing is normalised and no weight is multiplied. It runs inside every Relation run, but its own value has never been isolated. See Flock read.

Fresh panel. Rows that were never seen during design and stay sealed until a run is registered to score them. Every development gain must also report a fresh number. See the rules.

H

H4. The symmetry group of the 600-cell, a regular solid in four dimensions. Its 120 roots are the icosians. See E8, H4 and the 600-cell.

Hamilton gate. A gate for a feed-forward layer that turns the gate signal into a rotation in four dimensions and rotates the value by it, so no sigmoid is needed. A rotation keeps a vector's length, so the gate steers a signal rather than switching it off. It is built and tested (READY), and has never been trained. See Hamilton gate.

Hamming distance. The number of positions at which two bit strings differ. It costs one XOR and one bit count. The model uses it as a tie-break inside its reads. See VSA and Hamming distance.

Hinge loss. A loss that asks only whether the right answer beats its strongest rivals by a fixed gap. If it does, the loss is zero. If not, the loss is the shortfall. It needs no probabilities. The live version is an integer hinge. See rank-margin.

Hold. An owner order that stops a kind of work until the owner lifts it. Training, the second milestone's training and rental, and Stage B are all on hold. A FIT review lifts none of them. See charter, section 5.1.

Hopf map. A map that takes a point on a four-dimensional sphere (a unit quaternion) to a point on an ordinary sphere. It forgets one angle, called the fibre, so many states cast the same shadow. The kept-fibre idea is built as a helper but is not part of the current read, and the mechanism is PARKED. See the Hopf map and the kept fibre.

I

Icosian. One of 120 unit quaternions that form the binary icosahedral group, a double cover of the icosahedron's 60 rotations (the icosahedron is a 20-sided solid). They are the vertices of the 600-cell, and their coordinates need the golden ratio, which is why exact golden-integer arithmetic is used (see Z[φ] below). See E8, H4 and the 600-cell.

Instrument. A measuring tool, such as a test panel or a checker. If an instrument is faulty, that is a fix, not a negative result about the mechanism. See what the project knows.

Integer serving. Running the finished model with whole numbers only: adds, shifts, comparisons and table look-ups. This is D11. Zero-multiply audits are green on 44 native symbol ranges and 7 of 7 WebAssembly functions (measurement), but no trained model has been served this way. See serving and export.

K

K16. The runs of 18 October that opened a shortlist of K=16 cells. Four runs finished (two training objectives, A and R, with two seeds each). None was a KEEP. The two seeds of objective A got 65 and 463 of 14,287 first guesses right (measurement). See K16 outcome.

KEEP. The verdict for a run that meets its own pre-registered mechanism target without a significant loss on the headline number. The work then iterates. It is not a final proof. See the rules.

L

Lab. Any contributor, human or AI, working under the charter. Labs so far include Claude, Codex and DeepSeek, with Kimi in the project-manager seat. Labs choose work from NOW.md and may not type an owner release. See the rules.

M

M1 to M8 (milestones). The eight GitHub milestones that define the road to an alpha release. None is complete. In plain words:

#Meaning
M1It predicts text (a saved discrete model beats both count tables through the integer export)
M2It answers from memory (at least 256 of 512 development replies, and 40% on a fresh panel)
M3It remembers across sessions
M4It is served: exported to UORLUT01 and run from the command line
M5It is cheap on a laptop, with the cost measured
M6It reasons and codes
M7It runs the same in a library, a command line and a browser
M8It is released as one checksum-pinned file

Source: language model and where we're going.

Matmul (matrix multiplication, GEMM). Multiplying a long list of numbers by a large grid of learned numbers. It is nearly all the arithmetic of a transformer, and the project bans it everywhere: training, tests, tools and serving. A geometric feed-forward block is allowed. A dense one is not. See charter, section 3.3.

Mechanism. One geometric replacement for one part of a transformer, such as the read, the loss or the optimiser. The project tracks 27, each with its own page. See the mechanism board.

Mechanism status (ACTIVE, READY, PARKED). The only three statuses a mechanism can have:

  • ACTIVE: on the current model path (10 mechanisms).
  • READY: built and tested but not yet trained into a model (4).
  • PARKED: the tested forms failed or broke a rule, and the page lists what would reopen it (13).

There is no "retired" status, by D22. Source: mechanism board.

MLP (feed-forward layer). The block in a transformer that processes each token after attention, usually with big grids of multiplications and a gate. UOR-R4's candidates are the Hamilton gate and the SpiralCore/FBS projection; neither has been trained.

N

Nat. A unit of prediction error: the natural logarithm of how surprised the model was. Lower is better; bits per byte is a related score.

Notebook. One page per line of research, with one row per result: date, what ran, the number, the bar, the verdict and an artifact link. Notebooks plus NOW.md replaced the old running log. See research notebooks.

NOT_RUN. A record that a planned test was never executed. It is not a pass and it is not a failure. See what the project knows.

O

Orbit. A set of points that one group of moves carries into one another. The model uses a single orbit of 16 E8 roots, each a signed rearrangement of (2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0). See E8, H4 and the 600-cell.

Owner. Casey Allard, the project lead. He sets the charter, the holds, the spending and the milestone bars, and personally types each run release.

Owner release. The typed phrase by which the owner personally lets one pre-registered run start. One release covers all arms and seeds of one sheet. No lab types it. See charter, section 5.1.

P

PARKED. A mechanism status. See mechanism status.

PM seat. The project-manager role: it sequences work and keeps NOW.md. Kimi holds it, with a cover lab named by the owner. See the rules.

Pre-alpha. The project's honest stage. Parts are built and tested, but 0 of 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation. See STATUS.

Pre-registration (sheet). A one-page plan, written before a run, that states the bar, the noise, the controls, the seeds, the cost and what each outcome would decide. It is needed only before GPU training or evaluation and before any run a milestone claim rests on. See the rules.

Prime address. The exact name of a token: the (id + 1)-th prime number, so no two tokens collide. For example the 4,096th prime is 38,873. It is kept separate from the geometric address. See primes and zeta phases.

PrimeZeta codebook. The table that turns each token's prime into eight angles taken from the Riemann zeta zeros, and the angles into a starting vector. It gives all 4,096 tokens distinct vectors (measurement). The distinctness comes from a cell-balancing step, not from the angles; whether the zeta angles help at all has not been tested. See prime-zeta codebook.

Q

Q1. The first checkpoint of a full-length run, at 4,096 of its 16,404 batches; Q4 is the last. The 18 October dose with Relation was stopped at Q1 when admission collapsed. See admission.

Quaternion. A four-part number \(w + xi + yj + zk\). Multiplying by a length-1 quaternion turns a point in four dimensions without stretching it, and every such turn can be undone. Quaternions of length 1 form the 3-sphere. See quaternions and rotation.

R

Rank-margin. The project's loss: the right token must outrank its strongest rivals by a fixed margin. See hinge loss and rank-margin.

Read. The step in which the model looks back at earlier text to decide what matters for the next token: the project's bounded replacement for attention. There are three: Route, Flock and Relation.

Reach. For one test position, whether the right next token is among the candidates the model opens at all; counted over the 14,287 positions of the DEV panel. A model cannot guess a token it never opens, so a low reach caps the top-1 score, but a high reach alone is not skill (variant R of K16 reached 12,000 positions by opening almost the whole vocabulary).

READY. A mechanism status. See mechanism status.

Relation read. A Flock read plus the ability to follow simple links between positions, such as "the word right after the earlier copy of this word". This is how copying is meant to work. It has trained twice, and both runs stopped before a verdict. See Relation read.

Root. One of the fixed points of E8 used as a block value. See orbit.

Route read. An attention replacement that walks a small tree of addresses, stepping toward the nearest branch at each level, and picks up one earlier word at the end. It never scores the whole history. It is the base read of every trained discrete model, but its own contribution is unattributed. See Route read.

Rung 0. The first full-length run on the discrete path (seed 1, 16,404 updates, scored on the 14,287 development rows). Its bars were unreachable because only 1,920 targets were admitted, which pointed the work at admission. See route read.

S

Seed. The starting number of a random draw. A decisive run uses at least two seeds, so a result is not one lucky draw. See the rules.

SiLU. A smooth squashing curve used as an activation in the older decimal stack. It is built from a sigmoid, so it falls under the ban on squashing functions.

Softmax. A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities with exponentials and a sum over everything. Transformers use it inside attention and again to pick the next word. The project bans it, and every softmax-like squashing function, anywhere in the model, its training or its comparators. See charter, section 3.2.

SpiralCore. An exact-geometry source credited to Matthew. From the octonion multiplication table it yields moves that shuffle the eight coordinates and flip some signs. Each move can be undone exactly. The integer form is the core of the current model. See SpiralCore.

Studio. The single-page interface meant to be the shell of both the web and desktop clients. It is not yet connected to the new engine. See web client.

T

T2. A table built from the training text. It looks up the last word and returns the next word seen most often after it. It gets 6,300 of the 14,287 DEV first guesses right, and it is one of the two count tables a trained model must beat (measurement). See host diagnostics.

Ternary. Used in two ways here. A ternary weight or gate takes one of three values: −1, 0 or +1. A ternary tree has three branches per node. Dense ternary weights are PARKED because every weight is still touched for every word. See ternary and XOR.

Token. One numbered piece of text, a word or part of a word. The model never sees letters. See tokenizer.

Tokenizer. The component that cuts text into tokens and turns tokens back into text. The pinned one has 4,096 pieces (identity d36d3e87). See tokenizer.

Tokens/s (tokens per second). How many tokens the model reads or writes per second. It is the project's lead metric, with decode speed and context speed reported separately. It has never been measured for the current model. See charter, section 1.

Tauri. A toolkit that wraps a web page as a desktop app. The planned desktop client would use it to share the web interface.

Top-1 (and top-8). The number of DEV rows on which the model's first guess (or any of its first eight) is the right next token, out of 14,287. M1 requires the top-1 of the model, through the integer export, to beat the unigram and T2 tables. See charter, section 4.8.

Transformer. The design behind almost every modern language model. Its cost sits in three operations: matrix multiplication, attention against every earlier token, and softmax. UOR-R4 is not a transformer. See what is UOR-R4 and transformer vs geometry.

U

Unigram. A table of word counts that ignores context and always guesses by overall frequency. It gets 1,226 of the 14,287 DEV first guesses right. The best trained discrete model got 65 and 463 (measurement). See K16 outcome.

UOR. Short for Universal Object Reference, the foundation named as copyright holder in the project's MIT licence (LICENSE). A "UOR address" in this project is the prime-based name described under prime address.

UORLUT01. The container format for the finished model: one file of 4-bit codes and small integer tables, pinned by checksum. It is what the engine serves. See serving and export and releases and artifacts.

V

VSA (vector-symbolic architecture). A memory idea using long bit strings (4,096 bits per token) glued by XOR and compared by counting differing bits. It improved bits per byte by 0.014 to 0.023 on a banned CPU learner, so it is PARKED. See VSA and VSA and Hamming distance.

W

W2. The next queued test: FIT-reviewed and awaiting an owner release (cost about $0.91, estimated). It decides whether the wall is the model's representation or its learning law, and includes count-table arms the headline bars lack. See open questions.

WASM (WebAssembly). A compact, sandboxed machine code that browsers run. The integer serving engine is built for it, with 7 of 7 serving functions free of multiply, divide and float instructions (measurement). See web client.

Writer (shared vector writer). The one component that handles a token's vector on the way in, along the carry and on the way out, using the same format everywhere. It builds the cells and picks the nearest token among the admitted ones. See architecture.

Z

Z[φ]. Pairs of whole numbers (a, b) standing for a + bφ, where φ is the golden ratio. They add and multiply with no rounding, so icosian coordinates can be kept exact. See golden integers.

Zeta zero. A point where the Riemann zeta function is zero. The project uses a few fixed zeros as clock speeds: for a prime \(p\) the angle on channel \(k\) is \(\gamma_k \ln p\). It uses the numbers only and makes no claim about the Riemann hypothesis. See primes and zeta phases.

How the repository is laid out

Every top-level folder has one job. This page lists them, says which ones are about to move, and explains three names that are easy to confuse. It describes the repository as of 20 October 2026; the owner approved a layout pass that day, and this page changes with each step of it.

Folders

FolderWhat it holds
archive/Every dated record and retired file, byte for byte as it was. Nothing in it is edited. archive/CATALOG.md indexes it.
crates/The Rust code, one crate per folder: the model, the serving runtime, the harness and the tools around them.
data/The small evaluation panels kept in git. Large inputs (corpora, checkpoints) live in the private Hugging Face store instead.
docs/The documentation you are reading, plus the live lab records under docs/labs/ and the harness files under docs/harness/.
projects/Side projects related to UOR-R4 but not part of the model. See the projects page.
scripts/Shell entry points: GPU pods (scripts/pod/), storage and hygiene (scripts/storage/), harness wrappers.
third_party/Copies of outside Rust crates the build patches in. Their contents are pinned by hash.
tools/lab-runner (a workspace crate), notes for the uor-knowledge server, and one historical trainer (below).
web/The web client. web/studio/ is the Studio page served at /studio/ on the documentation site.
xtask/Repository tooling, run as cargo xtask <command>: link checks, the archive check, figures, the catalog and the site build.
conformance/The requirements ledger (ledger.toml, ids.toml, authorities.toml) and its behaviour specifications (features/suites/*.feature). The repo-model and repo-conformance crates read it to produce CONFORMANCE.md. Until 20 October 2026 these were the top-level model/ and features/ folders.
models/Four reference tokenizer files that older tests compare against. Moving to data/tokenizers/.
src/, tests/, profiles/The root Rust package, uor-r4-wasm-router: its library, its tests and its server profiles. Moving to crates/uor-r4-wasm-router/, so the top level holds only workspace settings.

One more change is planned: the normative reference pages that sit loose in docs/ will gather under docs/reference/, except for the few that code pins by path and hash, which stay where they are.

tools/r4-softmax-trainer/ stays for now. It is a historical trainer that uses a banned method. One file in it is compiled into the core crate, and that core source file is itself pinned by hash in a recorded evidence table. Moving the trainer would break that record. It will move once that binding is retired.

Hidden folders at the top

FolderWhy it is there
.github/Continuous integration and the pull-request template.
.cargo/Cargo build settings for the WebAssembly target.
.devcontainer/Editor container settings. Editors look for it at the top level.
.agents/Shared skills for coding agents, in the layout agent tools expect.
.kimi-code/, .codex-lab/Onboarding notes for two of the labs.
.uor-models/The runtime's local model store. Only a manifest is tracked; the contents are gitignored. About ninety Rust source files read this path, so it stays.

Files at the top

README.md, CHARTER.md (the rules), AGENTS.md (onboarding for agents), CONTRIBUTING.md, STATUS.md, ROADMAP.md, SECURITY.md, LICENSE, CITATION.cff and the generated CONFORMANCE.md, plus build settings: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain.toml, deny.toml, Justfile and book.toml (the documentation site).

Names that are easy to confuse

  • conformance/ is a requirements ledger, not a language model. It was called model/ until 20 October 2026 and was renamed to end that confusion.
  • models/ holds reference tokenizers used by older tests. It is moving to data/tokenizers/.
  • .uor-models/ is the runtime model store on each machine. It is gitignored; its contents come from the private Hugging Face store.

What is not in git

Build output (target/), each lab's scratch folder (local/), working folders for open pull requests (.worktrees/), large corpora (*.u16) and the runtime model store are gitignored on purpose. Where each kind of file lives, and the routine that keeps the laptop clean, are described in docs/labs/workspace.md.

The three products

UOR-R4 aims to ship one thing people can use: a small, fast language model that runs on your own laptop or in your own browser, with nothing sent to a server. The owner defined three products around it on 19 October 2026. The first is the model itself, saved as one file of whole numbers. The second is a web client that runs that file inside a browser tab. The third is a desktop client, an installable app that runs the same file natively and remembers your conversations. None of the three ships today. The project is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS, NOW). Nothing is released until a trained model passes milestones M1 to M8.

Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run with its artifact, hypothesis means an untested idea (docs/formal_vocabulary.md, glossary).

One model file feeds two clients that share one interface. Everything inside the dashed line runs on the user's own device.

The three at a glance

ProductWhat it is meant to beWhat exists todayMain gate
Language modelA geometric language model exported as one checksum-pinned integer file (UORLUT01)The serving engine, tested on a synthetic stand-in model. No trained model has been exported to itM1 to M4, then M8
Web clientA local model in the browser: download the file once, run it in WebAssembly on the deviceThe Studio interface (index.html), a WebAssembly build of the engine (UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#2654), and a paused Pages deployM7
Desktop clientA Tauri app sharing the web interface, with the native engine, file access, durable memory and offline use on M1-class laptopsA specification only. Fragments exist: Tauri hooks in the Studio, the memory store crate, a command-line engineM3, M5, M7

A fourth page, Releases and artifacts, covers the model file format, how a release would be cut, the Hugging Face repositories and how checksums tie them together.

Why the products look like this

Local by design. The mission is "fast local AI": a model that trains fast, runs fast and approaches frontier capability on ordinary hardware (charter, section 1). The lead metric is tokens per second. A product that needs a data centre would defeat the point.

One file, many hosts. The served model obeys one contract, called D11: no decimal (floating-point) arithmetic, no multiply or divide instruction and no transcendental functions, only adds, shifts and table look-ups (D11). A file that needs nothing more exotic than integer adds can run the same way in a browser, on a laptop processor or on Apple silicon. The charter says serving this file on the user's device is the product and is allowed. The rule that research compute must run on a GPU (D24) does not apply to it (charter, section 3.6).

One interface, two shells. The Studio, a single-page interface already in the repository, is the shell for both clients. The browser runs the engine as WebAssembly. The desktop app wraps the same page and runs the engine as native code, which should be faster (a hypothesis; no side-by-side timing exists).

A passing audit shows that a forbidden instruction is absent. It is not a trained capability, and it says nothing about how well a model answers.

The order things must happen in

The products depend on the model, and the model depends on milestones. Roughly:

  1. M1 to M3 give a model that predicts text, answers from exact memory, and keeps memory across sessions.
  2. M4 exports that model through D11 and serves it from the command line.
  3. M5 measures its cost on a laptop, and M6 adds reasoning and coding on the same model.
  4. M7 makes the browser worker, the command line and the Rust library produce bit-identical tokens. That is the web client's gate.
  5. M8 is the alpha release: one versioned, checksum-pinned model file that meets every earlier bar.

The desktop client has no milestone of its own yet. It rides on M3 for memory, M5 for laptop cost and M7 for the shared interface. The full definitions are in the project track.

The language model

The core product is a language model: a program that reads text and predicts what comes next, and so can hold a conversation. Most language models today are transformers that do billions of decimal multiplications per word. UOR-R4 tries a different route. It predicts text with geometry (prime-number addresses, rotations in four dimensions, exact look-up memory), and it ships as one file of whole numbers that an ordinary laptop or browser can run without a single multiply instruction. That file is meant to be the one thing every client loads. It does not exist yet. No trained model has been exported in that form, training is on hold pending review, and 0 of the 8 milestones are complete (NOW). Nothing ships until a trained model passes M1 to M8.

Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary.

flowchart LR
  T["Train on rented GPUs<br/>(crates/uor-r4-discrete)"] --> X["Export to one integer file<br/>UORLUT01"]
  X --> A["Audit: 0 multiply,<br/>0 divide, 0 float"]
  A --> S["Serve on the device<br/>(crates/uor-r4-integer)"]
  S --> C1["Command line<br/>uor-chat"]
  S --> C2["Web client<br/>WebAssembly"]
  S --> C3["Desktop client<br/>native"]

The model's life in one line. Training happens once, offline, on a GPU. Everything after the export runs on the user's machine using whole numbers only.

What the model is meant to be

A geometric model, not a transformer. The project calls it the UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model. Technically it is an autoregressive geometric state model with exact addressed memory: it keeps a running state, updates it with each token through rotations and table look-ups, and reads facts from an exact memory by address (architecture). The charter forbids the expensive parts of a transformer outright: no softmax or other squashing functions and no dense matrix multiplication, anywhere: training, evaluation, tooling and serving (charter, sections 3.2 and 3.3).

One model for every job. Conversation with durable memory comes first, then coding and reasoning, all on the same model (charter, section 1).

Fast and local. The lead metric is tokens per second on an ordinary machine, with decode and context reported separately. A small quality gap is acceptable if the model is much cheaper to run.

How it will be delivered

The deliverable is one checksum-pinned D11 integer artifact in the UORLUT01 format, released at milestone M8 (project track, M8).

  • D11 is the serving contract. Its five rules are: no floating point or maths library (R1); no multiply or divide instruction (R2); reading every weight for every token is an interim stage, not the end state (R3; the charter no longer treats dense table maps as an allowed stepping stone for new exports); no transformer backbone (R4); energy claimed only when measured (R5) (D11).
  • UORLUT01 is the file format. It holds an 8-byte magic string, a JSON header, 4-bit weight codes in groups with one scale byte each, and small integer tables for the few nonlinear steps (format.rs; proof by reading the code). The reader computes the SHA-256 hash of the whole file as it loads it, so a release can pin that hash. Details are on the releases page.
  • Training may use decimals; serving may not. Since 18 October, offline training may use floating point, but the shipped file is integer, and every float-trained candidate must report its export gap: its served score minus its float score on the same evaluator (D37, charter section 3.7).
  • The engine is crates/uor-r4-integer. It runs the file natively (the uor-chat and uor-r4-stack command-line programs) and as WebAssembly (UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#2654). The serving page shows how it multiplies without a multiply instruction.

The web client

The web client is meant to be a language model that lives in a browser tab. You open a web page once, it downloads the model file, and from then on the model runs on your own computer, inside the browser, in a sandboxed form of machine code called WebAssembly. Your prompts and the model's replies never leave the device, because there is no model server to send them to. The page you would use is the Studio, an editor-and-chat interface already in the repository. Today the pieces exist separately and are not joined: the browser engine works on a synthetic test model, the Studio still points at an older engine that was retired, the public site is frozen, and there is no trained model to download. Until milestones M7 and M8 pass, the web client is a geometry explorer and demonstration, not a product.

Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary.

One download, then everything runs in the tab. The only network traffic is fetching the static page and the model file.

How it is meant to work

  1. Load the page. The Studio is static HTML, JavaScript and CSS. The charter places it at /studio on the project's documentation site (charter, section 2).
  2. Download the model once. The page fetches one UORLUT01 file and checks its SHA-256 against the hash published with the release (releases). It then keeps the file in browser storage so later visits work offline. This cache is planned, not built (from reading the repository).
  3. Start the engine in a Web Worker. A worker is a background thread of the page, so typing stays smooth while the model computes. The worker loads the WebAssembly build of crates/uor-r4-integer and calls init, then loadStack on the model bytes.
  4. Generate. For each token the worker calls step. The engine uses only integer adds, shifts and table look-ups (the D11 contract), so the same file gives the same tokens in every browser. That is a design property; M7 has to measure it.
  5. Save and resume. saveSession writes the conversation state as a UR4SESS1 snapshot, and restoreSession brings it back byte for byte.

These function names are the real exports of the WebAssembly build: init, tickClock, loadStack, step, saveSession, restoreSession, weightsPerToken, allocEvents, leakedModels (record; proof by reading wasm_bindgen_exports.rs).

Why serving in the browser is allowed. Research compute must run on a GPU (D24). On 15 October that rule paused the browser engine, because serving in a browser runs on the user's processor (D36). The owner resolved this on 19 October: serving the exported D11 file on client devices, including browser WebAssembly, is the product, and D24 does not apply to it (charter, section 3.6).

Until then: an explorer, honestly labelled

It must not offer a chat box that implies a working assistant. The Studio's engine-status banner already says so. Privacy model

  • The model computes only on the device. No prompt or reply is sent anywhere by the engine. That is the M7 bar, and today it holds trivially, because there is no remote model to call.
  • Network use is not yet limited to static files. The target is the page and the model file only. Today the Studio also loads third-party code and fonts from CDNs (Monaco, pdf.js and three.js from cdnjs; marked, KaTeX and the three.js controls from jsDelivr; fonts from Google Fonts), and its search feature sends the typed query to en.wikipedia.org and api.duckduckgo.com. Features that open files from GitHub talk to GitHub. None of that is model compute, but a privacy claim must not hide it: the requirement is to self-host every asset and make web search opt-in, or remove it, before M7 (index.html, lines 11 to 25 and 5845 to 5906).
  • Integrity, not secrecy, of the model file. The SHA-256 check proves the file is the released one. The model is public, so there is nothing to hide in it.

Open questions

  • How large will the model file be, and is a one-time download of that size acceptable on a phone? Unknown until a model exists.
  • How fast is WebAssembly against native on the same file? No tokens-per-second figure for the browser has been recorded. The only native figures are from older float models: 68 to 80 tokens per second on 8 threads for a 29M model, which is evaluation throughput over 64 scored windows, not free-running decode (D11 serving record). No decode tokens per second exists for any D11 artifact.
  • Should the Studio's provenance be settled first? Its source is an import from a companion repository, Casey-allard/uor-r4-wasm-chat, which this audit did not inspect.
