D11 integer table serving (UORLUT01)

Status: ACTIVE. It is the end-of-pipeline contract: the finished model must ship as one integer artifact, and this engine runs it. The engine reproduces its reference answers exactly, and its zero-multiply audits are green. But no model built under today's rules has been exported through it yet, and the models it has served were not good enough. It is ACTIVE as the export boundary; no model built under today's rules has gone through it yet.

Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, hypothesis means an untested idea. See docs/formal_vocabulary.md.

In plain words

This is how a finished model runs on an ordinary laptop or in a web browser using only whole numbers: adds, shifts and table look-ups. There is no decimal arithmetic and no multiply instruction. A trained model is exported to a compact file, mostly 4-bit numbers. A checker then reads the compiled program and counts machine instructions to prove that no multiply sneaks in. The engine reproduces its reference answers exactly, and the checks are green. But it has only served older models that fell short of their bars, and no model built under today's rules has been exported through it.

What it replaces in a transformer

The arithmetic. A transformer runs on large matrix multiplications. Here the same weights are read through tables, so every product is a table read and an add. This changes how a model is computed, not what it is. The engine does not make a weak model better, and, as the history below shows, it still reads every stored weight for every token.

Left, how a dot product needs no multiply. Middle, the engine is exact and the loss is in rounding the weights. Right, the audit counts instructions in the compiled program.

Its chapter in the project's history

  • July to August. The first multiplier-free runtime came from the compiled-graph approach (r4g1-graph). Its contract said only serving must avoid multiplies and allocation (#157).
  • 25 September. Learned attention, recurrence and rotation from two 1.68-million-parameter models ran with integer arithmetic and tables, and the standalone integer library reproduced the saved distributions (#1397).
  • 26 to 29 September. An interim "D10" engine allowed multiplies and a softmax table. On 27 September the owner replaced it: D11 made multiplier-free, transformer-free serving the one contract for every lab (#1443). A first energy test found table emulation of every product used about 4.3 times more energy than float (#1449).
  • 8 October. The first chat model was trained, exported and served end to end (#1893). On 10 October three 29-million-parameter models served at 1.20 to 1.24 bits per byte, and four softmax-free serving reads missed their bar.
  • 12 to 13 October. The bans on softmax and matrix multiplication moved the older multiplier-allowing engines out of every build (D29).
  • 18 October. D37 made the integer export the boundary: training may use float, serving may not. The native zero-multiply audit went green (#2655) and a contributor-built WebAssembly runtime followed (#2654).
  • Next. Export one discrete model through the container and measure the export gap (milestone M4).

Under the charter, serving this artifact on client devices (CPU, browser WebAssembly, Apple silicon) is the product and is allowed.

How it works

Export. Training is offline and may use float. For serving the weights go into a UORLUT01 container. Weights are 4-bit codes in groups of 32. Each group has a one-byte scale (a 4-bit mantissa and a 4-bit exponent). A few small integer tables cover the nonlinear steps (square root, decay rates, SiLU, arcosh, exp).

One projection (definition). For a weight matrix \(W\) and an integer activation vector \(x\), the output is \(y_i=\sum_j w_{ij}x_j\), where each weight is a group scale times a 4-bit code, \(w_{ij}=s_g\,q_{ij}\) with \(s_g=m\,2^{e}\). The engine does not multiply \(q_{ij}\) by \(x_j\). For each activation it builds a 16-entry table \(T_j[q]=q\,x_j\), which needs only additions to fill, and then reads \(T_j[q_{ij}]\) for each weight. Four output rows are blocked to reuse the table. The scale \(s_g\) is applied by shifts and adds.

Products of two runtime values. A score, a gate or a value mix needs a true product of two numbers known only at run time. The engine builds a table of the sixteen multiples of one operand by repeated addition, reads it at each base-16 digit of the other operand, and sums the reads with shifts: \(ab=\sum_k 16^k\,T_a[d_k(b)]\), exact by the definition of base-16 digits (proof; stack_mul_u64 and stack_mul_u128 in kernels.rs). The quarter-square identity would also be allowed, but the serving engine does not use it. Normalisation uses an integer square root or a table. Sampling is integer min-p.

Session state. A conversation's state is saved and restored byte-for-byte (the UR4SESS1 format).

The five rules (D11). R1: no floating point and no maths library. R2: no multiply or divide instruction. R3: dense per-token access to a learned store is interim, not the end state (D5). R4: no transformer backbone. R5: energy is claimed only when measured.

The audit. The release binary is disassembled, and the multiply, divide and float instructions are counted over the serving symbols, natively and in WebAssembly. The audit proves absence of those instructions. It says nothing about model quality, and the SIMD kernels in the WebAssembly build are unintegrated fixtures that the 7-of-7 audit never exercises (record).

Geometry, as exact finite tables. The 120-element icosian group's Cayley table (about 14 KiB), a 1,025-entry arcosh table for Lorentz read scores, icosian-pair weights and the Q30 Hopf observation are stored as tables. The current integer crate selects typed H4 geometry and checked integer arithmetic for the discrete model's own export (native_geometry.rs).

The gap: about 30.2 million parameters are read per token for the 29M stack, which the sparsity rule (D5-b) calls non-compliant. Cache residency (D5-a) is unmeasured until hardware counters exist

What has been tried

"Gap" means served minus float score. "Bits per byte" (BPB) is the model's loss on a held-out chat stream, lower is better; the milestone bar is at most 0.90. The D10 engine is the older engine that allowed multiplies. A "D11 minus D10" loss of 0.0 therefore means the multiplier-free engine reproduces the older one exactly.

Reading these honestly. Two things are true at once. The engine is exact: every windowed comparison matched its reference to within about 1e-6 bits per byte (exactly, on the 64-window D11-minus-D10 checks), and the audits count zero forbidden instructions. And the models it served were weak, and it is not yet fast. The loss between float and integer is weight rounding, about 0.009 bits per byte on matched positions, not the engine. Table-based products on a dense model cost more energy and time than float. A dense model streamed through tables is still dense, which is why the project's sparsity rule asks for selected, addressed reads instead.

What has never been tested

  • Serving a model built under today's rules (discrete or lawful float) through the container. Its export gap is unmeasured.
  • Hardware-counter measurement of memory traffic per token (D5-a) and of parameters touched per token (D5-b). Milestone M5 has not run.
  • Whole-system energy per token with a validated sampler. The only earlier figures (5.7 and 21.0 millijoules per token) came from a truncated capture.
  • Integer serving of a product-key or other addressed memory read. The kernel is not built.
  • A comparison with the SIMD kernels on the serving hot path.
  • Free-running generation speed. The 184.58 tokens/s figure was input-driven forward throughput.

What stays frozen, and what would restore it

This mechanism is active, so nothing here needs reopening. Two sub-parts are held:

  1. The D10 engine and its SIMD crate stay frozen, non-mission comparators. They return only if an owner decision restores a serving tier that allows multipliers, which D11 withdrew.
  2. Serving of product-key or addressed memory needs an integer read kernel. The exporter refuses it today.

Open questions. What is the export gap of a discrete or allowed float model through the container, and does UORLUT01 need a new schema for table-native models? How many of the 30.2 million parameters touched per token can selected reads remove before tokens per second move, given that arithmetic count was not time? Are the audit scripts, which are Python, to be ported to Rust and run in CI?

Native geometric engine (typed values, version chains, grounded replies)

Status: PARKED. Its passes were on question sets the project wrote itself and never reached free prose. Its best score, 437 of 512 on the practice set, fell to 0 of 128 on fresh questions. Its ranking objective used functions the project now bans, and its October kernels were quarantined. The idea of one shared writer lives on in the discrete path. The owner decided on 19 October 2026 to repair the root crate and other legacy crates so they build again; that restores the build, not this mechanism. See what would reopen it.

Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, hypothesis means an untested idea. See docs/formal_vocabulary.md.

In plain words

This is a small language model written from scratch in Rust. It treats every word as an exact prime-number address and keeps its memory as rotations in four-dimensional geometry. It learned which earlier word or number to copy, add, or stop on, and which version of a changing fact to read, such as the first or the latest locker number. On questions the project wrote itself it answered exactly. It never wrote free prose. Its best score, 437 of 512 on the practice set it had been fitted to, fell to 0 of 128 on fresh questions.

What it replaces in a transformer

The whole network. This is not a transformer variant. Exact address lookups, version chains and small learned selector tables take the place of attention and feed-forward layers, and a readout of score tables predicts the next piece of text.

Left, how a changing fact is read by version. Middle, the best score and what happened on fresh questions. Right, how words become exact addresses and rotations.

Its chapter in the project's history

  • 3 to 8 September (build first). After weeks of frozen ladders and bookkeeping, the owner ruled that a process which forbids running code produces nothing (#1111) and restored a single Rust model path (#1125). The first source-free native artifact continued prompts from a 35,655,288-byte table without opening the training text (#1112). A "model v0" followed, with typed Stop, Copy and Add selection and a 663-answer regression set (#1140). The project was named UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model (#1174), and an honesty pass withdrew fabricated scorecards (#1198).
  • 8 to 17 September. Exact versioned memory and rules for abstaining. The first shared-core test failed (#1229). Typed attention was exported to exact Boolean tables (#1254), but passes came on constructed panels only (#1264).
  • 19 to 25 September. A falsification sweep found the trained number overstated the shipped artifact by 0.57 bits per byte (#1284). No geometric mechanism had beaten a matched ordinary control (#1371). Continuous loss improved while actual prose scored 0 of 5 (#1398). The next stage of the plan moved to the layered stack (geometric-stack).
  • 6 to 10 October (the October line). The records call it Line B. Cross-state fields over categorical H4 banks raised complete correct replies on a 512-row development panel from 8 to 437 (#2152 to #2162). A single fresh draw scored 0 of 128 (#2164). The rules in D21 and D22 followed: stop a line that does not move its milestone number, but a negative closes a configuration, never a mechanism.
  • 12 to 13 October. The bans on softmax and squashing made the pooled-ranking loss non-compliant (D23, D25), and 15 kernels were quarantined after a hidden dense contraction was found (D29). The discrete path (crates/uor-r4-discrete) took over, and it keeps this line's single shared writer.

How it works

Addresses and phases (definition). Each token has a full prime address, and ordered two-prime keys name contexts. Eight fixed zeta-zero phase channels, compiled to 16-bit turns, supply position-like phases.

Window fold (definition). A window of recent tokens is folded, in order, into exact H4 coordinates. H4 is the 4-dimensional symmetry of the 600-cell, whose 120 corners are the unit icosians. Sums are exact pairs \(a+b\varphi\) with \(\varphi^2=\varphi+1\). Products stay exact because

\[(a+b\varphi)(c+d\varphi)=(ac+bd)+(ad+bc+bd)\,\varphi \qquad\text{(proof, by } \varphi^2=\varphi+1).\]

The fold keeps signed chirality and evicts old entries with a bound.

Readout. Conditional score tables plus seven gated feature groups, with coefficients rounded to eighths and bounded shift-and-add arithmetic, predict the next piece.

Selectors on top. Small learned tables, each fitted on constructed families, choose: which source occurrence to read; whether to write an exact owner-value relation (sixteen versions kept); whether to Copy, Add or Stop on typed numeric literals; how deep to read; and which version intent (initial, previous or current) to follow along a validated chain, abstaining when the chain is truncated. A shared geometric writer emits the answer. Exact occurrence and version identity stay separate from the geometric addresses, and digests are never used as meaning.

October cross-state form. Trained 4-bit ("Q4") coefficients over categorical H4 banks (Context, Prefix, Generate), scored with exact integers. The training goal was a pooled-token ranking: for each token, push the correct answer above its strongest wrong rival, using

\[\ell=\operatorname{softplus}\!\Big(\log\frac{m_{\text{rival}}}{m_{\text{gold}}}\Big),\]

with \(m\) the score masses. That function is banned. The allowed replacement is the hinge \(\max(0,\ \delta-(s_{\text{gold}}-s_{\text{rival}}))\) of rank-margin.

Training and serving. Training used floating point. Serving executes the rounded integer scores. The preserved source is excluded from the current build by cfg(any()) and the facade in native_support.rs.

Reading these honestly. The pattern is the one the project's own rules warn about. Exact selectors, writers and version chains worked on authored panels, and a general language model never followed. Fixed geometry lost to an ordinary table given the same supervision (186 of 288 against 288 of 288). The 437 figure was fitting: the fresh draw reused 15 of the 24 literals the model had been fitted on, and still scored zero. What has never been tested

  • The engine at matched capacity against an ordinary control. It was set aside at 1.68 million parameters.
  • Free-running prose from this engine; continuous loss improved, generated prose scored 0 of 5.
  • A genuinely fresh qualification of any October model after the exposed-panel critique. The one fresh draw scored 0 of 128, and no successor ran.
  • A rank-margin or other allowed objective for the cross-state banks.
  • GPU execution of the September engine. Its fitting was recorded as host Rust.
  • Whether version-chain selectors transfer to free-form edited facts, not authored wording.
  • A D11 instruction audit of the complete native binary.

Open questions. Which Line B ideas survive into the discrete path: the Copy/Add/Stop selector, version chains, or the exact-relation writer? Do exact chains need a learned selector at all once the D19 object store holds exact records? Can the cross-state field be rebuilt as a SpiralCore read with a hinge objective and score above zero on fresh rows? What did the 75 development replies (of 512) that still fail do wrong, beyond output limits?

What would reopen it

  1. A new pre-registration with a TEST FITNESS: FIT review, after the owner lifts the separate hold on this line's training and rental. It replaces the softplus ranking with an allowed hinge and runs on GPU in its own scanned module (D37).
  2. A genuinely unexposed decisive panel: at least 200 fresh rows or at least 2 seeds (D22), not the 512-row practice panel.
  3. Rebuild and re-qualify the quarantined kernels without the hidden dense contraction (D29).
  4. Join the line to the shared integer vector writer, so the language path and the compile-and-emit path use one geometric representation.
  5. A result from the relation-read reranker (relation-read, D34) that needs exact multi-version identity memory. That is the natural route back for the version-chain selectors.

How research is done now

UOR-R4 is a research project, and for months it ran research the heavy way: one folder per pull request, a written plan before almost every step, and a review before each run. In the week of 12 to 18 October only 11% of the recorded lab work was a model result (see history). Since 19 October 2026 the owner's charter keeps the rigour but drops the bulk. Each line of research has one notebook page with one row per result. A written plan is required only before a GPU run or a run that a milestone claim rests on. Old records are kept, untouched, in archive/.

flowchart LR
  A["Question or idea"] --> B["Notebook page<br/>for its research line"]
  B --> C{"GPU training or<br/>evaluation, or a<br/>milestone claim?"}
  C -- no --> D["Build, test, run<br/>host checks"]
  C -- yes --> E["One-page sheet"]
  E --> F["Review by someone<br/>who is not the author"]
  F --> G["Owner releases<br/>the sheet once"]
  G --> H["Run on the GPU"]
  D --> I["New notebook row"]
  H --> I
  I --> J["Sealed artifacts and<br/>old records go to archive/"]

The path of one piece of work. Only the right-hand branch needs a sheet, a review and an owner release.

Terms follow the glossary. Claims are labelled proof, measurement or hypothesis as defined in formal_vocabulary.md. The rules below are the research clauses of the charter; section numbers point there.

The working rules

One notebook per research line (charter §5.6). A line is one sustained question, such as "how the discrete model reads context". Its notebook lives at docs/research/notebook/<line>.md. Each result is one row: date, what ran, the number, the bar it was tested against, the verdict and a link to the artifact. A dated evidence folder is kept only when a run seals artifacts. The one-page plan for the whole project is NOW.md; with the notebooks, it replaces the old running log (current-state.md).

A sheet only where it decides spend (§4.5). A sheet is a pre-registration of one page: the bar, the noise, the controls, the seeds, the cost and what each outcome would decide. It needs a review by a non-author, called a FIT review, before:

  • any GPU training or evaluation, and
  • any run that a milestone claim rests on.

A fresh-context subagent counts as a non-author. Builds, finite kernel tests and host checks need no sheet. Old float sheets come back only as new sheets with a new FIT. A FIT review releases nothing by itself.

One owner release per sheet (§5.1). The owner types one release phrase personally for each sheet. It covers all the sheet's arms, seeds and registered stop rules. Labs stage the commands and then check the records; no lab types a release for the owner.

Mechanism statuses (§4.1). Every mechanism is ACTIVE (on the model path), READY (built and tested but not yet trained in) or PARKED (the tested forms failed or broke a rule). A PARKED page lists what would reopen it. There is no terminal status. The mechanism board shows the current state. This is the rule from decision D22 (a negative closes a configuration, never a mechanism).

What a verdict closes. A negative result closes the exact tested configuration: the recipe, dose, window, key and objective. It never closes the mechanism, and stopping a novel mechanism takes an owner decision. A run that meets its own pre-registered mechanism target without a significant headline loss is a KEEP, and the work iterates. A tooling or numerical failure is a blocker to fix, not a negative. Source: D22 sections 1 and 2 in archive/integration/DECISIONS-2026-10-19.md.

Instrument first (§4.2). Before calling a result, decide whether the check itself is faulty. An instrument defect is a fix, never a negative. No target is set from a vacuous instrument, and no single number rules out a line. Findings shows why: a metric that read zero, a control that checked zero rows and a typed-in number each misled the project once.

Power and transfer (§4.3). A decisive run uses at least two seeds or at least 200 fresh rows. Its bar is never narrower than the measured noise. The mechanism must be trained in, not bolted on. Every gain on a development panel is reported together with a fresh transfer number.

Controls and pivots (§4.4). Compare against lawful non-neural baselines, which today means count tables. After three results on one line that do not move its headline number, write a pivot note: stop, or run one decisive test.

Plain verdict words. NOT_RUN means nothing ran; it is not a pass. UNAVAILABLE means a needed input was missing; it is not a negative. A passing test is not trained capability, and a passing control is not a language result (§4.6).

Preserve everything (§4.7). Nothing is deleted. Negatives, unique source and other labs' work go to the archive, byte-identical.

Where old records live

Every dated record before 18 October 2026 now sits under archive/, at the same relative path it had under docs/, except the reference documents that stayed in docs/ (such as docs/scaling_law.md and docs/inference_contract.md). Records dated 18 and 19 October stay in docs/labs/. The archive never changes: many experiment sheets are pinned by hash, and SHA256SUMS files cover the records. So read an archived record as a faithful copy of the day it was written, including any claim that was corrected later.

To find a record, use the generated index archive/CATALOG.md, with the same data in archive/catalog.jsonl. Its columns are date, lab, line, milestone, mechanism, verdict and path. It also holds the old-path to new-path map, so an old link still resolves. The catalog is an index, not a verdict. Follow its path and read the record before you rely on a number.

What the project knows

The project's record holds more lessons about what misleads than results about what works. The most useful knowledge is a set of 21 lessons, mostly about how to measure honestly, plus a short list of measured results. The honest summary is this. Several lawful parts exist and have passed their finite tests. No model on the current path has learned language: the best trained discrete model sits below a simple count table. The cause is not yet established.

flowchart TB
  A["Passes with the teacher's text supplied<br/>(teacher-forced)"] --> B["Passes on a panel the authors built"]
  B --> C["Passes on development rows<br/>the team has already seen"]
  C --> D["Passes on fresh held-out rows"]
  D --> E["Writes coherent text on its own"]
  E --> F["Same result from the shipped integer file"]
  F --> G["Faster or cheaper per token on a laptop"]

The ladder a result must climb before it counts as capability. The project has repeatedly stopped at the first three steps (lessons 3 and 4 below).

How to read this page

  • #N is issue or pull request N in UOR-Foundation/uor-r4. Each lesson cites the items it came from.
  • The lessons come from the audit's reading of the GitHub archive, items #1 to #2495. Some items were read in full and some by title only (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/eras/eras.json, field notes). Check the item before you rely on a number.
  • Each lesson records something that happened at a stated scope, so each is a measurement of that case. Where a lesson generalises, the generalisation is a hypothesis, and it never closes a mechanism (decision D22).
  • Mechanism names use the statuses ACTIVE, READY and PARKED. See the mechanism board.

The 21 lessons, by theme

The numbers are the audit's own, so you can trace a lesson back to its era in the history. Lessons are grouped by theme, so their numbers are not in order; other pages cite them by number.

Check the measurement first

  1. Check the instrument before trusting a result. A metric that read 0.0000 hid a real loss (the #99 metric, removed by the revert #102). An outside check on the same text differed from the pipeline's own score by about a factor of three, 11.17 against 3.84 bits per token (#300). Typed-in numbers were once merged as results (#1459). A lookup-table gain was retracted as a constant shift (#1881). A control that checked zero rows reported a pass (#2112).
  2. Measure the shipped form. The trained model and the shipped artifact differed by 0.57 bits per byte (BPB) (#1284).
  3. A teacher-forced or authored-panel pass is not coherent generation. Loss kept falling while prose stayed at 0 of 5 (#948, #1264, #1398).
  4. Development is not fresh. A frozen-upstream adapter scored 437 of 512 on rows the team had seen, then 0 of 128 on a fresh draw (#2162, #2164).
  5. A gate set before a run does not move after a miss, and a missing input is not a negative. Frozen floors survived every re-entry (#887, #931). An UNAVAILABLE report is not a zero (#661, #986).

What geometry bought and what it did not

  1. Fixed geometry usually tied or lost to a matched ordinary control. This held for W(3,3) (#929), for the project's geometric mechanisms as of September (#1371) and for fixed E8 or H4 codebooks against k-means (#1456). Kept exceptions: quaternion transport (#1460), quaternion and icosian weights (#2193, #2216) and seed reliability (#1798).
  2. Some geometry wins were storage or lexical artifacts. A zeta-grid headline was storage banding (#440); see also #487.
  3. Exact algebra reproduces perfectly but carries no meaning on its own. H4 and the 64-state SpiralCore worked as controls and supplied no semantics (#952, #985).
  4. Shift-and-add stores and E8 codebooks beat sign codes at equal bits (#243, #395).

Data and scale

  1. Data and teacher breadth beat model size and clever stores. On broad text the ceiling was the teacher (#437). Matching the training distribution beat adding parameters (#1913).

Memory and retrieval

  1. An exact log plus a prime sieve retrieves; the learned pointer copied recency. The pointer returned the most recent value, not the queried one (#1558). The sieve did the retrieval (#1559, #1607).
  2. Chat failures came from missing knowledge and fluency, not retrieval. Retrieval accounted for 2.2% of failing rows (#1708).
  3. Compliance needs a demand paired with its exact short answer. Instruction following was 0 of 6 until each demand was paired (#1918, #1958).
  4. Exact integer export and bit-exact serving work (#1254, #1893).

Learning

  1. Hard geometric selection gives unselected keys no gradient. It needs a training bridge (#2195, #2249).
  2. State and horizon were the levers, not training length (#1366, #1379).
  3. Binding failures came from the training recipe, not the architecture. A copied reference cell scored 99.17% where the bundled recipe failed (#1045, #1050).

Speed and cost

  1. Savings counted on paper are not tokens per second. Analytic multiply savings did not become speed (#2200, #2211). Integer serving first cost 4.3 times more energy than its float parent (on a dense model with every multiply replaced by a table read) (#1449).
  2. Check where compute goes. The output readout took 99.97% of per-token compute (#1287). Geometric operations were 0.05% of the stack's arithmetic (#2186).

How to work

  1. Keep dormant mechanisms behind gates; never delete them (#515, #1747).
  2. A process that forbids running code produces nothing (#1111). A negative closes a configuration, never a mechanism (#2165).

What is still open

The project has built and tested many of the parts of a language model. The few it has trained together (the discrete writer, the reads and the ranking loss) have not yet beaten a simple count table, and a full trunk of lawful parts has never been trained. The biggest open question is simple to state: can a model that uses no softmax learn to rank the right word above the wrong ones? Nobody knows yet. Beside it sits a list of tests that were never run, or that failed only because the test was set up badly. Most of them are cheap, and the cheapest decisive one is FIT-reviewed and queued, not yet released.

flowchart TD
  W2["W2: read-code capacity capture<br/>(FIT-reviewed, queued, about $0.91)"] --> Q{"Which wall is it?"}
  Q -- "representation (H_rep)" --> R["Fix the read and the address metric.<br/>Do not fund float training."]
  Q -- "learning law (H_law)" --> W3["W3: BVG-K batched discrete moves<br/>(about $12)"]
  W3 --> Q3{"Does integer top-1 beat<br/>both count tables?"}
  Q3 -- yes --> NX["Add the missing trunk slots,<br/>then export"]
  Q3 -- no --> W4["W4: one float-credit sheet<br/>(about $5 to $10 GPU)"]

The order of the next decisive tests in the sequence the owner approved (D39 item 4); each is FIT-reviewed, none is released. W1, the K16 run, has already finished with no KEEP.

Terms follow the glossary. Claims are labelled proof, measurement or hypothesis as in formal_vocabulary.md. Dollar figures are the chief architect's estimates, not recorded costs.

How the output head works, in two lines

The model first picks a shortlist of candidate cells, the nearest K of 256 by address. A row counts as admitted if the right token survives that cut. It then ranks the shortlist and takes the nearest token. So a model can fail at admission, at ranking, or at both. Source: docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md section 1 and K16 outcome.

The central unknown

Can a softmax-free read learn ranking? This is a hypothesis, and the biggest one. Every float read that learned had softmax helping it somewhere in training. The best read without softmax, arm W, is a recorded REJECT. It was worse by 0.0172 BPB (bits per byte) and ran 15% slower, and its gradient came from a softmax-shaped surrogate. The starling read reached recall 0.329 where softmax reached 0.999. Both verdicts close those configurations only (decision D22), not the idea. See findings for the numbers and flock read for the discrete read that replaces them.

What we know today: the best trained discrete model scored top-1 of 65 and 463 of 14,287 development rows, below a unigram count table (1,226) and a context-free successor table (6,300) (measurement, K16 outcome). The cause is open. The record rules out one suspect: aliasing did not explain the ranking failure. It leaves ranking capacity, the read, the address key and the training schedule.

FIT-reviewed and queued

These are the closest to a decision. A FIT review is not an owner release: spending waits for the owner (charter §5.1).

  1. W2, the read-code capacity capture (about $0.91, already reviewed as FIT, same lease). It decides whether the wall is the representation (H_rep: the stored code cannot separate the answers) or the learning law (H_law: the code could, but the update rule does not find it). It also adds the count-table arms that the headline bars lacked. Source: architect review section 6, docs/labs/course-correction-2026-10-18/audits/d37-reactivation-architect.md.
  2. The admission-preserving rerun of A8. Pre-registered and reviewed FIT, never run. Its controller and a separate finite qualification producer are merged. The qualification is NOT_RUN. Source: admission-anchor controller.

Every step that trains also needs an owner release (charter §5.1), and training stays HELD until the owner releases it.

Never tested, moderate cost

  • Ranking with admission intact. No run has had admission intact and then failed or succeeded at ranking (admission).
  • A rank objective that keeps cells occupied. The registered route after the K16-R run collapsed to 19 or 20 occupied cells (rank margin).
  • Full-epoch and frequent-token revisit schedules. One pass sees 43.3% of the training targets (proof, by arithmetic, model training).
  • The finite relational head. K16-A reached its 16,404 batches and can satisfy the prerequisite for the next stage (architect review §5; relation read).
  • Discrete Hamming binding (VSA) on the current writer (VSA).

Never tested, expensive or blocked

  • A trunk built only from lawful parts. Train it with float in a new scanned module, then export. The 24-kernel extract has passed finite controls only (geometric stack). No exporter exists for it.
  • The forced-copy oracle for the pointer. The cheapest decisive pointer test. It needs a lawful pointer first, because running it on the old softmax pointer would execute a banned model (pointer key).

Failed only on configuration

A negative closes the configuration, never the mechanism. These tests were flawed as set up, so they say little about the mechanism.

Not yet buildable

The map of lawful parts still has gaps that no test can fill until someone builds them (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md section 1).

  • Position. No mechanism is assigned. The only related result is about recurrent state, and it is confounded (see findings).
  • Normalization. None is designed.
  • Address as the read. Never built, and nothing yet consumes the object store.
  • A lawful exporter for any trained trunk, so the export gap is unmeasured.
  • A faster writer. The writer scans the whole vocabulary, about 5 million comparisons per row, which breaks the per-token sparsity goal at larger vocabularies (proof, by count, architect review §3.5).

What counts as success for the first milestone

The charter sets the M1 closing bar: integer top-1 through the D11 export beats both count tables on the same development panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported. A bits-per-byte bar returns later, once a lawful likelihood exists (charter §4.8). That settles the old open question about scoring a model with no likelihood, for M1 only. A lawful likelihood is still unbuilt. A conversation bar (M2) is further off, and a float student would need a new owner decision (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md section 4, stage 5).

How the project got here

UOR-R4 began in June 2026 as an attempt to run a language model without a transformer or heavy arithmetic, using the geometry of primes, rotations and symmetry groups. Over four months it tried five broad approaches. Each was replaced when it hit a wall, and each left lessons. The 32 steps below are the audit's "eras", read from the GitHub archive (items #1 to #2495). The work has been careful and open about its failures, and it has not yet produced a model that holds a conversation.

Five phases and 32 eras on one time axis, with the number of catalog records per day underneath (1,051 of the catalog's 1,173 records carry a date). Era spans come from the archive audit; the daily counts come from archive/catalog.jsonl. The figure draws Phase E to 19 October; the era snapshot below ends on 15 October.

Terms follow the glossary. #N is an issue or pull request number in UOR-Foundation/uor-r4. Every row below is a measurement of what a recorded item said, at that item's scope, unless marked otherwise. Eras overlap on their edges, and some items were read by title only (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/eras/eras.json, field notes).

Phase A: compile a teacher into tables (10 June to 26 August)

In plain words: watch a real language model, the "teacher", and compile what it does into lookup tables and a graph that a CPU can run with no multiplications.

In plain words: teach a home-grown Rust model to remember exact facts and versions, then find out why it still could not write prose.

The research lines

A research line is one sustained question the project worked on, such as "how does the discrete model read earlier text". The audit sorted all 1,173 recorded pieces of work into 20 lines. This page lists them, shows when each ran, and says in a word where each stands. Seventeen lines have at least three records and get their own page. None of them has produced a model that holds a useful conversation: the project is pre-alpha and 0 of its 8 milestones are complete (docs/integration/NOW.md).

When each line ran. The September lines end as the October discrete line begins; the tooling and operations lines run alongside.

How to read the table

  • Records are catalog entries. They mix lab records, lane results, reviews and plans, so they show where effort went and not how many experiments ran. Source: archive/catalog.jsonl, counted with jq on the field line.
  • Results are the records whose outcome is positive, negative, inconclusive or diagnostic-stop. The rest are plans, tooling, process, review, operations and blocked runs. A blocked record is a run that could not start; it is not a negative.
  • Span is the first to last dated record in 2026. Some records carry no date and are left out of the span.
  • A positive record reports that the target the record itself set was met, at the scope it states. Many are narrow, scored on a panel the authors wrote, and none is a language result.
  • State follows the project's vocabulary. Active means on the current model path. Parked means the tested forms failed or broke a rule and the mechanism stays open (decision D22). Closed means the line stopped (a line label only: its mechanisms keep their board status); a negative closes a configuration and never a mechanism. Preserved is evidence kept inactive.

Research line: discrete attention for the language base (M1)

This is the line that carries the project today. It asks one question: can a model that uses only integers and small geometric moves learn to read earlier text well enough to predict the next word? So far the answer is no. The best trained discrete model gets the next word right in 65 and 463 of 14,287 development rows, below a plain word-count table that gets 1,226.

flowchart LR
  A["Sep to early Oct<br/>Float readers and<br/>attention latches"] --> B["13 to 14 Oct<br/>First integer GPU path,<br/>first pilot (A2)"]
  B --> C["15 to 18 Oct<br/>Admission wall;<br/>56x faster scoring"]
  C --> D["18 Oct<br/>Four 16-cell runs (K16)"]
  D --> E["19 Oct<br/>No keep; address cells<br/>and their dose (A8)"]
  E --> F["Next: admission-<br/>preserving rerun"]

Two terms used below. Admission is the shortlist of words the read can see; a word outside it can never be chosen. Top-1 means the right word ranked first.

What it set out to do

Give the discrete model an attention-like read of context. Under the owner's rules (no softmax, no matrix multiplication, integer serving) the read must be a tree walk (Route), a small neighbour set rotated into the query's frame (Flock) or a link-following rule such as "the word after the earlier copy of this word" (Relation). The line's yardstick is milestone M1: a saved discrete artifact that, after export to integer serving and on each of two seeds, beats a unigram table and a successor table on the same development rows (charter, item 8 of the research clauses).

What happened, in order

  1. Float readers and latches (19 Sep to 5 Oct). A hard capture-and-hold gate let saved models answer 128 of 128 original and stress rows, against 47 to 59 for same-size controls (latch). Fresh complete replies stayed low: a directed cue relation scored 0/32 and its cue-only control 1/32 (cue carrier).
  2. First integer GPU path (13 to 14 Oct). All eleven construction controls passed, then 25 of 25 (discrete learning, driver cost). The first training pilot (A2, 1,640 batches) raised top-1 from 17 to 82 and top-8 from 173 to 1,169 of 14,287, while the loss total rose from 13,816,032 to 13,884,032 (pilot). The diagnosis: the starting table had only 16 distinct vectors for 4,096 tokens (diagnosis).
  3. The admission wall (15 to 17 Oct). Re-scoring saved checkpoints with 8 to 16 kept cells never reached the 4,894 admission bar (best 2,400 at 16), so capacity had to be trained in (sweep). Repeated qualification restarts (five by the last record) stopped on build, interface and lint errors and then on a 99-against-100 timing count (restart 5). A host check found that a context-free successor table already scores 6,300 of 14,287 (host diagnostics).
  4. Speed (16 to 18 Oct). In a three-batch diagnostic, over 99.99% of each proposal's time was one scoring kernel; a row-parallel version gave equal losses about 56 times faster (3.843 s to 0.0691 s) (rows parity).
  5. The paired test and the 16-cell runs (18 to 19 Oct). The first paired attention test (Dose 1) was stopped by the owner at 904 and 1,065 batches, before any checkpoint, to switch to the row-parallel driver (a diagnostic stop, not a verdict). The paired row-parallel run that followed (Dose 2) reached its registered collapse stop at 4,096 batches in both arms (the Relation read and a frozen control): admission on 3,847 copy-successor rows (development rows where copying the word after the previous occurrence would be right) fell from 2,034 to 225 (Relation) and 205 (frozen control) (Q1 diagnosis). Four runs of the 16-cell experiment (K16) used two training objectives, an address-margin loss (A) and an occupancy-rank loss (R), with two seeds each. They accepted 407, 130, 410 and 129 moves. The occupancy-rank loss collapsed to 19 or 20 occupied cells; the margin loss lost admission. Verdict: no KEEP (no run met its own target), and the fresh slice stays sealed (outcome call).
  6. Address cells (19 Oct). Placing each token's cell near its predecessors' cells lifted starting admission from 127 to 1,351 of 3,847 at zero training; a shuffled control got 476 (pre-flight). Training then eroded it in the address-cell dose (A8): Relation 1,351 to 551 (stopped), frozen control 857 (A8 dose). A controller that audits admission every 64 batches is built; its GPU qualification has not been run (NOT_RUN) (controller).

What it taught

Check the instrument first (lesson 1 in what the project knows): a register-count mismatch, a mismatched JSON key and a hash-domain bug each blocked a run or rejected a valid artifact without testing any mechanism. Development is not fresh (lesson 4), and a pass is not a language result. The mechanisms in play are discrete learning, admission, address cells and the three reads linked above.

Current state

M1 is not met. No trained discrete artifact beats the unigram table. The cheapest approved next steps are the read-code capacity capture (W2) and the admission-preserving rerun of the address-cell dose (A8) (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md, section 4). Any further training needs a new owner release.

Research line: the prime-zeta codebook (M1)

Every word needs a starting address. The discrete model had been starting from a seeded table that left 4,096 words sharing only 16 distinct addresses. This line built a fixed, repeatable table instead: each word gets a prime number, and the prime is turned into a vector through the phases of the Riemann zeta zeros. All 4,096 words now get unique addresses. The line has three catalog records, and one of them says plainly what the construction does not show.
Catalog idm1-prime-zeta
Time span14 Oct 2026 for the one dated record; two older reference records are undated
MilestoneM1 (1 record); none for 2
Records3
Outcomespositive 1 · inconclusive 1 · review 1
StateACTIVE as the baseline start and the fallback inside the address-cell table (prime-zeta codebook). No trained result against its controls

Counts: archive/catalog.jsonl. Terms follow the glossary; ACTIVE, READY and PARKED are defined on the mechanism board.

flowchart LR
  A["Token id"] --> B["Prime p<br/>(4,096th = 38,873)"]
  B --> C["Zeta phases<br/>gamma x ln p"]
  C --> D["Snap to E8 roots<br/>(integer table)"]
  D --> E["256 cells, 16 words each;<br/>4,096 unique vectors"]

The construction, run once offline on the host. The model only sees the finished table of small integers.

What it set out to do

Replace the random start that caused the first pilot's ranking trouble. In that pilot the initializer produced only 16 distinct vectors for 4,096 token identities, so most words could not be told apart by the read (A2 diagnosis). The prime-zeta construction was registered as a zero-training check that a deterministic, arithmetic table could fix that.

How it works

Token \(v\) gets the prime \(p_{\mathrm{id}(v)+1}\), so the vocabulary maps one to one onto the first \(V\) primes. For each of the first 512 pinned zeta-zero ordinates \(\gamma_k\), the phase is \(\theta_k(p)=\gamma_k\ln p \bmod 2\pi\). Four channels per 8-dimensional block are quantized to integers and matched to the nearest of 16 roots of the E8 lattice by an exact integer inner product. A word's writer cell is the pair of roots of its first and last block, a 16 by 16 grid of 256 cells with exactly 16 words each. A uniqueness pass then gives interior blocks distinct roots. Floating point appears only in this one-time host step (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/mechanisms/prime-zeta-codebook.json, field how_it_works).

What happened, in order

  1. Older reference work (undated). Replacing a stub router with sixteen zeta-window projections raised top-1 from 0.17 to 1.00, but only on a six-sentence fixture (record). An audit checked every consumer of the stored zeta state vector before widening its storage (audit).
  2. 14 Oct: construction qualified. The generator was built, with no training and no corpus rows. All 4,096 of 4,096 tokens receive unique vectors, 17 of 17 base CUDA controls and 6 of 6 prime-zeta controls pass, and the tables match across macOS and Linux (construction record).
  3. 18 to 19 Oct: used as a starting point. Starting from the injective table fixed aliasing but spread tokens over all 256 cells, so only 127 of 3,847 copy-successor rows had the right cell in view at 8 kept cells, below the 500 gate (pre-flight). Address-structured cells (see the M1 line) lifted that to 1,351 at zero training, and prime-zeta remains the fallback inside that table.

Where it stands

ClaimKindSource
4,096 of 4,096 tokens get unique vectors; 0 collisions; 256 of 256 cells occupiedmeasurementconstruction record
The two matched controls (shifted zeta ordinates, permuted primes) also give 4,096 unique vectors, so uniqueness comes from the quota and uniqueness pass, not from the primesmeasurementsame
Do prime-zeta phases give similar words similar addresses? Primes are assigned by token id, which is arbitraryhypothesis (untested)prime-zeta-codebook.json, never_tested
A trained model starting from prime-zeta beats its controlsnot runsame

What it taught

An injective table is necessary, not sufficient. Uniqueness solved aliasing, and it did not solve admission. Two kinds of check are separate here: a construction passing its tests, and a trained model gaining anything from it. A passing control is not a language result.

Current state

ACTIVE. The held trained-in test against the two nulls (a shifted-ordinate null and a permuted-prime null) at matched budget with at least two seeds is the next step. Prime-zeta is a deterministic function of token id, so identical seeds give identical tables; seed variance needs another declared axis.

Research line: the float route to rung 0 (M1)

"Rung 0" is the first, smallest training test of a model that obeys every rule: no softmax, no matrix multiplication, geometric parts only. This line tried to reach it with floating-point training, then rebuilt each part until it was lawful. The central case was the "starling" read, which picks about seven neighbouring earlier tokens instead of using softmax. It could not learn from scratch. On 13 October the owner moved training to the integer path, and this line was preserved as inactive evidence.

flowchart LR
  A["Sep<br/>Reviews: frozen state<br/>adds 0.022 bits"] --> B["11 to 12 Oct<br/>Starling read tests,<br/>quaternion weights"]
  B --> C["12 Oct<br/>Softmax ban;<br/>lawful parts rebuilt"]
  C --> D["13 Oct<br/>18 finite GPU controls"]
  D --> E["13 Oct<br/>D32 stops float<br/>model computation"]

Seven days of experiments, then a rebuild, then an owner decision that paused the route.

What it set out to do

Reach a first rule-compliant training result. The plan of 12 October named the pieces: a hard rank-hinge loss in place of cross-entropy, an exact flock selection on the 600-cell, a raw-score output head, a rotation gate in place of sigmoid gating and a geometric projection in place of dense maps (design). Rung 0 would pass only if the margin loss fell steadily and the rate of unviolated targets reached five times the no-model rate on both seeds.

What happened, in order

  1. September reviews. A frozen recurrent state added only 0.022 bits over a count table, so no readout work was justified (result).
  2. 11 Oct: the starling read. Trained from scratch, it scored mean recall 0.009 (chance 0.0045) where an L2-softmax control scored 0.617, because hard selection gives unchosen keys no gradient (record). A temporary dense helper raised the address hit rate from 10% to 73% but recall stayed at 0.011 (anneal). Gating by content instead of address did not help (content).
  3. 12 Oct: partial recoveries. A dense bootstrap teacher got 3 of 5 seeds to softmax-level recall, against 1 of 5 without it (bootstrap). A light distillation weight gave 0.380 (sweep). Training twice as long gave 0.78 on 5 of 5 seeds on a 512 synthetic test, a provisional KEEP (target met, at an unequal budget) (recall). At 1,536 context the read collapsed to 0.241 against 0.999, because each cell kept only its last four keys (context). A persistent tree fixed retention but recall stayed at 0.329 (tree).
  4. Quaternion weights (11 Oct). Quaternion-structured projections beat a dense model of equal parameters by 0.018 bits per byte, six times the noise, with four times fewer matrix weights than an equal-width dense model (record).
  5. 12 to 13 Oct: lawful rebuild. Source landed for the rank-hinge loss, the Hamilton gate, geometric recurrence gates and the SpiralCore and FBS projection. Finite GPU checks passed: 18 controls on the complete path (rung 0 path). No training followed.
  6. 13 Oct. The owner's D32 decision banned float model computation. The float qualification attempts were stopped and kept: 31 of 33 controls passed at the last complete replay; the 34-control replay was NOT_RUN. This was a scope change, not a mechanism negative (record).

Key results

ResultKindSource
Starling from scratch: recall 0.009 against 0.617 for the L2-softmax controlmeasurementstarling read
Starling with persistent tree at 1,536 context: 0.329 against 0.999 for softmaxmeasurementtree
Quaternion weights 1.495866 against 1.513594 bits per byte for dense at equal parametersmeasurementrecord
18 finite GPU controls pass on the complete rung-0 path; no trainingmeasurementrung 0 path

What it taught

Hard geometric selection gives unselected keys no gradient, so it needs a training bridge (lesson 12 in what the project knows). Every float read that learned had softmax help it in training, so whether a softmax-free read can learn ranking from scratch is the biggest open question (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md, section 5). A scope change is not a negative (lesson 21).

Current state

Preserved evidence, not a live line. The surviving parts are READY, never trained: Hamilton gate, recurrence gates and SpiralCore/FBS. Flock read is ACTIVE on the discrete path and spin weights is PARKED. Archived float sheets return only as new sheets with a fresh review.

Research line: grounded replies from exact memory (M2)

This line tried to make the model answer a question from a fact it was told earlier, and to say "I don't know" when it was never told. Facts sit in an exact store, so storing and fetching are not the hard part. The hard part is getting a trained model to read the right fact and write it out. One model reached 437 of 512 correct replies on the rows the team had been tuning on, then 0 of 128 on fresh rows.

flowchart LR
  A["Sep<br/>Reviews and scoped<br/>memory sessions"] --> B["28 to 29 Sep<br/>Always-on store read<br/>fails its gate"]
  B --> C["9 Oct<br/>Chat model cannot<br/>copy a stored number"]

The development score rose in steps on a panel the team could see. The fresh draw, run with no further training, did not follow.

What it set out to do

Build the second capability after a language base: a reply that is correct because it came from an exact record, not from a guess. Exact storage is easy and was never the problem; an exact store scored 1.000 whenever its register was right (exact memory dossier). The line tested which learned reader or writer could use it.

What happened, in order

  1. September. Fifteen records dated 3 Sep are source audits and acceptance reviews of a text-to-clause adapter and a native bridge. A pre-registered exact-pair cache lowered the count reference by 0.238 bits per target on exposed project Markdown, not general prose (result). An always-on exact-store read failed its gate on all three seeds, with held-out accuracy of 0.03 to 0.16 against a 0.90 bar (G1). A diagnostic put 77.7 percent of held-out failures at query-entity tagging (decomposition).
  2. 1 to 5 Oct. Adapting only the readouts raised complete own-prefix source replies from 4/20 to 18/20 (coadapt), yet a prospectively frozen fresh panel gave 0/8 (frozen transfer).
  3. 9 Oct. Traces showed why stored numbers failed. The copy pointer attended the repeated sentence frame, never the second digit of the value (0 of 13 rows), and the 4,096-piece vocabulary has no multi-digit tokens (positional read). Several attempts to build legal parameter changes with an exact solver stopped on numeric errors, which are blockers, not negatives.
  4. 10 Oct. Whole-answer replies on the 512-row development panel went 8, 22, 145, 175, 177, then 437 after training each token against its strongest wrong rival (260 gains and no losses on that last step) (pooled rank). Five other recipes lowered it (8 to 2, 8 to 4, 8 to 0 and 145 to 139 replies). The saved 437 model then scored 0/128 against a bar of 52 on fresh role and value combinations (fresh).
  5. 10 to 12 Oct. Training the read to land on the asked value was flat at first (19/40 against 20/40). A powered rerun over three seeds cut wrong-value failures from 47 to 30 of 120, and at four times the length from 49 to 23 (scaled). Both met their bars, so each was a KEEP (target met without a significant loss elsewhere), but on a softmax read. A whole-path source reference was built; CUDA execution has not been run (NOT_RUN) (recovery). The softmax ban (D23, 12 Oct) and the M2 training hold stopped further runs.

What it taught

Development is not fresh (lesson 4 in what the project knows). An exact log retrieves; the learned pointer copied recency (lesson 9). Chat failures came from missing knowledge and fluency, not retrieval (lesson 10), and binding failures came from the recipe (lesson 20). Hard selection needs a training bridge (lesson 12). Research line: durable memory and the object store (M3)

Milestone M3 asks that a conversation's memory survive between sessions and that answers stay grounded in it. This line built the storage half: an exact object store that keeps bytes once in a hashed tree, can fetch any range with an integrity check, and can copy itself between machines. The store works and is well tested. Nothing in the model reads from it yet, so M3 has not been measured.

flowchart LR
  A["3 to 5 Oct<br/>Chat-memory<br/>diagnostics"] --> B["14 to 15 Oct<br/>Design, build, byte tests"]
  B --> C["17 to 18 Oct<br/>Replication, audit,<br/>repair, cross-language"]
  C --> D["Not yet<br/>A model that reads it;<br/>M3 bars"]

Most of the work sits in the third box. The fourth box has not started.

What it set out to do

Give the model a memory outside its weights: exact bytes, deduplicated, verifiable and portable, tied to token occurrences. The early records (3 to 5 Oct) tested whether a model could use an exact selected value in chat. With the exact value supplied, 16 of 20 development cases answered correctly against 0 of 20 with the read off (source binding). That is an open-development diagnostic only.

What happened, in order

  1. Design (14 Oct). Data is folded into hashed records that can be rebuilt or range-read with checks. A node id is 12 bytes. A 32,768-byte fixture record kept 70,972 bytes, a reminder that deduplication is not universal compression (design).
  2. Build (14 to 15 Oct). A Rust reader fetched 203 byte ranges with identical bytes from an eager and an indexed backend (reader). The store folded and rebuilt source bytes exactly; a repeated fixture kept 380 bytes for 7,776 raw bytes. Twenty integration tests and 13 tokenizer tests passed (store).
  3. Replication and audit (17 to 18 Oct). About 25 records add a peer protocol. A receiver holding an older 1 MiB version fetched 22 records, 1,014 bytes, in three rounds (peer). Batching a cold 52 MB pull over a high-latency link took 91.50 s against 236.19 s (batch). Pipelined fetches ran about 2.8 times faster with an emulated 8 ms delay, which is not a real wide-area measurement (pipelined). Other records add pinning, failover, repair, retries and a verified audit command. Twelve warm receivers pulling at once took 0.864 s against 3.506 s one at a time (concurrency).
  4. Second language (18 Oct). A pure-Python client audited and pulled a 256 KiB artifact from the Rust server over loopback, byte for byte (conformance). The test suite stands at 60 passing (batch plumbing).

Key results

ResultKindSource
Exact value supplied: 16/20 development cases correct, 0/20 with the read offmeasurementsource binding
Repeated fixture: 380 retained bytes for 7,776 raw bytesmeasurementstore
1 MiB delta pull: 22 records, 1,014 bytes, 3 roundsmeasurementpeer
WAN cold pull with batching: 91.50 s against 236.19 s (2.58 times)measurementbatch
Cross-language conformance: PASS, 262,144 bytes pulled identicalmeasurementconformance

What it taught

A byte store is a reliable component, and its tests show that it stores and returns bytes exactly. They say nothing about whether a model can use it, and a passing control is not a language result. The record also shows where effort went: 27 of the 33 records are tooling, and most are network plumbing built before any model consumed the store (a count from the catalog; the reading is a hypothesis).

Current state

READY. Nothing consumes the store and no M3 bar has been run (board). The next step is to wire it in and run the M3 bars. Exact addressed memory as a read is still unbuilt (exact memory).

Research line: integer serving (M4)

This line is about running a finished model on an ordinary laptop or in a browser using only whole-number arithmetic, adds and table lookups: no floating point and no multiplication. In the records the engine reproduced its float models exactly on the old stack, and the multiply-free audits pass on the WASM serving symbols. What is missing is a trained model worth serving: the models tried scored 1.20 to 1.24 bits per byte against a 0.90 target, and no model that obeys all the current rules has been exported.

The engine was settled early. The quality gap was never in the engine.

What it set out to do

Make fast, cheap, local inference real: one served model, integer-only (D11), reachable from a command line, with tokens per second and energy measured on the owner's laptop. The product is serving; panel scoring and training stay on the GPU.

What happened, in order

  1. August. A source-free integer n-gram table predicted 22.26% of held-out targets against 5.41% for unigram, and one exact tie-break added 0.95 points (table, tie-break). The skip-mix lane beat base by +28.45 per mille top-1 (record). A vector (SIMD) scan sped one path up 1.60 times against a 2 times bar (record).
  2. 8 Sep. The alpha publication was withdrawn: the scorecard had used constant or flag evidence (record).
  3. 9 to 10 Oct: the gap is the model. The published 0.877 float against 0.933 served compared different numbers of windows. On a matched retrain the pair is 0.8776 against 0.8868 bits per byte (protocol pin). The recorded criterion is still "not met and not claimable", and the matched float model sits at 0.924 on the attribution record's own table. At identical positions quantization cost 0.0041 and the engine cost -0.0000008 (attribution). The integer engine matched float exactly (maximum logit difference 0) while three served models scored 1.20, 1.24 and 1.24 against the 0.90 target (D11 serving).
  4. 10 to 11 Oct: lawful pieces. Replacing the served softmax read with rank-weight tables cost 0.017 to 0.26 bits per byte more across four arms, all missing a 0.01 bar (softmax-free read). Weights built from two icosian table entries and a 2-bit mantissa reached 1.5148 against 1.4944 for float quaternions and 1.5136 for dense of equal size (icosian mantissa). The integer engine refuses product-key memory entirely, so the speed case there is unmeasured (port).
  5. 18 Oct. An outside contributor's WebAssembly integer runtime was merged after hardening: 165 tests pass and 7 of 7 serving symbols show no multiply, divide or float. The vector (SIMD) kernels are not integrated and the demo is not runnable from a clean clone (record).

Key results

Integer engine equals float: negative log-likelihood difference 0.0, maximum logit difference 0measurementD11 serving
Served quality 1.20138, 1.24402 and 1.24233 bits per byte; target at most 0.90measurementsame
Speed fell from 63.41 tokens/s at 384 context to 30.43 at 4,096, so replacing the quadratic read buys at most about 1.7 timesmeasurementcontext curve

What it taught

Check the instrument before blaming the engine (lesson 1 in what the project knows): most of the apparent served-versus-float gap came from comparing different numbers of windows. Measure the shipped form (lesson 2). Savings counted on paper are not tokens per second (lesson 13). Exact integer export and bit-exact serving work (lesson 17).

Current state

The zero-multiply and bit-exact properties are verified on the old stack and on the WASM serving symbols. The engine has not served any model that obeys the current rules, and the WASM record lists its SIMD kernels as unintegrated fixtures, so its contract is not yet exercised end to end. The 19.9M-parameter stack that missed the old M1 bar read every weight on every token, and two of the integer schemas serve softmax through exponent tables, which the current rules ban (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md, section 1). The next step is to export one discrete artifact and measure its export gap (board). Product serving, including tokens per second and energy on the laptop, is allowed; panel scoring of an exported artifact is still GPU research compute.

Three of the four steps corrected an earlier claim.

What it set out to do

Show that a geometric, table-driven model uses less energy per token on a laptop than an ordinary model. The plan of 25 September proposed ternary table-lookup serving with recurrence and exact memory, to be judged by measured joules per token. Its energy figures were derived from operation counts, not measured (plan).

What happened, in order

  1. 28 Sep: a sealed record was edited. The sealed root of the cost profile for the D11 serving contract had been edited in place and resealed. The correction records the hashes, the overwritten fields and a duplicated evaluation record (lineage correction).
  2. 11 Oct: the metric changes. The owner directed that generated tokens per second is the headline comparison, reported with panel acceptance and never alone. A direct test swapped a layer's feed-forward block for an addressed lookup memory. Analytic multiplies fell by 90%, but generation ran at about 385 ids per second against about 637 for the control, 1.65 times slower. Training took 245 s against 104 s for 2,000 steps, 2.4 times longer (tokens per second). A same-day correction relabelled the arms as feed-forward block against lookup memory, not read against address.
  3. 18 Oct: cost provenance. Energy evidence must separate cache residency from sparsity. Earlier cost figures for the injective-initialisation draft are relabelled planning guesses, not measurements: 1.31 s per batch survives only as an extrapolation, and 5,361 seconds meant a resource lifetime, not a per-batch time (record).

What it taught

Savings counted on paper are not tokens per second (lesson 13 in what the project knows). Check where compute goes: the output readout took 99.97% of per-token compute in one model, and geometric operations were 0.05% of the stack's arithmetic (lesson 14). A table read is the intended primitive of the native integer path, but that path refuses product-key memory today, so the lookup's cost there is unmeasured (native address port).

Current state

Not started. M5 needs a lawful model to measure, and none has been exported (serving line). Product serving and its tokens per second and energy on the client device are allowed measurements (charter, item 6).

Research line: the geometric stack

The "geometric stack" was a layered float model whose layers carried state with quaternion rotations. It was trained offline and then converted to 4-bit integers for serving. It matched an ordinary transformer on loss, served bit-exactly, and still wrote useless prose. It also used softmax, SiLU and matrix multiplication in training, so the owner's later bans made it a historical form. Some of its pieces live on as READY mechanisms that have never been trained.

flowchart LR

The stack's arc: a good loss number, then repeated attempts to turn it into a model that talks.

What it set out to do

Train a deeper model with recurrence, geometric reads and exact memory, then compress it to integers and serve it without multiplications. The steps followed the owner's learning ladder (decision D8: reference baselines, then joint learning, then conversion to the discrete form): reference baselines, a joint recurrent learner, then conversion to the discrete form.

What happened, in order

  1. Baselines and the recurrent learner (24 to 25 Sep). A neural reference reached 1.574 nats against 2.392 for the best 5-gram-plus-cache baseline (baselines). Both float recurrent arms reached about 2.11 nats and passed the engineering gate, but the quaternion arm trailed the ordinary control, so no geometric advantage was shown (result).
  2. Integer forms (25 to 27 Sep). Four-bit quantization-aware training missed its +0.05-nat retention gate (+0.059 and +0.080) (result). Learned rounding passed (2.114 and 2.111 nats) and an integer bridge kept every source answer, about 28 times slower than float (learned rounding, bridge). A standalone integer command reproduced all 4,096 saved distribution hashes and ran 4.5 to 6.6 times faster after one optimization (serving). Continued language training lowered loss but produced 0 of 5 acceptable stories (continuation).
  3. Geometric reads (26 to 28 Sep). A Lorentz (hyperbolic) read beat a dot-product read by 0.018 nats on code in 3 of 4 seeds, then lost to the matched dot reset when adapted (+0.046 and +0.013 nats) (cycle 3, adaptation). The stack matched a 7M-parameter transformer on repository code (1.998 against 2.011 nats), but generated code was useless (cycle 4). An exact relation store was perfect in distribution but its learned read trigger fired 0 of 826 times on held-out phrasing (exact relation store probe, D2).
  4. Quantization (28 to 29 Sep). Round-to-nearest 4-bit export cost +0.0362 nats against a 0.02 gate (representation measurements). Quantization-aware training brought the integer engine within +0.0106 nats of its float model, bit-identical to a NEON reference (QAT).
  5. Contest and withdrawals (6 to 11 Oct). In the D20 contest, a three-seed test of the geometric read against a parameter-matched control found no winner: the geometric arm scored 0.0073, 0.9995 and 1.0000 in class against about 0.25 for the control (D20 run). A claimed 12-times faster fused kernel was withdrawn because the pod never ran it (record).

What it taught

Loss and prose are different things: a good number coexisted with 0 of 5 stories (lesson 3 in what the project knows). Fixed geometry usually tied or lost to a matched control (lesson 6), and the quaternion-transport win is a hypothesis until a parameter-matched, lawful control exists. Compute went to the readout, not the geometry (lesson 14).

Research line: the September native geometric model

This line was the project's first attempt to build a language model from scratch in Rust out of geometric parts. It gave the model an exact memory of what was said and small learned "readers" that choose what to look at. It produced many narrow wins on hand-written test panels and no model that writes prose. The ideas that survived went into the discrete model that now carries the project.

The line in five steps. Most of the green results sit in the second box and were scored on panels the authors wrote.

What it set out to do

The compile-a-teacher approach (R4G1) had stalled: it could copy a teacher but not write text on its own. This line asked a different question. Can a model whose parts are exact geometric objects, such as prime-number addresses, rotations in four dimensions (H4) and versioned records of what was said, learn to read context and answer from it?

What happened, in order

  1. Attention in geometric coordinates (27 Aug to 3 Sep). Small positive tests changed a decoded continuation: for example real 2/2 against 0/2 when the binding was permuted (paragraph test). Not all passed. Full H4 causal attention scored 3/12 while plain fixed-tangent attention scored 12/12 (direct causal test), and a gauge-covariance test scored 13/24 against an 18 gate (V4). A recall control (Zoology) reached 99.17% (11,900/12,000) with an ordinary softmax cell, which showed the earlier binding failures came from the training recipe (record).
  2. A parameter-free readout ladder failed. Four variants of reading retained state all missed the frozen prompt-gain floor of 0.0433 (best 0.0390) (block-delta).
  3. Rust engine and exact memory (4 to 13 Sep). Dozens of narrow positives on authored panels, for example 50/50 against 12/50 for a contextual phrase start and 64/64 against 0/64 for fresh historical targets (contextual start, historical query). Each is scoped to a familiar grammar. The fixed geometric readout alone scored 0.13% against 21.5% with geometry disabled (recovery).
  4. Joint fits failed (12 to 13 Sep). Eight negative records on calibrated emission, block learning and tied sampling each broke earlier behaviour or missed a gate. A 64-update addressed-attention pilot produced no useful answers (pilot).
  5. Learned readers (19 to 25 Sep). A competing-source reader beat exact recurrence on a built panel but harmed natural text by +1.29 bits per token against a +0.05 tolerance (result). H4 shared transitions scored 186/288 where an ordinary finite table scored 288/288 (result). Four integrated-attention trials (A1 to A4) lifted correct source admission from 1/24 to 17/24 but never produced a complete correct answer (0/12 per arm) (A3).
  6. End of the line (25 to 28 Sep). Bounded admission lost the first noun in 11 and 8 cases against a maximum of 2 (result). Icosian direction codes changed the dense read's top choice at 41 to 46 percent of positions and were rejected as address codes (audit).

Key results

What it taught

  • A pass on an authored panel is not language. Many positive records state their own scope as an authored panel, a familiar grammar or development rows only (lessons 3 and 4 in what the project knows).
  • Fixed geometry tied or lost to a matched ordinary control (lesson 6), and exact algebra reproduced perfectly without carrying meaning (lesson 8).
  • Binding failures came from the recipe, not the architecture (lesson 20).
  • Several first readings were later withdrawn by principal reviews, for instance a gain that did not reproduce after a threshold defect (lesson 1).

Research line: compiling a teacher into tables (R4G1)

This was the project's first idea. Watch an ordinary language model (the "teacher"), compile what it does into lookup tables and a graph, and run those on a laptop with no multiplications. It worked as a compiler: it copied the teacher's top choice about as often as the teacher's own tables did. It never wrote coherent text on its own, which is why the project moved on.

flowchart LR

From a compiler that copies a teacher to the point where the objective had to change.

What it set out to do

Compile a teacher into an integer-only graph (called R4G1) that a CPU can run with no floating point, no multiplications and no allocation while serving. Its rules are in inference_contract.md. Compilation itself may use a teacher; only the served runtime must be lawful.

What happened, in order

  1. July. Planning documents, a runtime contract and a format for the graph. The cyclic phase-clock design was an open proposal that authorized no work (phase clock). Held-out Hopf routing used only 7 of 512 sectors (record).
  2. August: retrieval and baselines. Three retrieval negatives turned out to be one measurement bug: a dead cosine term. With a content query, mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.7179 to 0.8542 (reassessment). A certified GPT-2 dense teacher ran at 0.704 times the conventional cost against a 3.0 gate, bit-exactly (record). The attested SmolLM2 baseline was ratified at 29.5203% top-1 (21,293 of 72,130 positions) against 28.1214% for the older runtime (record). A one-token skip-mix lane followed the reference in 41 of 87 favorable pairs, then in 58 of 87 after the candidates were injected, clearing the 53-of-87 bar (spot check, fix).
  3. 20 to 24 Aug: the walls. The best prompt-conditioning arm gained +16.2 per mille against a 20 per mille floor (bake-off). No sealed final partition existed for planning, so reasoning was NOT ESTABLISHED (certification). The skip-mix lane worsened free-running cycle collapse from 710 to 1000 per mille, so corrective rounds were not launched (reachability).
  4. 23 to 27 Sep: the ordinary lexical model. One shared Generate, Copy and Stop model passed 32 of 32 authored preflight cases but was 2.25 bits per target worse than a tuned count table (result). Doubling joint-fit steps added only +0.025 bits against a 0.30 bar (joint fit). Packed 4-bit storage kept eight output pairs identical and cut retained coefficient bytes from 6,702,340 to 847,876 (87.35%) (comparison).

What it taught

The teacher set the ceiling, not the store (lesson 5 in what the project knows). A metric that read zero, or a cosine term that never fired, hid real results, so check the instrument first (lesson 1). Gains measured while the teacher's text was supplied never became coherent text the model wrote itself (lesson 3). Exact integer export and bit-exact serving work (lesson 17), and the project kept that contract. Dormant mechanisms were kept behind gates, never deleted (lesson 16).

Current state

PARKED. The R4G1 graph never produced coherent free text and needs a transformer teacher, which the current rules ban. What happens to its crates is an open owner question (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/mechanisms/board.md, D36 item 3). The integer runtime contract remains the model for D11 serving (the integer-only serving decision) (M4 line).
