Research line: SpiralCore wire transport (side exploration)

This line is a side road, not the model. SpiralCore is a set of exact geometric tools that the project also uses inside the model. Here, someone imported a separate use of it: compressing and routing network traffic between programs. All seven records are dated 18 October. They fix bugs, add tests and record loopback timings. None of them touches the language model, and none is a language result.
Catalog idspiralcore-wire
Time span18 Oct 2026 only
MilestoneNone
Records7
Outcomestooling 7
StateSelf-contained side exploration, off the model path

Counts: archive/catalog.jsonl. Terms follow the glossary; ACTIVE, READY and PARKED are defined on the mechanism board.

flowchart LR
  A["Import<br/>Python, Rust and<br/>interposer, with benchmarks"] --> B["Review fixes<br/>receive lock, streams,<br/>fd reuse"]
  B --> C["Fork safety<br/>shutdown change undone"]
  C --> D["Counters and matrix<br/>18 of 18 legs pass"]

One day of import, review and repair.

What it set out to do

Test whether the exact byte-transport ideas in SpiralCore can shrink repeated network exchanges. The project's own review of the SpiralCore documents on 14 October found the byte transport and exact geometry sound, while the proposed attention head was incomplete and unproven. In the supplied tests a 1 MiB cold exchange used 62,579 bytes and a warm repeat 438 bytes (review). The wire work asks a narrower question about transport only.

What happened, in order

  1. Import. The standalone wire compression and transport code (Python, Rust and an interposer) was imported as a self-contained side exploration with loopback benchmarks. On a Rust peer, a 1.25 MiB compressed exchange took 2.86 ms on average (range 2.10 to 3.30) against 1.92 ms for plain TCP; for 1 KiB, a round trip took 41.8 microseconds against 55.1. So on loopback the wire layer was faster for the 1 KiB round trip and slower for the 1.25 MiB exchange (import).
  2. Review fixes. Four findings from Codex's review of the merged transport were repaired: a receive lock, stream cleanup, a workspace path and committed build outputs. Smoke tests pass; no model compute ran (fixes). A second round repaired a file-descriptor reuse race, stream registration order and half-close handling, with four smoke tests passing (round two).
  3. A fix that broke something. Adding a socket shutdown on close woke a blocked reader but broke fork safety, and the next record replaced it. The final interposer closes a shared socket after a fork without killing the parent's connection; fork and negative-control smoke tests pass on macOS and a Linux guest (round three, fork-safe).
  4. Counters and reproducibility. A one-character bug made a reused route report only its last connection's bytes. The fix reports two connections, 3,357 wire bytes and a ratio of 0.0041 against 0.0030 for the last connection alone, and a regression test fails without it (counter fix). The interoperability matrix was made reproducible off the owner's machine, with 18 passing legs and none failing, and claims that cited nonexistent verify tools were withdrawn (matrix).

Key results

ResultKindSource
Interoperability matrix: 18 pass, 0 failmeasurementmatrix
1 KiB round trip: 41.8 us over the wire layer against 55.1 us plain, on loopbackmeasurementimport
1.25 MiB compressed exchange: 2.86 ms mean against 1.92 ms plain TCP, on loopbackmeasurementsame
Route counter fix: 3,357 wire bytes over two connectionsmeasurementcounter fix

What it taught

Loopback numbers are not wide-area numbers: the benchmarks are one-machine timings, and one 2 MiB probe figure (16.7 ms) is a single uncontrolled run. A fix can break a neighbouring property, so the fork-safety smoke test mattered. Claims about checks that do not exist were withdrawn when found, which is lesson 1: check the instrument (what the project knows). Nothing here is evidence about language.

Current state

A side exploration, kept for its tests. It uses no model, trains nothing and moves no milestone. The related exact-memory work that does matter to the model is the object store, which has its own peer protocol.

Research line: data and tokenizer

A language model never sees letters. It sees numbered pieces of text, and it learns from whatever text it is given. This line holds the small set of records about both choices: which tokenizer cuts the text, and where training text comes from. The project has used one 4,096-piece tokenizer for every current corpus, panel and model. A larger one is prepared as a tool but never trained. The newest records plan a one-time, owner-approved corpus written offline by a large open model.

What it set out to do

Fix a single text-to-piece mapping so every corpus, test panel and trained file refers to the same pieces, and decide where enough good training text can come from.

What happened, in order

  1. Corpus sizing (16 Aug). A historical scaling-law document measured a coverage knee near 1.5 million records, then a correction said the sweep was not fixed-partition evidence and gives no estimate of the exponent (scaling law).
  2. Teacher rehearsals. A pinned small teacher compiled a 20,000-token corpus into table-native artifacts, explicitly not a quotable quality baseline (record). A how-to for refreshing a corpus with the frozen integer runtime alone labels the result self-distilled, kept apart from teacher-fidelity numbers (record).
  3. Reuse audit (3 Sep). External repositories were audited for licences and interfaces. No new dependency was admitted and matrix multiplication was rejected as a backend (audit).
  4. Dialogue format (26 Sep). A contract binds training, panel and chat encoders to one tokenizer identity and a shared role format. So far only the integer session path uses it (contract).
  5. 19 Oct: two preparations. A deterministic Rust command can train a byte-level BPE tokenizer of 16,384 pieces; it does not change the active tokenizer (trainer). Decision D41 lets one open model (gpt-oss-120b) write a training corpus offline once, then never run again for the student. The estimated production corpus of about 30 million tokens costs about $52 to $63 on one large GPU, and executing it needs a separate owner release (D41). A host-only checker that validates such a corpus against its registered sheet passes 32 of 32 self-tests, with no generation run (verifier).

Key results

ResultKindSource
No multi-digit tokens in the 4,096-piece vocabulary; 12 of 13 numeric memory rows failedmeasurementnumeric diagnosis
Donor corpus estimate: about 30M tokens, $52 to $63estimate (not a measurement)D41
Corpus checker self-tests: 32 of 32 passmeasurementverifier

What it taught

A tokenizer is a hidden hypothesis. The missing multi-digit pieces look like an obvious cause of the numeric-memory failures, but an untrained probe found that the number codec already stores two-digit values in order, so the failure sits in the learned read and emit path (probe). A number-aware tokenizer was planned and never built or run (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/mechanisms/tokenizer.json, field never_tested). A data source that is borrowed, such as a teacher, sets the ceiling (lesson 5 in what the project knows). Self-distilled numbers must stay apart from teacher-fidelity numbers.

Current state

Nothing has been trained on any tokenizer except d36d3e87. The never-run tests are 4,096 against 16,384 pieces, a number-aware tokenizer, and whether tokenizer choice interacts with the address placement of the discrete model. D41 releases no training hold: generating a corpus is not training the student (scope note).

Research line: evaluation panels and graders

A model is only as well measured as its test. This line built and audited the project's test sets (panels) and the programs that mark them (graders). Its main finding is humbling: a single canned reply scored as well as the trained chat models on the abstention half of the test, so the early "reply" scores did not show what they seemed to show. The panels are now frozen and graded by deterministic code, not by a neural judge.

flowchart LR

  B --> C["9 Oct<br/>Failures traced to<br/>numbers and cut-off replies"]
  C --> D["13 Oct<br/>Deterministic grader:<br/>canned reply ties"]
  D --> E["14 Oct<br/>Stricter grader v2"]

Each step made the test harder to fool, and each lowered the score the project could claim.

What it set out to do

Settle how progress is judged before more compute is spent. Two panels matter. A 64-row held-out memory panel (40 memory rows, 24 questions that cannot be answered) was drawn from public word lists and sealed with its pass bar before any model saw it. A 232-row open reply panel measures chat quality.

What happened, in order

  1. August to September. A committed evaluation constitution fixed content-pinned suites and leakage checks, and asserted no capability result (constitution). A trajectory-state diagnostic found that none of the free-running failures was state-addressable (0 per mille) (record). The latest evaluation-policy entry stopped a predictive block-delta test at a gain of 0.0390 against a 0.0433 floor, with no generation (policy).
  2. 9 Oct: freeze, then score. The memory panel was sealed (26 files, 26 verified), and a binding-swap control passed 0 of 40 (freeze). The pre-declared test of a 29M chat model scored 10 of 40 against a bar of 34, and 1 of 24 on abstention, where a constant answer did better (v5 acceptance). The 214M model's 31 of 40 reproduced exactly, even on a laptop CPU (v4 reproduction).
  3. 9 Oct: why replies fail. Of 189 failing replies, 152 (80.4%) were neither fluent nor relevant, and 125 (66.1%) ended mid-clause; 85 of those ran to the 64-token cap, and a 50% larger budget rescued only 2.4% of them. No judge-free property separated accepted replies from rejected ones. One canned greeting made up between a fifth and a quarter of the accepted rows (open reply panel). On numeric memory rows 12 of 13 failed, and the 4,096-piece vocabulary holds no multi-digit tokens (numeric diagnosis). Judge-free checks can mark only 88 of the 232 reply rows exactly, 37.9% (deterministic checks).
  4. 13 to 14 Oct. A deterministic Rust grader replaced the neural judge. Re-scoring showed one canned abstention reply scores 40 of 88 and copying the last value ties the model at 20 of 40, so the reply headline was suspended (grader). Version 2 stopped a wrong number that contains the right digits from passing, and left old scores unchanged (11 of 96 and 15 of 96) (grader v2).

Key results

ResultKindSource
v5 memory rows 10/40 (bar 34/40); whole panel 11/64measurementv5 acceptance
One canned abstention reply scores 40/88 on the open panel; the model scored 1/88measurementgrader
12 of 13 numeric memory rows failed; 0 multi-digit tokens in the vocabularymeasurementnumeric diagnosis
88 of 232 reply rows exactly checkable without a judgemeasurementdeterministic checks

What it taught

Check the instrument first (lesson 1 in what the project knows). A model score means little until a constant reply and a copy rule have been scored on the same panel. A pass on a built panel is not general capability (lesson 3). The panel rules are now in the charter: lawful non-neural baselines, which today means count tables, are the standard control.

Current state

The reply and memory panels and graders are frozen and unchanged. The M1 closing bar is now integer top-1 beating the unigram and successor tables, not chat replies (charter, item 8). The reply headline stays suspended, and the charter brings bits per byte back as a bar only once a lawful likelihood exists.

What it set out to do

Make GPU work cheap, repeatable and safe. The rules are owner rules: touch pods only through the project's uor-pod tool, keep to the cost caps, save durable output off the pod before it is destroyed, and never use the laptop CPU for research model compute. What happened, in order

  1. September. A read-only storage review deleted nothing (review). An owner-authorized cleanup recovered about 21.6 GiB of regenerable caches and debug dependencies, and preserved models, research, binaries and downloads (cleanup).
  2. 9 Oct. Hard-coded account details were removed from the pod tool so outside contributors can rent GPUs. Its dry-run suite reached 240 of 240 with 16 new checks; two timing-flaky tests were fixed so the suite passed in 10 of 10 runs under load, where the unfixed version failed 6 of 6 (open pods, deflake).
  3. 13 Oct. A missing import in a CUDA-only test broke every pod's parity check; adding it restored 43 passing parity tests at a cost of about $0.05 (record). The tool gained a Vast.ai backend at about half Runpod's price for the same card: an empty RTX 5090 pod reached a CUDA build and passed 38 of 38 parity tests in 137 s at $0.469 per hour (Vast). Pods now fetch toolchains from a private Hugging Face store; a warm pod is ready in 57 s against 330 s cold (store). Vendored CUDA and Rust dependencies were cleaned of banned code (cuBLAS, softmax and tanh kernels, matmul crates) and 31 of 31 finite controls passed, at an observed cost estimate of $1.23 (vendor boundary).
  4. 17 Oct. Three timing attempts stopped before running anything: the rented GPU had driver 580.105.08 instead of the admitted 580.95.05, then driver 595.71.05, then the right driver on a different physical GPU than the one qualified. Each recorded zero instrument invocations (first, third). An opt-in setting now allocates only hosts advertising one exact driver (driver-aware selection).
  5. 18 Oct. The tool checks a per-file checksum manifest of the laptop archive, and reads uploaded results back from the store, before it destroys a pod (archive verify, store read-back).

Research notebooks

A notebook is one page per line of research, and each page is a table with one row for every result. Instead of a new folder and a new status entry for every pull request, the project now adds one row to the right notebook when a run produces a number. You can read a page top to bottom and see what was tried, what it measured, what bar it had to clear and what was concluded.

flowchart LR
  A["A run or check<br/>produces a number"] --> B["One new row at the<br/>bottom of its notebook"]
  B --> C{"Did the run seal<br/>artifacts?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Dated evidence folder<br/>linked from the row"]
  C -- no --> E["The row is the record"]
  D --> F["Older folders move to archive/"]

How a result becomes a row. Only a run that seals artifacts keeps its own dated folder.

The format

Each notebook lives at docs/research/notebook/<line>.md. A line is one sustained question, such as "how the discrete model reads context". The charter sets this format (CHARTER.md, section 5.6), and the owner chose it in answer to question 4 of the 19 October 2026 review.

Every result is one row with six columns:

ColumnWhat goes in it
DateThe ISO date the result was recorded (YYYY-MM-DD).
What ranOne or two plain sentences: the test or check, on what, with what budget.
NumberThe measured value, with its denominator and the baseline it is read against.
BarThe pass line that was fixed before the run, or "none registered" when the run was a diagnostic or a qualification check.
VerdictOne of the five words below, with a short qualifier.
ArtifactA link to the record or the sealed evidence folder that holds the proof.

Rules for keeping a notebook:

  • Append at the bottom. The newest row is last. Rows from one day appear in the order the work ran where the records show it.
  • One row per result. A repeat of an earlier run gets its own row. A change of plan, a review or a tooling step is not a result and gets no row.
  • A dated evidence folder only when a run seals artifacts (checkpoints, receipts, logs with checksums). The row links to it. A result with nothing to seal needs no folder.
  • Numbers are measurements from a recorded run, unless the row says proof or hypothesis, as defined in formal_vocabulary.md. A passing control is not a language result, and NOT_RUN is not a pass.
  • Rows are never edited to change a verdict. If a later run corrects an earlier one, add a new row that names the earlier one.

The five verdict words

VerdictMeaning
positiveThe run met the bar or passed the controls it registered, at the scope stated in the row.
negativeThe run missed a registered bar. It closes that exact configuration (recipe, dose, window, objective) and never the mechanism (D22).
inconclusiveThe run produced a number, but no bar was decided, or the evidence cannot separate the explanations.
diagnostic stopA registered stop rule or the owner ended the run early so the cause could be found. It is not a negative.
blockedA fault in the tooling, the machine or the source stopped the run before it could measure. It is not a negative, and it is not a result about the model.

Notebook: discrete attention for the language base (M1)

This is the running table of results for the line that carries the project today. It asks whether a model that uses only integers and small geometric moves can learn to read earlier text well enough to predict the next word. The rows below run from 13 October to 19 October 2026. None of them is a trained language result: the best trained discrete model gets the right next word first in 463 of 14,287 development rows, while a simple count table (T2) gets 6,300.

flowchart LR
  A["14 Oct<br/>A2 pilot: rank counts up,<br/>loss total up"] --> B["15 Oct<br/>Wider shortlist at test time<br/>fails: 2,400 vs 4,894"]
  B --> C["18 Oct<br/>Row-parallel scoring:<br/>about 56x faster"]
  C --> D["18 to 19 Oct<br/>Four K16 runs:<br/>no keep"]
  D --> E["19 Oct<br/>Address cells at zero training:<br/>1,351 vs 127 of 3,847"]
  E --> F["19 Oct<br/>A8 dose stopped at<br/>batch 4,096 for diagnosis"]

The turning points in the rows below. Each box is one or more rows; the numbers are in the table.

The longer story of this line is on its line page. The mechanisms involved are described in address cells, admission, rank margin and relation read.

Terms used in the table

  • DEV panel. The open development panel of 14,287 rows. Each row is a context and the true next token. P_succ (the copy-successor subset) is 3,847 of those rows; it is the subset where the answer follows an earlier occurrence of the same token.
  • Admission. The read can only choose among a shortlist of candidate cells (K of them, usually K=8). A row is admitted when the true next token's cell is on the shortlist. A token outside it can never be chosen, so admission is a ceiling on top-1.
  • Top-1 / top-8. The true token ranked first / within the first eight.
  • Batches. Training steps. A full registered dose is 16,404 batches.
  • FIT. An independent review of a run's pre-registration sheet before spending compute. A FIT releases nothing by itself.
  • Control (C-R1 to C-R6, V2 and the like). A check built to fail if the instrument is wrong. A passing control is not a model result.
  • Status words (positive, negative, diagnostic stop, blocked) are defined in the format page.

What the rows say, in plain terms

  • The integer path is built and its finite controls pass. Those are construction results, and they say nothing about language.
  • Training moves the rank counts up but has not yet beaten the context-free count table. The best trained result in the rows is 463 of 14,287, against 6,300 for T2 and 1,226 for the unigram table (CHARTER.md, section 4.8).
  • The main obstacle found so far is admission: a token outside the shortlist can never be chosen. Widening the shortlist at test time did not fix it (row of 15 October). Placing cells by address structure fixed it at the start (1,351 against 127 of 3,847), but training then pushed target cells out of the shortlist (the A8 row).
  • Six of the 30 rows are blocked by tooling or build faults and are not results about the model. The row-parallel kernel (about 56x faster proposals with identical losses) is the largest measured speed change.
  • The next step recorded in the A8 row is a choice among three diagnoses by the PM: an acceptance rule that refuses moves which eject a target cell, a per-checkpoint cell census, or a finer checkpoint cadence. Each new training run needs a reviewed sheet and a typed owner release.

Notebook: prime and zeta starting codebook (M1)

This notebook records tests of one idea: give every token a fixed starting vector built from numbers rather than from random noise. Each token gets a prime number by its rank, and the phases of the Riemann zeta zeros, read at the logarithm of that prime, turn the prime into an eight-dimensional integer vector. The one result so far shows that the vectors are distinct and the GPU code accepts them. It does not show that the vectors help the model read.

flowchart LR
  A["Token id v"] --> B["Prime by rank:<br/>p = prime number v+1"]
  B --> C["Zeta phases:<br/>gamma_k times ln p, mod 2 pi"]
  C --> D["Quantize to integers<br/>(29-bit phase, 30-bit unit vector)"]
  D --> E["Nearest E8 root cell,<br/>balanced over 256 cells"]
  E --> F["Integer codebook table<br/>read by the GPU model"]

How one token becomes one table row. The steps are the construction described in the record linked below; the table is built once, offline, on the host.

Background: primes and zeta explains the phases, and the prime-zeta codebook page gives the mechanism's status. The line page for the model that reads this table is discrete attention.

Host checks on macOS and Linux, then the GPU controls. No training.4,096 of 4,096 tokens get distinct vectors (0 collisions, 256 of 256 writer cells occupied); 17 of 17 base and 6 of 6 prime-zeta CUDA controls pass; 0 updates applied, 0 corpus rowsBit-exact table across seeds 0, 1 and 2; no floating-point instruction in the GPU code; 0 collisions over all 4,096 tokens; 17 of 17 base controls; the codebook must separate structurally from both nullspositive (construction only; the learned comparison against the nulls is deferred to a training sheet)prime-zeta-construction

What the row says, in plain terms

  • This is a measurement of a build, not of learning. Distinct vectors mean the table does not merge tokens. An earlier seeded table did merge them, and capped top-1 at 1,986 rows (k16-outcome-call).
  • Whether prime-zeta routing beats the permuted-prime null or the shifted-phase null on learned move selection or corpus loss is not tested. The pre-registration defers it to the first downstream training sheet, and training is held until the owner releases one.

Later use in another notebook

The prime-zeta table became the injective starting table (one distinct vector per token) in the discrete-attention runs of 19 October. Those results are rows in the discrete-attention notebook, not here: the injective table alone admitted 127 of 3,847 copy-successor rows, below its bar of 500 (injective-preflight-and-c2-qualify), and placing the cells by address structure raised that to 1,351 (address-cells-preflight).

Notebook: durable memory (M3)

This notebook tracks whether conversation can be stored so that it lasts across sessions and comes back exactly as it went in. The idea is to fold text into a deduplicated store of small records and rebuild the bytes from them, with a hash check that proves nothing changed. The one result so far is a tested piece of source code, not a memory that the model uses.

flowchart LR
  A["Source bytes"] --> B["Fold into small records<br/>(deduplicated, hashed)"]
  B --> C["Exact object store"]
  C --> D["Rebuild from records"]
  D --> E{"Same bytes and<br/>same whole-object hash?"}
  E -- yes --> F["Round trip holds"]
  E -- no --> G["Reject: nothing is published"]

The round-trip test behind the row below: rebuild(fold(bytes)) must return the original bytes, checked against a fresh SHA-256.

Background: the object store mechanism and exact memory.

The rules of the project, in plain language

UOR-R4 is trying to build a fast language model that runs on an ordinary laptop and does not use the expensive machinery inside today's chat AIs. A short rulebook, the charter, keeps every contributor pointed at that goal. This page explains what the charter says, why each rule exists, what the project's labs may and may not do, and who makes which decision. It is a guide to the charter, not a replacement: if the two ever disagree, the charter wins.

flowchart TD
  idea["Idea or experiment"] --> rules{"Inside the constraints?<br/>Geometry only, no squashing,<br/>no matmul"}
  rules -- "No" --> owner["Only the owner can<br/>change the charter"]
  rules -- "Yes" --> need{"Needs GPU training or evaluation,<br/>or will a milestone claim rest on it?"}
  need -- "No: builds, kernel tests,<br/>host checks" --> doit["Just do it"]
  need -- "Yes" --> sheet["Pre-registration: one-page sheet<br/>bar, noise, controls, seeds,<br/>cost, what each outcome decides"]
  sheet --> fit{"FIT review by someone<br/>other than the author"}
  fit -- "Not fit" --> sheet
  fit -- "FIT" --> release["Owner release:<br/>one per sheet, typed by Casey"]
  release --> run["Run on the GPU via uor-pod"]
  run --> row["Notebook row: date, what ran,<br/>number, bar, verdict, artifact"]
  doit --> row

How work moves from an idea to a recorded result. Only the Yes branch that needs GPU spend or a milestone claim goes through a sheet, a review and an owner release.

Why there are rules at all

The owner's stated goal behind every ban, in his own words from 18 October 2026, is "to ban expensive operations" and to optimise for "fast local ai that can train fast and run fast" and reaches "almost frontier level capability" (CHARTER.md §1, from decision D37). Each rule removes a cost that a dense neural network pays, or protects the evidence that tells the project whether its geometric replacement works. When a case is unclear, the charter says to choose what trains and serves fastest on a laptop through the geometric path, and to write the choice down.

The project's headline metric is tokens per second: how fast the model reads and writes text, with decode speed and context speed measured separately. A small quality gap is acceptable (CHARTER.md §1). The project is pre-alpha, 0 of its 8 milestones are complete, and no model holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS.md; see the mechanism board).

These are rules, so the labels "proof", "measurement" and "hypothesis" from docs/formal_vocabulary.md do not apply to them. The "why" given for each rule below is the reason the charter itself states. It is not a measured result.

The constraints and the reason for each

The charter's section 3 lists thirteen technical constraints. Here they are in everyday terms. Terms are defined in the glossary.

#RuleWhat it means in practiceWhy the charter gives
3.1Geometry onlyEvery mechanism, training signal and fix comes from the project's geometry (prime addresses, rotations, E8/H4 structures). The flock rule for attention looks at about 7 nearest neighbours, not a dense teacher.The bet is that geometry replaces expensive dense operations.
3.2No squashing functionsNo softmax, log-softmax, cross-entropy, softplus, sigmoid, tanh or GELU anywhere, including in losses, sampling and comparators, and including renamed or lookup-table versions.They are expensive and hide a dense global normalisation.
3.3No matrix multiplicationNo dense matmul in training, evaluation, tooling or serving, including wrappers and hand-written loops. A geometric feed-forward block is allowed; a dense MLP is not.Matmul is the cost the project exists to remove.
3.4Presence countsBanned code may not sit in any compiled or loaded module. NVRTC (runtime GPU compilation) is banned. The checks uor-harness ratchet d23 and d25 only ever tighten.Code that is present eventually runs.
3.5Research compute is GPU-onlyTraining, evaluation, qualification and reference runs use the GPU. Spend GPU only where a run can change a decision.Host runs gave wrong timing and wrong evidence, and the GPU is where the speed is.
3.6Serving is integer, on your deviceThe shipped model uses no float, transcendental, multiplier or integer-divide instruction. Running it on a laptop CPU, in a browser (WebAssembly) or on Apple silicon is allowed, and so is measuring its speed and energy. Panel scoring, qualification and milestone evaluation of an exported artifact remain GPU research compute; only product serving and measuring its tokens/s and energy run on client devices.The product is fast local AI on ordinary hardware.
3.7Float only offline, with an export gapFloat training is legal offline in a separately scanned module. Every float candidate reports how much accuracy it loses when exported to integers; a loss above the two-seed noise band disqualifies it.Float trains faster, but only the integer artifact ships.
3.8Zeta exceptionFloat is allowed for complex-plane zeta-zero parts and prime log-phases. Everything downstream is discrete.Zeta phases are complex numbers by nature.
3.9Efficiency is measuredReport sparse access, bytes per token, bounded candidates and exact memory together.Unmeasured efficiency is not efficiency.
3.10No neural comparisonsNo neural comparators, controls, teachers or graders until the owner says the model works end to end. Panels are graded by deterministic checks. The one exception is a one-time donor pass (D41) with binding conditions.A neural comparator would hide a dense model behind the geometry.
3.11Rust firstNew code is Rust, built on the uor-foundation crates. Python only where Rust cannot do the job.One fast, checked language keeps training and serving on one path.
3.12Exact identity stays separate from addressOne shared vector writer serves input, carry and output. Every artifact binds its data, seed, configuration and parameters.One representation avoids translation costs, and exact identity cannot be recovered from a geometric address.
3.13HygieneTyped errors instead of panics, no committed binaries, corpora or secrets, and API keys are never read or printed.It keeps the repository small and the keys out of it.

Source: CHARTER.md §3; the first column gives its clause numbers.

What labs may do, and what they may not

A lab is any contributor, human or AI, working under the charter. The rules in sections 3 and 5 give these limits.

Labs may:

  • Choose their own work from NOW.md, post a one-line intent note, claim a branch and carry on unless redirected (CHARTER.md §5.3).
  • Build, run finite kernel tests and run host checks without any pre-registration (§4.5).
  • Train in float offline once a sheet, FIT and typed release exist (training is currently held; §3.7, §4.5, §5.1), and report the export gap on the same evaluator.
  • Serve the integer model on a user's device and measure it (§3.6).
  • Review their own pull request at the exact head, from a fresh context (§5.5), and use a fresh-context subagent as the non-author FIT reviewer (§4.5).

Labs may not:

  • Use a banned operation anywhere, including in comparators, or in renamed form (§3.2, §3.3).
  • Run research compute on the CPU, or spend GPU on work that cannot change a decision (§3.5).
  • Start GPU training or a milestone-bearing run without a sheet, a FIT review and a typed owner release (§4.5, §5.1).
  • Use a neural comparator, teacher or grader, apart from the single D41 donor pass (§3.10).
  • Type an owner release themselves. Casey types it personally with UOR_LAB unset; labs only stage the commands (§5.1, from D40).
  • Cancel a healthy run because a self-set budget ran out, or touch another session's GPU or files (§5.4).
  • Stop a mechanism. That needs the owner (§4.1).
  • Delete research. Negatives, unique source and other labs' work go to the archive unchanged (§4.7).
  • Exceed 4 pods or $8 per hour across all labs (§5.4).

The project-manager seat (Kimi, with a cover lab named by the owner when Kimi is offline)The order of work. Keeps NOW.md with the roster. Operating notes may never contradict the charter.CHARTER.md §5.2
LabsWhich task to pick from NOW.md, how to implement it, and the exact-head review of pull requests.CHARTER.md §5.3, §5.5
SubagentsReviews, adversarial tests and research. They never make critical decisions: a change to a bar, a status, a constraint or a spend goes to the manager or the owner as a decision card.CHARTER.md §5.2

Two rules guard the owner's role. A pending owner question means wait. And Casey's own words beat any written acceptance text, with his directions recorded verbatim the same day (CHARTER.md §5.1). The training hold, the M2 hold and the Stage B hold remain until the owner releases them, and a passing FIT review releases none of them.

How evidence is judged

Section 4 of the charter is about not fooling ourselves.

  • A negative closes one configuration, never a mechanism. Mechanisms carry one of three statuses: ACTIVE (on the model path), READY (built and tested, not yet trained in) or PARKED (a tested form failed or broke a rule; the reopen conditions are listed). There is no "retired" status for a mechanism (§4.1). Rules can be retired; mechanisms cannot.
  • Instrument before verdict. If a check fails, first ask whether the measuring tool or the mechanism is at fault. A broken instrument is a fix, not a negative (§4.2).
  • Power. A decisive run uses at least 2 seeds or at least 200 fresh rows, with bars no narrower than the measured noise, and reports a fresh transfer number with every development gain (§4.3).
  • Controls and pivots. Compare against lawful non-neural baselines such as count tables. After three results on one line that do not move its headline number, write a pivot note: stop, or run one decisive experiment (§4.4).
  • Claims. Write "measured X on Y against Z". A test pass is not trained capability, and NOT_RUN is not a pass (§4.6).
  • The first-milestone closing bar. For milestone M1, the integer model's top-1 accuracy through the D11 export must beat both the unigram table (1,226 of 14,287) and the T2 successor table (6,300 of 14,287) on the same development panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported (§4.8).

Where each old decision went

Before 19 October 2026 the project's rules lived in 43 numbered decisions (D0 to D41, including a variant called D0-b) and in a long instruction file. The owner replaced them with one short charter. This page lists every decision and says what became of it: the rule lives on in a numbered charter clause, it was folded into a broader clause, or it is history only. Nothing was deleted. Every decision keeps its original heading in the live index, so old links still land, and the full original text is preserved unchanged in the archive.

flowchart LR
  old["Old decision<br/>D0 to D42"] --> q{"Does the rule still<br/>bind today?"}
  q -- "Yes, as written" --> kept["Kept<br/>own charter clause"]
  q -- "Yes, as part of a wider rule" --> merged["Merged<br/>into a broader clause"]
  q -- "No: superseded, one-off<br/>or expired" --> retired["Retired<br/>history only, in the archive"]

The three fates. "Retired" applies to rules only. A research mechanism is never retired; see the mechanism board and D22.

How to read the table

  • Kept means the decision survives with its meaning and has a home in the charter.
  • Merged means its content now lives inside a clause that also covers other decisions.
  • Retired means it no longer binds. It was superseded by a later decision, was a one-off order, or had a time limit that has passed. Its text stays in the archive.
  • Clause numbers such as 3.6 refer to sections of CHARTER.md. Section 1 is the mission, 2 the products, 3 the technical constraints, 4 the evidence rules, 5 the workflow and 6 the retired list.
  • The fate column follows the final DECISIONS.md index adopted with the charter (decision D42). It differs from the working rule map in one place: it files D14 as merged, because its owner boundaries and GitHub authority survive while its council is retired.

Change log for the project's rules

This is the dated record of every change to the project's rulebook, the charter. Only the owner changes the charter, and every change is written here as a new entry, newest first. If you want to know why a rule is the way it is, or when it last moved, start here. The log began on 19 October 2026 with the charter's adoption.

flowchart LR
  a["Old rules<br/>D0 to D41, AGENTS.md"] -- "19 Oct 2026<br/>checkpoint 1" --> b["CHARTER.md<br/>adopted"]
  b -- "owner changes only,<br/>one dated entry each" --> c["Next entry<br/>in this log"]

The charter replaced the older rules in one step on 19 October 2026. Later changes are added to this log as dated entries.

How an entry is written

An entry gives the date, what changed, which charter clauses it touches, and who decided. The owner's own words are recorded verbatim when they are the reason. Old text is never edited or deleted: it moves unchanged to the archive/ folder, and the live decision index keeps one line saying where each decision went (see the decision map).

20 October 2026: workspace reset

Decided by: the owner (Casey), in chat, on the workspace-reset review page. Source: docs/labs/workspace.md and archive/storage/README.md.

The owner approved four decisions. One line each, with the clause it touches:

  1. Results storage. iCloud UOR-R4/results/ and X10 Pro backup 2026-10-01/workspace/ (198 GB together) become a read-only cold archive with its index committed to GitHub in archive/storage/. All new results go to the private HF store caseyallard/uor-r4-store under results/<lab>/<topic-date>/, with a SHA256SUMS. (Clause 5.6.)
  2. One clone. One local clone, ~/uor-r4, with the owner checkout on clean main. Each lab works in ~/uor-r4/.worktrees/<lab>-<topic>, keeps scratch in ~/uor-r4/local/<lab>/<topic>/ and builds into ~/uor-r4/target/<lab>. Nothing project-related lives elsewhere on the laptop. After a task merges, upload what is worth keeping, then remove the worktree, the branch (both sides), the claim and the scratch. uor-hygiene runs after every merge. (Clause 5.9, new.)
  3. Branches. main, gh-pages and gh-pages-preview are long-lived and never deleted, and are listed in the registry docs/harness/branches.json. Every other branch is <lab>/<topic>, one per open PR, deleted after its merge. (Clause 5.5.)
  4. Freeze exception. The freeze on discretionary harness features is lifted for the hygiene tooling only, at the owner's request. The freeze is otherwise unchanged, and its wording in clause 5.3 is not edited. (Clause 5.3.)

19 October 2026: charter adopted at checkpoint 1

Decided by: the owner (Casey), in chat, at checkpoint 1 of the repository renormalisation. The charter replaces the stacked directions in AGENTS.md and decisions D0 to D41 as the project's rules (decision D42). Source: CHARTER.md, the final DECISIONS.md index, and the checkpoint notes in charter-diff-notes.md.

The owner answered eight questions. One line each, with the clause it changed:

  1. Client serving (Q1). D24's ban on CPU compute governs research compute only. Serving the exported D11 integer model on client devices (CPU, browser WebAssembly, Apple silicon), including measuring tokens per second and energy, is allowed. D36's "browser counts as CPU model compute" clause is replaced. (Clauses 3.5 and 3.6.) Panel scoring, qualification and milestone evaluation of an exported artifact remain GPU research compute; only product serving and measuring its tokens/s and energy run on client devices.
  2. Pre-registration (Q2). A one-page sheet with a non-author FIT review is needed only before GPU training or evaluation, and before any run a milestone claim rests on. A fresh-context subagent counts as non-author. Builds, finite kernel tests and host checks need none. (Clause 4.5.)
  3. Releases (Q3). One typed owner release per pre-registered sheet, covering its arms, seeds and stop rules. D40 is unchanged: Casey types it personally. (Clause 5.1.)
  4. Records (Q4). One notebook page per research line, with one row per result. Dated evidence folders exist only for sealed artifacts. NOW.md plus the notebooks replace current-state.md, and STATUS and ROADMAP change only with state. (Clause 5.6.)
  5. Coordination (Q5). The owner plus one project-manager seat (Kimi, with a cover lab named by the owner). Labs self-direct from NOW.md. The D14 three-seat council is retired, and operating notes may not contradict the charter. (Clauses 5.2 and 5.3.)
  6. First-milestone bar (Q6). For M1, bar (d) is replaced: integer top-1 through the D11 export must beat both the unigram table (1,226 of 14,287) and the T2 successor table (6,300 of 14,287) on the same development panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported. BPB (bits per byte) returns later as a bar once a lawful likelihood exists. Bars (a), (b), (c) and (e) are unchanged. (Clause 4.8.)
  7. Harness (Q7). The harness stays as a shared view with automatic presence and no manual heartbeat cadence. The merge queue serialises itself. The adopt_policy hold is dropped, and claims record the charter version. Discretionary harness features are frozen until a model beats both count tables; mandated Rust ports (D27) continue. (Clauses 5.3 and 5.5.)
  8. Legacy crates (Q8). The four older crates (uor-r4-graph-compiler, uor-r4-graph-certify, uor-r4-api, uor-r4-proof-model) and the root crate are repaired on the current core instead of archived. Repair restores the build only; their mechanisms stay PARKED. (Clause 2.4.) The draft had recommended archiving them; the owner chose repair.

Approved in the same session: archive everything byte-identical with nothing deleted; side projects under projects/; documentation as GitHub markdown plus an mdBook site with the Studio at /studio; the web client as a local in-browser WebAssembly integer model; the desktop client as a Tauri app (specification only); and D22 kept, so mechanism statuses are ACTIVE, READY and PARKED with no terminal state. Source: CHARTER.md and decision D42 in docs/integration/DECISIONS.md.

UOR-R4 Charter

Adopted 19 October 2026 by the owner (Casey), at checkpoint 1 of the repository renormalization; replaces the stacked directions formerly in AGENTS.md and D0–D41.

Old text moves byte-identical to archive/. Bracketed ids are sources.

1. Mission

Build the UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model: a fast language model that is not a transformer. It predicts text with geometry (prime addresses, zeta phases, E8/H4/icosian rotations, SpiralCore/FBS routing) and exact memory, on an ordinary laptop or in a browser. Conversation with durable memory first, then coding and reasoning, on one model [AGENTS:mode, D19, AGENTS:both-lines]. Pre-alpha; no capability is established.

The owner's rule: "USE GEOMETRY. THAT IS THE END OF IT. NEVER USE ANYTHING ELSE." [OWNER:0]

The owner's goal behind every ban (18 Oct, verbatim): "my goal with all of these bans is to ban expensive operations and to always optimize for what is best for the project goal... fast local ai that can train fast and run fast and reach almost frontier level capability ... we have so many mechanisms, at this point we just need to stitch the right ones together and optimize all of the things that aren't, which will likely be found in the details" [OWNER:26, D37]. When unclear, choose what trains and serves fastest locally on the geometric path, and write it down [D37:why-bans]. The lead metric is tokens per second (decode, and context separately); a small quality gap is acceptable [OWNER:5].

2. Products

  1. Model: the geometric model, exported as one D11 integer/table artifact; built in crates/uor-r4-discrete, served by crates/uor-r4-integer [AGENTS:ownership].
  2. Web client: the Studio at /studio on the mdBook site, running the integer model locally in the browser as WASM [renorm decision 7, D36].
  3. Desktop client: a Tauri app sharing the web UI, the native integer model with D19 memory, offline, on M1-class laptops; spec only [renorm decision 8].
  4. Legacy crates are repaired, not archived: uor-r4-graph-compiler, uor-r4-graph-certify, uor-r4-api, uor-r4-proof-model and the root crate are repaired to build on the current core; repairing restores the build only, and their mechanisms (r4g1-graph, native-geometric) stay PARKED. [D36, owner 19 Oct]

3. Technical constraints

  1. Geometry only. Every mechanism, training signal and fix comes from the project's geometry; keep R4/S3, Hopf and paired-H4/icosian roles distinct (E8 = H4 ⊕ φH4, fixed). Flock reads use local rules (~7 nearest neighbours), not a dense teacher. Why: the bet is that geometry replaces expensive dense operations. [OWNER:0, OWNER:6, D20, D32:hamming-one-factor, AGENTS:typed-geometry, AGENTS:e8-shorthand]
  2. No squashing functions. No softmax, log-softmax, cross-entropy (implicit softmax), softplus, sigmoid, tanh, GELU or normalized exponential, anywhere: runtime, losses, gradients, sampling, teachers, surrogates, comparators, including renamed or table forms. Why: they are expensive and hide a dense global normalization. [D23, D25, OWNER:1, HR:no-squash]
  3. No matmul. No dense matrix multiplication or GEMM anywhere: training, evaluation, instruments, serving and tooling, including wrappers and hand loops. A geometric feed-forward block (Hamilton gate and projections) is allowed; a dense MLP is not. Why: matmul is the cost the project exists to remove. [D25:no-matmul-anywhere, D30, OWNER:2, OWNER:14, HR:no-matmul]
  4. Presence counts. Banned code may not exist in any compiled or loaded module or vendor path; NVRTC is banned; CUDA is prebuilt by nvcc. Ahead-of-time nvcc kernel builds run on the GPU pod (authorized by D30); the laptop runs CPU-only builds and static checks. The ratchets uor-harness ratchet d23|d25 only go down. Why: code that is present eventually runs. [D29, R5, OWNER:no-nvrtc, HR:banned-module]
  5. Research compute is GPU-only. Training, evaluation, qualification, and model and parity reference execution run on the GPU; a host fallback is a defect to fix with a kernel. Spend GPU only where a run can change a decision. Why: host runs gave wrong timing and wrong evidence, and the GPU is where the speed is. [D24, OWNER:4, OWNER:20, HR:gpu-only]
  6. Serving is integer, on the user's device. The exported artifact has no float, transcendental, multiplier or integer-divide instruction (D11 R1–R5); the frozen runtime does no steady-state allocation, and a dense model disguised as lookup tables is excluded. Serving it on client devices (CPU, browser WASM, Apple silicon), including measuring tokens/s and energy, is the product and is allowed; D24 does not apply, and D36's browser-as-CPU clause is replaced. Panel scoring, qualification and milestone evaluation of an exported artifact remain GPU research compute (§3.5); only product serving, and measuring its tokens/s and energy, run on client devices. Why: the product is fast local AI on ordinary hardware. [D11, D36, D39:float-horizon, HR:serving-integer, AGENTS:frozen-tla; owner 19 Oct]
  7. Float only offline, with an export gap. Float forward, gradients and optimizers are legal offline, in a separately scanned module, never in the discrete crate. Every float candidate reports its export gap on the same evaluator; a gap above the two-seed noise band disqualifies it. The D32 discrete path stays active; its qualification uses exact arithmetic. Why: float trains faster; only the integer artifact ships. [D37, D39:export-gap, R13, HR:float-offline, KIMI:d37]
  8. Zeta exception. Float is allowed on the complex plane for zeta-zero parts, prime log-phases and the C4→R4/C8→R8 phase maps; everything downstream is discrete. Why: zeta phases are complex numbers by nature, and the bans target expensive operations, not geometry. [D32:zeta-exception]
  9. Efficiency is measured. Report sparse access, bytes/token, bounded candidates, multiplier-free kernels and exact memory together, naming D5-a (residency) or D5-b (per-token sparsity, the end state). Why: unmeasured efficiency is not efficiency. [I1-I5, D5, D38]
  10. No neural comparisons (comparators, controls, teachers, graders) until the owner says the model works end to end; panels are graded deterministically. Sole exception: D41's one-time distill-d1 donor pass, on its binding conditions: the student consumes hard targets only (no logits, probabilities or distributions), the donor never executes in student preparation, training, evaluation, serving, grading or any panel, a generation receipt is bound at generation, and a typed D40 owner release is required at dispatch. Why: a neural comparator would hide a dense model behind the geometry, against geometry only. [D28, OWNER:memory-no-transformer, D41]
  11. Rust first, building on the uor-foundation crates; Python only where Rust cannot; no ad-hoc scripts. Why: one fast, checked language keeps training and serving on the same geometric path. [D27, OWNER:20, HR:rust-default]
  12. Exact identity stays separate from geometric address; one shared vector writer serves input, carry and output; every artifact binds its data, seed, config, parameters and format. Why: one representation avoids translation costs, and exact identity cannot be recovered from a geometric address. [POLICY:shared-vectors, AGENTS:shared-vector, AGENTS:artifact-determinism]
  13. Hygiene: Result errors at library boundaries; no unwrap/expect/panic on recoverable paths; keep forbid(unsafe_code) in portable runtime and format crates; no committed binaries, corpora or secrets; never read or print API keys. Why: hygiene keeps the repository small and fast to clone, and keeps keys out of it. [AGENTS:errors, HR:no-artifacts, HR:no-credentials, AGENTS:no-keys]

4. Evidence

  1. A negative closes a configuration, never a mechanism. Mechanism statuses are ACTIVE (on the model path), READY (built and tested, not yet trained in) and PARKED (failed or broke a rule; reopen conditions listed). There is no terminal status. Stopping a mechanism needs the owner. [D22, D12, D2, POLICY:gates-promote, renorm decision 5]
  2. Instrument first. Classify a failing check as instrument or mechanism before calling anything; an instrument defect is a fix, never a negative. No target is set from a vacuous instrument; no single number rules out a line. [D31, R12, R14, D39:gcap]
  3. Power. Decisive runs use ≥ 2 seeds or ≥ 200 fresh rows, with bars no narrower than measured noise, the mechanism trained in, and a fresh transfer number with every development gain. [D22:power, D22:transfer, D17]
  4. Controls and progress. Compare against lawful non-neural baselines (count tables). After three results on a line that do not move its headline, write a pivot note: stop, or one decisive run. [D21, D6, D9, POLICY:progress-control]
  5. Pre-register only where it decides spend. A one-page sheet (bar, noise, controls, seeds, cost, what each outcome decides) with a non-author FIT review is required only before GPU training or evaluation, and before any run a milestone claim rests on. A fresh-context subagent counts as non-author. Builds, finite kernel tests and host checks need no sheet. Archived float sheets return only as new sheets with a fresh FIT. [R4, D37:archived-sheets, AGENTS:mech-briefs; owner 19 Oct]
  6. Claims. "Measured X on Y against Z"; label proof, measurement, hypothesis; NOT_RUN is not PASS; tests are not trained capability. [HR:claims, POLICY:evidence, AGENTS:invariant-formal, PROTO:status-vocab]
  7. Preserve. Nothing is deleted: negatives, unique source and other labs' work go to the archive byte-identical. [R6, HR:archive]
  8. M1 closing bar. Bar (d) is replaced, for M1: integer top-1 through the D11 export, on each of two seeds, beats both the unigram table (1,226/14,287) and the T2 successor table (6,300/14,287) on the same DEV panel, with tokens/s reported. BPB returns as a later milestone bar once a lawful likelihood exists. Bars (a), (b), (c) and (e) are unchanged. [D39, owner 19 Oct]

5. Workflow

  1. The owner decides this charter, §3, holds, spending caps, milestone bars and exceptions like D41. Training, M2 and Stage B stay HELD until released; a FIT releases nothing [AGENTS:holds-oct12, D37]. One typed owner release per pre-registered sheet covers all its arms, seeds and pre-registered stop rules. Casey types every release personally, with UOR_LAB unset; labs stage the commands [D40, R15; owner 19 Oct]. A pending owner question means wait; Casey's words beat written acceptance text; record directions verbatim the same day [OWNER:9, OWNER:10, OWNER:11].
  2. Coordination. GitHub main is the single source of truth [PROTO:github-authority]. The owner plus one PM seat: Kimi, with a cover lab named by the owner when Kimi is offline. Formal Vocabulary, Notation, and Claim Classes

  • Version: 0.1.35
  • Status: Normative for all new specification, plan, proof-model, and certificate text.
  • Source: docs/hologram_formal_analysis_direction.pdf §§1, 7, 13; tracker #122; issue #123.
  • Related: terminology for existing graph-compiler concepts lives in docs/transformerless/GLOSSARY.md; this document governs claim language and mathematical notation. Where the two overlap, this document wins for claim classification and the glossary wins for structural terms. The route-scope decision is ADR-0004, and current execution follows the native geometric AI policy. Geometric Intelligence Evaluation retains historical experiment protocols. A preserved #973 terminal contract is R4PredictiveBlockDeltaPromptCapacityV5.

Current authority (2026-09-05). This document governs claim language and typed mathematical distinctions. The project plan owns the goal, and current-state.md owns the implemented model and next work. Dated results and table cells naming a "current" reference, a parked operation or an unimplemented boundary retain their original artifact scope; they do not select a new task or prohibit a versioned native successor. Preserve their measurements without importing a reference model's capability or runtime guarantees into the active model.

This spec separates the statement classes that the research notes previously mixed — architectural definitions, compiler optimization objectives, empirical certification claims, and structural runtime guarantees — and fixes the symbols that recur across the compiler, artifact, certificate, and proof model.

1. Claim classes (role of a statement)

Every equation and every normative mathematical statement in repository documents MUST carry exactly one of these role labels, written inline in bold (**Definition**, **Objective**, **Guarantee**, **Assumption**, **Empirical Criterion**):

LabelMeaningWhere it may appear
DefinitionIntroduces an architectural object or mathematical term. True by convention; never "proven".Anywhere
ObjectiveA quantity the offline compiler attempts to optimize. Never a runtime invariant, never a theorem.Compiler-side docs/code only
GuaranteeA structural property of the compiled artifact or runtime. Requires a claim status from §2 and a proof artifact, witness, test, or explicit Unproven record.Artifact spec, runtime docs, proof model
AssumptionA condition a proof or certificate requires but the implementation does not itself establish.Proofs, certificates
Empirical CriterionA measured property with a declared distribution, protocol, sample count, and uncertainty. Never stated as a proof.Certificates, evaluation docs

Design aspirations are not theorems: an optimization target (arg max …) is an Objective, and a measured approximation (P_θ(a|c) ≈ P_θ(a|Z(c))) is an Empirical Criterion until the protocol behind it is declared.

2. Claim status (evidence behind a statement)

Every Guarantee and every Empirical Criterion MUST also carry one of these statuses. The statuses are the machine-readable vocabulary of the proof-status matrix (crates/uor-r4-proof-model/src/proof_matrix.rs); the mapping is normative.

StatusMeaningProofStatus mapping
StructuralEstablished by construction or by a named machine-checked test, fuzz target, or formal proof artifact that has actually run for the declared evidence.Verified
WitnessedEstablished per execution by a bounded, replayable witness an independent verifier replays without the teacher.Verified (witness path)
EmpiricalMeasured on a pinned corpus with protocol, confidence intervals, and provenance identifiers, per docs/transformerless/EQUIVALENCE_AND_EMPIRICAL_PROTOCOL.md.DifferentialPass
AssumedRequired by a proof or certificate but not established by the implementation.recorded as an assumption entry
UnprovenAsserted as a goal but currently without evidence.Unverified (blocks verify_all)

ExecutableSpec in the proof matrix means the obligation has a runnable specification but no activated binding check yet; documents must label such claims Unproven (or Assumed where applicable), never Structural.

2.1 Wording rule (automated check, dormant by default)

The prohibited phrases are "machine-verified", "machine verified", "exact equivalence", "exact teacher equivalence", and "provably equivalent". They are prohibited in normative documents (docs/**, crate READMEs) unless the same line links a proof artifact or certificate, or the phrase is explicitly disavowed on that line. The uor-r4-claim-wording gate enforces this when explicitly activated (see §6). The project does not claim exact teacher equivalence (disallowed per this rule), does not claim human-level reasoning, and does not treat plausible language output as evidence of coherent internal state transitions.

SDefinitionSemantic state space; every observation projects into a state s ∈ S. Regions are subsets R_i ⊆ S; beliefs are predicates over S; goals are desired subsets of S.Compiler/reference-only abstraction (issue #124). The deployed runtime carries a fixed-capacity approximation: the runtime state (frontier, rolling context code, token shortlist) in crates/uor-r4-core.
G = (V, E)DefinitionCompiled semantic graph: V packed semantic states, E typed transitions.crates/uor-r4-graph-format GraphView over the R4G1 NODE/EDGE sections (docs/transformerless/R4G1.md).
H(x)DefinitionHolographic encoding of observation x: a family of overlapping projections {h_0, …, h_k} with partial recoverability, distributed evidence, progressive fidelity. The deployed path today is still the single compiled Boolean semantic code; the certifier additionally defines and measures overlapping projection families for issue #126.Runtime binding: sign-bit signature path in crates/uor-r4-core (see "Semantic code H(x)" in the glossary). Measurement contract binding: crates/uor-r4-graph-certify/src/holographic_encoding.rs and its deterministic fixture tests.
T : S × A → SDefinitionTyped graph dynamics: transition function over states and actions/semantic operators A.Compiler/reference-only (issue #124). Deployed precursor: forward transition edges E_f / R4G1 ROUT section.
RDefinitionReconstruction / behavioral-recovery operator; R(H(x)) ≈ x read behaviorally as the divergence condition below.Compiler/certifier-only; exercised through the fidelity-certification harness (score.rs, Gate C).
C : Θ → GDefinitionThe compiler as a map from teacher parameter space Θ to the space of compiled artifacts. Compilation is lossy semantic compression: parameters → behavioral probing → latent graph induction → Boolean synthesis → packed immutable artifact.crates/uor-r4-core compiler pipeline; graph generalization in crates/uor-r4-graph-compiler.
P_θ(·‖c)DefinitionTeacher distribution over next tokens for context c, pinned HF revision, deterministic mode.TeacherOracle next-token surface (crates/uor-r4-core).
P_G(·‖H(x))DefinitionRuntime/graph distribution produced by the compiled artifact.Graph scorer (crates/uor-r4-core score.rs; R4G1 adapter src/r4g1.rs).
D(·, ·), εDefinitionDeclared divergence measure and empirical tolerance for the behavioral reconstruction condition (below).docs/transformerless/EQUIVALENCE_AND_EMPIRICAL_PROTOCOL.md.

Behavioral reconstruction condition (the testable form of R(H(x)) ≈ x):

Empirical Criterion. D(P_θ(· | x), P_G(· | H(x))) ≤ ε for a declared divergence D and tolerance ε, measured on a pinned held-out distribution with confidence intervals. Status: Empirical; never a structural claim.

4. Objectives versus runtime invariants

These are Objectives — quantities the offline compiler optimizes. They must never be stated as runtime properties:

QuantityRoleBinding
J = L_teacher + λ·C_runtime + μ·C_artifactObjectiveCompiler cost model: teacher behavioral loss, inference cost, artifact size/complexity (issue #129).
min_Z I(Z;X) − β·I(Z;Y_future)ObjectiveInformation-bottleneck compression target: discard surface detail, keep future-relevant information (issue #127).
H(A | R), H(S_future | R)ObjectivePredictive-entropy criteria for splitting, merging, or removing regions (issue #127).
π* = arg max_π [ V(G | T(B,π)) − P(C,π) − R(U,π) ]ObjectivePlan-ranking target for bounded future-state optimization (issue #131). Not a theorem.

These are Guarantees — structural properties of artifact and runtime, each with a proof-model entry. Their current statuses are the proof-matrix records; a document citing one MUST cite the same status:

GuaranteeStatusEvidence
Allocation freedom on the prediction hot pathStructuralallocation_proof counting-allocator harness; allocation_census.rs (proof matrix: PDF §16)
Bounded packed rangesStructuralrange_bounds_proof (Theorem 8)
Deterministic top-K (canonical tie-break)Structuraldeterministic_topk_proof (PDF §23)
Forward/reverse index consistencyStructuraltheorem7_proof (Theorem 7)
Score arithmetic safety (no overflow/panic)StructuralKani-1 harness (kani_proofs.rs)
Fixed-capacity container invariantsStructuralKani-2 harness (kani_proofs.rs)
Inference operation-set conformanceWitnessed (Structural after machine-code audit)INFERENCE_OPERATION_CONTRACT.md + P-4 source scans (transformerless/mod.rs)
Termination, bounded frontier width, valid references, canonical serialization, provenance completenessper proof matrixR4G1 two-stage validation + proof-model entries; anything lacking an executed evidence artifact is Unproven

5. Term discipline (overloaded words)

Avoid (unqualified)Use insteadRule
"intent"Future-state optimization: belief = estimated current state, goal = desired future-state subset G ⊆ S, constraint = forbidden subset F ⊆ S, action = transition operator, plan = bounded trajectory π = (a_0, …, a_n) with T^π(s_0) ∈ G and T^π_i(s_0) ∉ F for all intermediate i (Definition, PDF §12).Unqualified "intent" is informal prose; it must not appear in a labeled statement.
"semantic atom"Semantic region — multiresolution, overlapping, proof-addressable; explicitly not an atom (glossary)."Semantic atom" is prohibited in normative text.
"equivalence"Qualified forms only: byte reproducibility (identical pinned inputs ⇒ identical artifact bytes) or behavioral equivalence (an Empirical Criterion, valid only on the declared distribution, per the equivalence protocol).Unqualified "equivalence" is informal; "exact equivalence" hits the §2.1 wording rule.
"reasoning"Precise mechanisms: typed state transitions, graph navigation, bounded planning (trajectory evaluation over T).Bare "reasoning" is informal; plausible language output is never evidence of it (§2.1).
"transformerless"Zero source-attention calls and no dense full-prefix Q·K matrix/softmax kernel on the exact promoted decoder path; the replacement uses bounded geometric support shown load-bearing by disabled/permuted interventions.Does not imply multiplication-free, integer-only, allocation-free, coherent, or production-ready. Name retained source components and the checkpoint/scope.
"geometric intelligence"Name the measured mechanism: geometric support change, memory-causal logit effect, student-prefix rollout, or another declared empirical result.Geometry being present or visually structured is not evidence of intelligence.

Existing documents predate this convention. Their already-qualified uses ("behavioral equivalence", "not semantic atoms", "equivalence-tested") conform; unqualified uses are hereby marked informal and are migrated opportunistically, not by wholesale rewrite.

6. Enforcement

  • The uor-r4-claim-wording crate (Rust port of the retired scripts/check_claim_wording.py) scans docs/**/*.md and crate README.md files and fails on §2.1 violations. Run locally: cargo run -q --locked -p uor-r4-claim-wording -- ..
  • Current PR and merge-group CI run the focused native checks described by the execution policy. Four historical required statuses acknowledge compatibility only. Run the claim-wording script when changing claims; broader legacy release checks remain separately activated. Neither status names nor unrun jobs are evidence.
  • The proof-status matrix (proof_matrix.rs) is the machine-readable registry for §2 statuses; verify_all fails on any Unverified entry.

September 7 direction reconciliation: the product name is UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model. Read the canonical plan, current artifact/results, capability assessment and project map first. This document retains technical and dated experiment/reference material; earlier “active/next” sequences do not supersede those pointers. Native bounded inference and contextual/copy attention exist; general prose, general reasoning and frontier capability remain unqualified. Offline Rust training matmul is allowed; final serving has no matrix products or transformer backbone. No new model result was run for this documentation update.

For the current Rust model, use the CLI options and examples in the native geometric workflow. The explicit r4 geometric command family configures preparation, training, evaluation, generation and the local service; model context and operator settings travel with the artifact. The canonical plan owns architecture and budget policy, while current-state.md owns implementation status. Native options do not wait for a historical stage or later Rust port.

Retained compiler and reference configuration

The inventory below covers existing compiler/runtime and measurement lanes across earlier architectural eras. TLESS_*, R4G1_*, teacher and release variables apply to their named paths. Defaults for plain ask/chat, source tokenizers and older HTTP engines do not select the r4 geometric model. These references preserve compatibility and reproducibility; they do not reintroduce a Python model dependency or change the current project goal.

The listed environment variables give their defaults and owning modules. Where a listed CLI flag and variable both exist, the flag wins.

Legacy override contract. The capacity and sampling helpers (capacity_override_usize / capacity_override_f64) share one rule: unset is κ-neutral — behaviour is bit-identical to not setting it. Set-but-invalid, or zero, panics. A knob that silently did nothing would be indistinguishable from a knob that does not work, and both failures are invisible. Underscore separators are accepted (R4_GATE_C_SAMPLE=10_000).

Tokenizer adapter selection

Registered source tokenizers are selected by CLI/API fields, not environment variables. CLI commands that accept --source also accept the atomic pair --tokenizer-family FAMILY --tokenizer-version N. Both flags must be present or absent. When absent, discovery succeeds only when the source directory has one unambiguous supported definition; a directory containing both tokenizer.json and spiece.model requires the explicit pair. Unknown pairs and any attempt to combine a registered adapter with legacy --checkpoint input fail closed.

For raw SentencePiece sources, use family sentencepiece-unigram. Version 2 is the current, reference-correct adapter; automatic discovery of one unambiguous spiece.model selects it. Version 1 remains registered only as the immutable published behavior whose unknown id decodes to the literal model surface <unk>. N is part of the semantic identity, not a compatibility range: consumers do not substitute a newer or older version. Both versions read the pinned 32,000-piece spiece.model; neither applies the T5 Hugging Face wrapper's 100 sentinel tokens or EOS-appending post-processor.

The host adapter performs text normalization and encoding. The deployed tagged tokenizer.bin is decode-only and carries the complete adapter binding (family, version, source-model CID, and policy digest). Serving requires a matching host encoder for prompt text. Missing/mismatched identity, unavailable encode, invalid token ids, and decode failures are errors; an explicitly tagged tokenizer does not fall back to a legacy tokenizer. SentencePiece observation records have no original-source byte anchors because normalization and unknown collapse do not preserve a total input-offset map.

Normative deployed-quality evaluation (#933)

These knobs drive the teacher-free R4G1Runtime evaluator. Worker partitions are deterministic and reductions are replayed in canonical position order, so changing the worker count changes wall time but not report bytes. Once an evaluation phase launches it writes monotonic progress plus its phase terminal; a missing control, timeout, or absent identity is UNAVAILABLE/skipped and cannot authorize production.

R4_CERTIFY_R4G1_EVAL_BUDGET_SECSSample/census wall-clock budget3,600

The historical certify-C diagnostic above and this normative command share the two budget variable names but retain distinct defaults: 600 seconds for the non-binding diagnostic, 3,600 seconds for r4 deployed-quality. Explicit CLI flags override their environment variables.

Every invocation against a valid, non-symlink bundle root first creates evidence/deployed_quality_invocation_terminal.jsonl. The create-once JSONL journal is synced after its started row and again after exactly one completed, failed, or best-effort interrupted terminal row, so argument, bundle-discovery, cross-surface, witness, sample-gate, projection, and evaluator failures are all durable. A synced started row without a terminal row means the process was externally interrupted or otherwise unresolved; signals, power loss, and SIGKILL cannot be guaranteed to run cleanup code. An absent, symlinked, or non-directory bundle cannot safely host in-bundle evidence and therefore fails before journal creation. Reusing the same staged bundle is refused rather than overwriting its first invocation.

The invocation journal is local, non-semantic evidence. It is excluded from the generation CID, production admission, and release archives, as are the resource sidecar and terminal transcript described below. Phase progress and phase terminal files under graph/ remain authoritative only after that phase actually launches.

Production admission accepts only a schema-2 release-bundle.json whose component digests and compiler/selector identities reproduce from the loaded graph, teacher artifact, corpus pair, tokenizer, tokenizer adapter, score report, cover report, and deployed-quality report. A sampled report remains research evidence even when all measured rows are favorable.

The release CLI exposes the same contract directly. --mode full cannot bypass the cheap instrument: it first runs the exact 6,000-position prefix of the canonical label-free, story-distributed order on the same bundle/evidence generation. Any structural, reachability, non-futility, planted-control, cross-surface, or witness falsifier emits STOP: and returns without starting the census. PROCEED: launches the census. A typed INCONCLUSIVE: extends the same immutable nested order to 18,000 positions; if that interval still overlaps the gate, it can launch only the census and only when the measured reachable ceiling remains sufficient. Before any census launch, the authorizing stage's measured throughput is scaled to the full population; a projection beyond the configured evaluation budget or one hour refuses launch and requires a revised run contract. No sample report can authorize production admission.

cargo run --release -- deployed-quality \
  --bundle .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging \
  --compiler-revision <full-40-character-revision> \
  --mode sample --positions 6000 --workers 8

For a canonical run, wrap the command so host identity, effective workers, wall time, peak child RSS, free storage, bundle growth, exit status, and every graph evidence-file size are durable even when the evaluator fails. A create-once JSONL beside the summary samples the complete child process tree's CPU share, RSS, process count, host-memory headroom, and filesystem headroom every five seconds. The wrapped evaluator still streams its phase counters, throughput, and ETA. On the canonical macOS host, /usr/bin/script -e -F preserves that stream in a separate terminal transcript and propagates the child exit status; require a new transcript path before launch just as the wrapper requires a new sidecar. The resource summary, live-sample JSONL, and transcript are explicitly non-semantic and are never admission inputs. The inventory snapshot is captured when the child exits. If the live-sample JSONL is placed inside the bundle it is therefore present in that snapshot; the subsequently written resource summary and the outer transcript's final trailer are not. Both resource paths are append-only: the wrapper refuses to overwrite either one, and it verifies that its --bundle exactly matches the wrapped command's --bundle (evaluation) or --bundle-root (graph emission) before launch. It also records --workers or --jobs as the effective requested worker count. Use --samples-output to select the JSONL path; otherwise it is <output>.samples.jsonl.

test ! -e .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging/graph/deployed_quality_full.log
/usr/bin/script -q -e -F .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging/graph/deployed_quality_full.log \
  python3 scripts/run_deployed_quality.py \
  --bundle .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging \
  --output .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging/graph/deployed_quality_full_resources.json \
  -- target/release/r4 deployed-quality \
  --bundle .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging \
  --compiler-revision <full-40-character-revision> \
  --mode full --positions 6000 --workers 8

Teacher-parity controls govern host-side verification only and do not enter artifact identities or deployed serving. S private sequence states must share one immutable weight allocation and advance in one physical exact batch; the one W-thread pool must schedule disjoint output rows without nested oversubscription. Every output row must keep the pinned uor-matmul dot reduction intact; splitting or reassociating the reduction dimension is not permitted. Results return to canonical prompt/position order before metrics are reduced.

The 36 logical teacher-forced positions are executed once in six physical batches with registered widths 8, 8, 8, 7, 4, 1. That transcript retains each canonical lane at its distinct final teacher-forced prompt prefix (lengths 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4 for the pinned tokenizer), rather than truncating different prompts to a colliding common prefix. S4 clones the templates, appends the already-computed teacher next token to each logical seed, and times only new causal continuation steps. Exact batches carry the per-lane sequence positions explicitly, so variable histories do not serialize the cohort. There is no duplicate live-teacher prefill and no independent full-model S4 warm-up. Preparation, decode, and one-shot elapsed time remain separate evidence fields.

Before measurement, the harness reserves the bounded model-wide batch buffers, exact input/output transpose buffers, and one exact scratch slot per dedicated worker, then exercises the worker pool/backend with a tiny known product. Its elapsed time, retained capacity, capacity-growth event count, and actual added capacity bytes are recorded as excluded preparation. Measurement counters are reset without discarding those buffers. Every transcript and S4 physical forward must subsequently report zero workspace-growth events and bytes; otherwise the run fails rather than presenting allocation churn as steady-state throughput.

Conditional source, artifact, store, graph, tokenizer, or corpus evidence is reported as AVAILABLE, UNAVAILABLE, FAILED, or NOT_RUN. An absent fixture is never a parity PASS merely because the enclosing test executable returns success. The progress/event/report schema and the launch gate are specified in the #932 run record.

The durable artifact set is:

ArtifactSchema idDefault pathRole

For uor-r4.exact-multicore-probe/2, probe_deadline_policy means that no new exact forward is admitted after 3,600 seconds; an already-active fixture load or exact forward may finish, then the probe records ABORTED, and elapsed time at or beyond the deadline cannot qualify. The report's required events object binds the sibling file_name, full-byte content_cid, byte_len, record_count, final_record_number, final_event, final_status, final_qualifies_full_run, and non-cyclic report_body_cid. FINAL is synchronized before the report is atomically committed, carries sequence == final_record_number == record_count, and must be the last JSONL record. Admission validates the current sidecar before teacher weights load; missing, truncated, appended, or tampered bytes refuse the run.

Schema /1 bytes describe the superseded fixed-sweep design and remain historical evidence. Schema /2 binds the adaptive candidate set, fastest-exact selection policy, and the complete registered admission shape: 36 transcript logical forwards in batch widths 8, 8, 8, 7, 4, 1; eight continuation tokens across eight lanes; 100 logical forwards in 14 physical shared-weight batches; zero-based maximum sequence position 13; and private-state capacity 14. A smaller operator cap may produce diagnostic evidence but cannot qualify the binding suite. reference_workers names the first measured exact candidate, equal_to_reference binds every candidate's raw trace to it, and the cheap worker-pool/backend prestart is recorded separately and excluded from timed forward rates. CPU and RSS fields are diagnostics: they must be structurally valid and truthful, but a platform-reported UNAVAILABLE value does not by itself refuse exact admission. A later change to field meaning, type, requiredness, units, or artifact partition requires another schema id rather than reinterpreting an existing record.

Served model identity (#655-F)

The canonical served model id on every serving surface (OpenAI /v1 routes, native /api/chat, WS, WASM) is r4. Requests may omit model, send r4, or send the deprecated pre-flip alias uor-r4 (accepted for a compatibility window); responses and /v1/models always report r4, and OpenAI wire ids are r4-prefixed (chatcmpl-r4-…, resp-r4-…, msg-r4-…, system_fingerprint: r4-{mode}). The CLI client subcommand's --model default is r4. Per-bundle logical/physical names are metadata (/uor/v1/status), not the served identity. Engine/tier names (r4g1, …) are unrelated to the model id and unchanged.
