Managed source-execution-era resolver (2026-08-15)

-attention-v2 and -attention-v2-dense-v2 are reserved physical-root suffixes; downloaded source basenames ending in either are refused before mutation. Suffix stripping uses longest match. The base and exact-suffix reload names are aliases for one logical model, attach to sources/<logical-name>/, and report the selected physical root plus optional attention/dense records. A missing source is allowed for the #718 decode-only path; a present-invalid source is terminal.

Every managed operation inspects all three roots before choosing one. A malformed/nonregular binding, an unbound populated suffix, a future version, an impossible attention+dense pair, duplicate semantic identities, or an unfinished lower-precedence identity is terminal and byte-preserving. Current startup/reload also requires the canonical corpus pair and graph-cover/cover_report.json to carry the same registry-exact execution pair as the root sidecars. Historical v1 and dense absence remain readable where documented. These checks reconcile metadata. The cover-graph PROV/1 byte section itself landed with #637 phase 3 (PR #738): cover now emits a PROV/1 section unconditionally (a deliberately-empty record when no identity flags are supplied).

Normative Specification: Canonical Artifact Byte Equality Under Compiler Parallelism

Preserved graph-artifact contract. The byte-equality rules below remain normative for their named TLA/R4G1 artifacts. New route manifests have their own identity contract under #961; this document does not establish geometric attention or chat. See the Geometric Intelligence Programme.

Version: 0.1.0
Status: Normative Specification
Issue: #167
Parent: #122
Depends On: #165 (Deterministic Compiler Executor), #166 (Compiler Stage Ownership & Parallelization DAG)
Normative Invariant Source: R4G1.md §7 (D2: "identical graph content + format version ⇒ identical bytes", Gate E), plan §4.1, AGENTS.md determinism invariant

1. Primary Invariant Statement

Normative Invariant (verbatim): Parallel execution may change compilation time, but must not change the canonical graph artifact produced from the same pinned inputs, compiler version, configuration, and target-independent compilation mode.

All R4 compiler pipeline stages (whether Parallel-Safe, Parallel with Deterministic Merge, Bounded Parallel, or Sequential Canonical Finalization) must conform to this invariant.

2. Required Execution & Reduction Mechanisms

To enforce strict byte-identical canonical outputs across sequential and parallel multicore executions, the R4 graph compiler mandates the following mechanisms:

  1. Stable Input Ordering & Shard Numbering:

    • Observations, traces, and samples are partitioned into deterministic shards based strictly on content-addressed IDs or stable positional indices.
    • Dynamic worker scheduling order or thread dispatch timing must never dictate shard numbering.

  2. Stable Candidate Ordering & Tie-Breaking:

    • At every candidate selection point (e.g., region induction, XOR-polynomial candidate ranking, routing program selection), tie-breaking must follow a deterministic total order.
    • For candidate scores, ties are broken strictly by candidate ID / content hash (ScoreQ fixed-point score descending, then candidate ID ascending).

  3. Deterministic Reductions & Sorting:

    • Parallel map-reduce operations must partition reductions by content-addressed key and perform deterministic ordered merges.
    • All canonical outputs (nodes, edges, regions, certificates) must undergo stable canonical sorting prior to binary encoding into R4G1 format.

  4. Floating-Point & Summation Policy:

    • Order-sensitive floating-point parallel reductions are strictly forbidden for canonical output calculations.
    • Compiler stages computing canonical graph quantities must use fixed-order summation or integer/fixed-point accumulator types (ScoreQ, saturating integer arithmetic).
    • Compiler-internal float heuristics (e.g., loss diagnostics) may use floating-point operations provided canonical topology, IDs, offsets, and binary payload bytes do not depend on summation order.

  5. Random-Seed Policy:

    • All pseudo-random processes (such as clustering initialization or randomized graph exploration) must consume pinned random seeds recorded in the compile report.
    • Seed generation and PRNG state transitions must be positionally deterministic and independent of thread scheduling or multicore worker counts.

  6. Thread-Count Invariance:

    • The compiled graph topology, node/edge IDs, section offsets, payload bytes, content CIDs, and performance/verification certificates must be 100% bit-identical across any thread count \(N \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\}\).

3. Forbidden Nondeterministic Patterns

The following implementation patterns are explicitly forbidden within the R4 graph compiler pipeline:

  • Forbidden Pattern 1: Assigning canonical node or edge IDs during unordered parallel discovery.
  • Forbidden Pattern 2: Using thread completion order or worker arrival sequence as semantic ordering.
  • Forbidden Pattern 3: Mutating or appending to shared global graph data structures from parallel worker threads.
  • Forbidden Pattern 4: Iterating over non-deterministic hash map key orders to emit canonical output structures.
  • Forbidden Pattern 5: Order-sensitive floating-point parallel reductions feeding canonical graph attributes.
  • Forbidden Pattern 6: First-finished-candidate-wins race conditions in candidate selection.

4. Verification Harness & Compliance

The compiler crate (uor-r4-graph-compiler::reproducibility) provides ParallelReproducibilityHarness. The harness executes:

\[\text{Harness}(\text{inputs}) \implies \text{Artifact}_{\text{seq}} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=1} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=2} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=4} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=\text{max}}\]

The harness asserts:

  1. ArtifactBytes(seq) == ArtifactBytes(par, N) (100% byte equality)
  2. Digest(ArtifactBytes(seq)) == Digest(ArtifactBytes(par, N)) (BLAKE3 digest parity)

The proof model (uor-r4-proof-model::structural_guarantees) currently provides an executable-spec check via verify_parallel_reproducibility_compliance; end-to-end compiler artifact-byte parity remains validated by compiler-path tests.

5. Traceability & Claim Classification

  • Formal Claim Classification: Canonicalization and deterministic output under parallelism is a Guarantee with Structural proof status (harness-backed).
  • CPU Portability: Reproducibility is strictly CPU-native and GPU-free (zero CUDA, OpenCL, Metal, WebGPU, BLAS, or hardware vendor dependencies).

Minimalist R⁴ Terminal Client & Local Vendor API

Preserved interface reference: this page documents the existing terminal client, launcher, and HTTP surfaces from the TLA/R4G1 serving era. It does not show that the route-native geometric-intelligence programme can answer a prompt. There is no working source-free geometric chat path yet; #961 -> #952 -> #953 must establish lexical state, recursive attention, and generation before this interface can carry that claim. The interface exposes r4 client plus vendor-shaped endpoints such as POST /v1/chat/completions, GET /v1/models, and GET /uor/v1/status. Provider, engine, and multiplication-free claims apply only to the exact legacy execution tier and artifact selected for a request; the existence of the endpoint is not evidence about which mechanism produced its response.

1. Single-Command Launcher (./r4-app.sh)

The simplest way to run R⁴ interactively is with the zero-dependency ./r4-app.sh launcher:

./r4-app.sh

  3. Background Server: Launches r4 serve in the background on port 8000 (or $PORT).
  4. Interactive Client: Automatically opens the interactive client once ready.
  5. Signal Cleanup: Traps EXIT, INT (Ctrl-C), TERM, HUP (window close), and QUIT (Ctrl-\) signals to cleanly terminate the background server process.

Release pipeline (#741)

Paused, 19 October 2026: .github/workflows/release.yml skips all three jobs. The legacy-crate repair restored the compliant library surfaces of the graph and root packages, but neither release asset can be built under the D23/D25/D29/D30 bans. The r4 CLI serves R4G1 through the retired transformerless compiler/runtime and the source-backed teacher, and the wasm frontend is the R4G1 browser engine D36 already paused. The commands below (r4 package-release-bundle, r4 install-release) are therefore not built. The M8 rewrite for a D11 served artifact (UORLUT01) re-enables the pipeline.

Preserved runtime reference: this pipeline packages the existing TLA/R4G1 frontends and bundle contracts. It is not the release pipeline for a route-native geometric-intelligence product, and a successful legacy release does not establish source-free attention, generation, correctness, or chat. Current product sequencing is defined by the Geometric Intelligence Programme.

Adopted by maintainer decision on 2026-08-19 (recorded on #741/#655): the "package + build release pipeline now" option — both frontends, a GitHub Release as the distribution artifact, an explicit verified fetch command, and a versioning convention that binds each tag to its exact code and bundle identity. This pipeline publishes nothing by itself: every piece below is inert until the maintainer pushes a v* tag, and even then the release starts as a draft that only the maintainer publishes.

Versioning convention

A release tag vX.Y binds, in one auditable place:

  • code identity — the tag's commit SHA (in the release notes and on the tag itself);
  • contract identity — the inference-contract version from docs/inference_contract.md (in the release notes);
  • bundle identity — the blake3 component digests (normative graph, sections-absent and label-shuffled control graphs, signature artifact, plain-TLA comparator store, tokenizer, score/compile reports, normative deployed-quality report, raw cross-surface parity evidence, and raw witness replay) declared by the attached schema-2 release-bundle.json. The quality report in turn content-binds the corpus pair, tokenizer adapter, compiler revision/configuration, selector semantics, held-out partition, controls, raw parity/replay evidence, and exact production decode profile. Schema-1 manifests remain readable only as historical research evidence and cannot authorize serving.

A tag with no bundle assets attached is a code-only release; the verified fetch command simply reports the missing asset.

What the tag triggers (.github/workflows/release.yml)

Pushing vX.Y creates a draft release and attaches both frontends:

  • r4-vX.Y-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz — native CLI, linux;
  • r4-vX.Y-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz — native CLI, macOS arm64;
  • r4-wasm-vX.Y.tar.gz — the wasm frontend (wasm-pack build, the same build the Pages deploy runs);
  • a .sha256 beside each.

CI cannot compile the model (hours of teacher-bound compute against a pinned snapshot), so the model bundle is attached by the maintainer:

Maintainer steps to cut a release

  1. Pick the bundle (current candidate per the decision record: the smollm2-360m-broad compile) and package its sidecar:

    r4 package-release-bundle \
  --compiled .uor-models/compiled/<name> \
  --model-id r4 --capability instruction-chat \
  --source .uor-models/sources/<source> \
  --tokenizer-family hf-byte-bpe --tokenizer-version 1 \
  --compiler-revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"

  2. Archive exactly the attested component files (the packaged layout — nothing else; r4 install-release refuses archives carrying any unattested entry). Local invocation journals, resource sidecars, and terminal transcripts are operational evidence and are deliberately not packaged:

    cd .uor-models/compiled/<name>
tar -czf /tmp/release-bundle.tar.gz \
  graph/score.r4g1 graph/score_sections_absent.r4g1 \
  graph/score_label_shuffled.r4g1 tless_artifacts.bin tless_store.bin \
  tokenizer.bin \
  graph/score_report.json graph/deployed_quality_report.json \
  graph/cross_surface_parity.json graph/witness_replay.json \
  graph-cover/cover_report.json corpus.meta corpus.records \
  tokenizer_adapter.json

  3. Tag and push: git tag vX.Y && git push origin vX.Y — the workflow drafts the release and attaches the frontend builds.

  4. Attach the bundle and publish:

    gh release upload vX.Y /tmp/release-bundle.tar.gz \
  .uor-models/compiled/<name>/release-bundle.json
gh release edit vX.Y --draft=false

The explicit verified fetch

r4 install-release --tag vX.Y            # from UOR-Foundation/uor-r4
r4 install-release --tag vX.Y --repo owner/name --name custom-install

install-release (src/release_install.rs) downloads the two bundle assets, requires exactly the schema-2 production inventory above, hard-verifies every manifest component digest, and independently reproduces the deployed-quality bindings from the extracted graph, teacher artifact, exact plain-TLA comparator store, corpus, tokenizer, adapter, reports, both planted control graphs, raw cross-surface rows, and independently replayed witness rows. It refuses unknown files, symlinks, missing/tampered raw evidence, legacy/sample/off-serving evidence, or any identity mismatch, never overwrites an existing install, and only then moves the bundle into .uor-models/compiled/<name>. A failure at any step installs nothing. The fetch is always explicit: no serving path, first request, or setup step triggers it — exactly #655's "first request must not silently download" scope line.

What this pipeline deliberately does not do

  • It does not flip any serving default or canonical model identity — that is #655-F, separately gated on its own preconditions and a fresh maintainer sign-off.
  • It does not auto-publish: drafts require the maintainer.
  • It does not compile models in CI.

Side projects

This folder holds research projects that are related to UOR-R4 but are not part of the language model. Some feed ideas into the model (the model's prime and zeta-zero geometry draws on one of them). Others, like a network transport or a Lean proof of a matrix kernel, run alongside it. None of them is on the model's training or serving path, and none of them is evidence that the model works. The model itself is pre-alpha: 0 of 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS.md).

The seven projects and where each connects to the model. Solid boxes keep their source in git. Dashed arrows into the model mean consulted or drawn on; the dashed arrow to the cylinder points to the large originals kept outside git.

Why these projects live in this repository

The owner decided (19 October 2026) that side projects stay in this repository under projects/, with one README each, rather than moving to separate repositories. Two reasons follow from that decision. First, the history of the model cannot be read without them: the model's prime-routing and zeta-phase ideas draw on the Prime Analysis program, and the SpiralCore references were consulted when the SpiralCore/FBS mechanism was designed (the mechanism itself follows a separate v63 reference and a hosted v69 file; see the mechanism page). Second, most of this material existed only on one laptop, with no version control and no remote. Putting the source in git and the bulky files in a checksummed store fixes that.

Three rules keep the side projects from being mistaken for model results:

  1. Nothing here changes the model's status. A proof scaffold, a transport benchmark or a Python probe is not a trained capability. See the claim rules in docs/formal_vocabulary.md.
  2. Old claims keep their original scope. Files imported from the owner's earlier workspaces carry labels such as "canonical" that applied to their own old repository, not to this one.
  3. Source goes to git, bulk goes to the store. Code, Lean files, LaTeX and short notes come into the project folder. Images, PDFs, corpora and run outputs stay in the private store and are checked by hash.

Until 20 October 2026 the owner's laptop kept working copies of these projects in a gitignored research/ folder at the top of the repository. That folder is retired. The source is here, and the full tree is in the private store under research-archive/2026-10-19/, which was checked file by file against the laptop copy on 20 October. The folder's old README is kept in archive/research-root-README.md.

MSA: Modular Structural Arithmetic

Modular Structural Arithmetic (MSA) is a small formal system for arithmetic with a few special numbers in it. It was written by Alex, a collaborator, and given to this project with his consent as source reading. The folder holds two short papers and nothing else: no code, no data, no experiments. It is a third-party idea that earlier route-attention and selector work in this repository pointed to. It is not part of the language model, and no result here measures anything about the model.

flowchart LR
    G["gamma = 24, the generator"] -- "doubling" --> M["mu = 48, the mediator"]
    M -- "doubling" --> E["epsilon = 96, the manifestation"]
    G -. "mu x mu = gamma x epsilon = 2304" .- E
    E --> P["Reduce modulo a prime p: do the roles and doublings survive?"]

The three constants of Structural Arithmetic and the question Modular Structural Arithmetic asks about them.

What the papers contain

Structural Arithmetic (SA), 10 pages. SA starts from ordinary arithmetic (Peano-style axioms for successor, addition and multiplication) and adds three named constants: \(\gamma=24\) (the generator), \(\mu=48\) (the mediator) and \(\varepsilon=96\) (the manifestation). Each doubles into the next, \(\delta(\gamma)=\mu\) and \(\delta(\mu)=\varepsilon\), which the paper calls the doubling cascade. It also states the "fundamental equation" \(\mu\times\mu=\gamma\times\varepsilon\). Numbers are classed by role as generators, mediators or manifestations, with axioms about how the roles are closed under operations such as greatest common divisor and least common multiple, and an induction schema over the structures built this way.

Modular Structural Arithmetic (MSA), 6 pages. MSA is described as a conservative extension of SA: it adds reduction modulo a number \(p\) and asks which moduli keep the structure intact. Three predicates carry the idea:

  • \(\mathrm{DP}(p)\), doubling-preserving: the reduced doubled constant equals the doubled residue, with no second reduction (for example mod 7 it fails: \(2\times6=12\) is not 5).
  • \(\mathrm{RP}(p)\), role-preserving: the three constants stay distinct mod \(p\).
  • \(\mathrm{SP}(p)\), structural-preserving: both of the above.

The paper then states special cases as axioms. For example, mod 11 the constants become 2, 4 and 8 (the "11-theorem"), and mod 7 they become 3, 6 and 5, which sum to a multiple of 7 (the "7-vanishing"). It also axiomatizes a "modular resonance" and a resonance period.

Checks anyone can do by hand (proof, by arithmetic). \(48^2=2304=24\times96\); \(24,48,96 \bmod 11 = 2,4,8\); \(24,48,96 \bmod 7 = 3,6,5\) and \(24+48+96=168=7\times24\). These confirm the numerical facts the axioms state. They do not show that the axiom system is consistent or that its larger claims, such as the characterization of doubling-preserving primes (axiom MSA9), hold; the papers present these as axioms, and this page has not checked that they follow from the others.

Why it is here

The repository's earlier route-attention and selector work referenced MSA as part of a modular-structure research direction (research/msa/README.md). This page claims no tie to the model's geometry, and none has been tested. Any such link would be a hypothesis needing its own experiment.

Prime Analysis: the Prime Phase and Chebyshev psi spectral program

Prime numbers look random, but their running count wobbles around a smooth curve in a way that has long been tied to the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. This project asked whether that wobble (the Chebyshev residual \(\psi(x)-x\)) carries a structure that can be recovered and used to predict where primes fall. It is a pile of research notes, slide decks, simulations and scripts. Its own README calls it a late, concluding collection of the prime-router studies; the ancestry runs from the AI-Research workspace to a Python prime router, to this program, to the Rust model. The model's ideas about prime addresses and zeta phases draw on it. It is not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and not evidence that the language model works.

flowchart LR
    A["Primes up to x"] --> B["Residual: psi of x minus x"]
    B --> C["Detrend, resample on a log grid"]
    C --> D["Hilbert transform: phase of the signal"]
    D --> E["Look for stable frequencies and compare with zeta zeros"]
    E --> F["Time-ordered 70/30 split: predict the held-out part"]
    E -.-> G["Idea the model draws on: prime log-phases and zeta zeros as fixed phases"]

The program's pipeline as its own notes describe it. The dashed arrow is a transfer of an idea, not a transfer of a result.

The question and the method

Let \(\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\) be the Chebyshev function, where \(\Lambda\) is the von Mangoldt function. The explicit formula writes the residual as a sum over the non-trivial zeros \(\rho=\tfrac12+i\gamma\) of the zeta function:

\[\psi(x)-x \;=\; -\sum_{\rho}\frac{x^{\rho}}{\rho}\;+\;\text{small terms}.\]

Each zero contributes an oscillation whose frequency is set by \(\gamma\). The program treats the residual as a signal and asks whether those oscillations can be seen and extrapolated. The notes describe a fixed ("fingerprint-locked") pipeline: causal detrending (no use of future data), resampling on a uniform log grid, analytic phase through a Hilbert transform, and time-ordered 70% train / 30% test splits so that prediction is judged out of sample.

The program also developed a geometric side: the R4 Prime Router, Hopf-base sector discretization, and an H4 x H4 coupled field. Those briefings are one source of the model's prime-routing language.

Riemann-Lean: a Lean 4 scaffold for a prime-number proof chain

This project is an attempt to write a proof about prime numbers in a proof assistant called Lean 4, where a computer checks every step. The goal was to connect how primes are spread out to the Riemann hypothesis, a famous open problem about the zeros of the zeta function. The result is a scaffold: a chain of statements with the pieces needed to prove them, plus 185 Python scripts that probe whether the needed inequalities hold. The Riemann hypothesis is not proved here, and nothing in this folder is evidence about the language model.

flowchart TD
    P["Python probes: a1 to a4, o1 to o5, k1, tau12, fixed_error_psi"] --> C["Constants and majorant checks"]
    C --> L["Lean files: PrimeRiemannBridge spine, 17 files (plus 6 scratch probes)"]
    L --> T["Theorem chain: O1 to O5, L1 to L3"]
    X["Pinned in lake-manifest.json: mathlib and its own dependencies, Lean v4.28.0"] --> L
    T -.-> G["Goal: bridge to the Riemann hypothesis, not reached"]

Probes feed constants into the Lean spine. Mathlib is pinned, not copied; the project README also names Lean-RH, PhysLean, Carleson and PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, which are not pinned and not imported. The last arrow is the goal, not a result.

What is in the project

  • formal/lean/: the PrimeRiemannBridge theorem spine. The folder holds 23 .lean files: 17 spine files plus 6 small scratch probes (dot-prefixed .codex_* files, a few lines each). The project README states no axioms; a search of the 23 files finds no axiom declaration (two comment lines only). It comes with lakefile.toml (which requires only mathlib), lake-manifest.json (mathlib and its transitive packages), a Lean v4.28.0 lean-toolchain, and three verification scripts.
  • 185 Python scripts at the top level: probes, ledgers, majorant checkers and proof-obligation tooling, grouped by prefix (a1 to a4, o1 to o5, k1, tau12, fixed_error_psi, spinning_top, build_*).
  • data/: reference data (19 JSON files: 12 arXiv listings and 7 zeta-zero tables from LMFDB and Odlyzko; sizes not re-checked here).

A "majorant" is an upper bound that dominates the quantity being studied; most scripts check numerically that such a bound holds in a range, or turn a bound into a constant for the Lean files. A numerical check in a range is not a proof for all numbers.

Casey Allard started this as a standalone local project. It was never part of the AI-Research or Prime-Analysis repositories (research/riemann-lean/README.md). The external Lean dependencies are fetched with lake exe cache get or lake update; their sources are not stored here because they are third-party, large and regenerable.

Relationship to Prime Analysis

The prime-analysis/ project holds a folder named formal-math-lean, which contains 185 Python files. Comparing the two trees byte by byte shows all 185 are identical to the ones here (measurement, checked on the local copies on 19 October 2026). The folder in Prime Analysis contains no .lean files. So this project is the canonical home of the Lean spine and of the probe scripts, and the Prime Analysis copy is a duplicate to be recorded, not imported twice. Which of the two the owner wants as canonical is an open decision; the inventory favours this one because it is small and holds the Lean source.

SpiralCore: networking protocols and compression

SpiralCore is a set of geometry ideas (by Matthew) that the language model borrows: a fixed graph of rotations in eight dimensions, with exact bookkeeping of the path taken between two points. This project poses a different question about the same family of ideas: could they help move and shrink data across a network? That question is posed here, not yet tested: the code that exists uses plain zlib framing with no SpiralCore routing. The folder also keeps two SpiralCore references. It is a side project. It is not wired into the model's training or serving, and nothing here is evidence that the model works.

flowchart LR
    A["App or unmodified program"] --> B["Wire layer: UORADP01 framing, zlib or raw per direction"]
    B --> C["Network"]
    C --> D["Wire layer at the far end"]
    D --> E["Service"]
    R1["Reference: SpiralCore v68 HTML"] -. "consulted" .-> M["Model mechanism: SpiralCore/FBS projection"]
    R2["Reference: Atomic Ternary FBS r3.1 PDF"] -. "consulted" .-> M
    R1 -. "future: not built yet" .-> B

Left: the wire transport that exists today. Right: the two preserved references, which were consulted but are not the build source of the model's mechanism (that follows a v63 reference and a hosted v69 file). The dashed line from the reference to the wire layer is a plan, not code.

What is in the project

The project has two parts that arrived at different times.

1. The wire transport exploration (code). One framing for compressed traffic, exposed four ways: a pair of proxies (a plain app talks to a local edge, the edge talks compressed to a gateway, the gateway talks to the service), a socket library the app links directly, a process interposer that makes unmodified programs use the wire (on macOS through DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES, on Linux through LD_PRELOAD), and opt-in multiplexing of several streams over one connection (UORADM01). The framing starts with a UORADP01 handshake, then length-prefixed frames with a raw-flag bit, so each direction can send zlib-compressed or raw data. There are 36 tool files (16 Python, 17 shell, 3 C) and a Rust crate, wire-rs, that is not part of the model's Cargo workspace.

This work lives at wire/ (82 files). It was copied from a separate review repository at commit 032d903, which keeps the full history.

2. The owner-supplied references (documents). Two sources the owner brought in on 13 September 2026, preserved byte for byte:

Also kept: provenance.json (original paths, byte counts and hashes) and a plain-text extract of the mathematics. The scripts in the HTML file were not executed during import, and its embedded fixture claims were not re-run (research/spiralcore-v68/README.md).

How the pieces fit

The HTML reference defines a fixed graph of rotations over the 16 roots of one E8 anchor orbit, and a search that returns an ordered history between two roots. The model's SpiralCore/FBS mechanism follows a related convention (the v63 reference, implemented in crates/uor-r4-core/src/spiralcore_operator.rs, and a hosted v69 file reviewed on 9 October), not this v68 file. The idea is the same family: an output block picks one stored atom and moves it along a short path of signed coordinate swaps (see the mechanism page and the geometry explainer). The wire transport does not use any of this yet. Its framing is plain length-prefixed zlib, chosen for interoperability.

Code

The wire transport code lives in wire/. It is standalone and is not a member of the repository workspace.

A separate warm-cache networking exploration (DeepSeek, #2808) lives in warm-cache/; it does not share code with wire/ and is not a workspace member either.

WASM-GEMM-GNAF: a Lean proof project about a matrix-multiply kernel

This project tries to prove, with a proof assistant called Lean 4, that one specific small program is the best possible program of its kind. The program is a matrix-multiplication kernel (GEMM) written for WebAssembly, the portable code format that runs in browsers. "Best possible" has a precise meaning set by the project: lowest score on a fixed cost formula, among every program that does the same job. The proof is not finished. The project's own result today is the honest answer "incomplete". It is a side project: it does not train, serve or test the language model, and the model's own rules forbid dense matrix multiplication, so this work is unrelated to how the model computes. It is outside every model build and every loaded path; whether the model ratchet's scan scope covers this folder was not checked for this page.

flowchart TD
    A["Authority: pinned UOR-GNAF draft.2 spec and the fixed claim WGG-GO-1"] --> B["Lean model of WebAssembly: encode, decode, step, cost"]
    B --> C["Cost objective: 36 charged coordinates, weight one each"]
    C --> D["Proved: a best program exists if any program exists"]
    D --> E["Still to show: a concrete program exists, and it equals the committed binary"]
    E -.-> F["Release theorem: global optimality. Not established"]

The proof structure. Solid boxes are done; the last arrow is the goal, which has not been reached.

What the project is

It is a Lean 4 library of 141 files (about 3.4 MB) with a normative specification (SPEC.md), an obligation ledger (CERTIFICATION.md), a claim registry (model/claims.json), pinned copies of its authority documents under authority/, fixtures, tooling and its own licences (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your option). It lives at proof/.

"GNAF" is the name of the authority document the project follows, UOR-GNAF version 1 draft 2, whose text is pinned by a SHA-256 hash. The requested claim, GlobalOptimal, ranges over all finite byte sequences that decode and validate as a WebAssembly module under the chosen profile. It does not range over a hand-picked family of kernels.

How it works

The project defines a cost vector with 36 charged coordinates and a canonical score, the weight-one sum of those coordinates. It models the binary format and the step relation of a subset of WebAssembly, and shows that its cost instrumentation does not change what a program computes. One key fact: each coordinate is at most the score, so every set of programs below a given score is finite. That lets a minimum exist.

With that, the project proves that if some valid program exists, a lowest-scoring one exists and satisfies the optimality statement. What is left is not a bound but an exhibition: build one concrete program with proofs that it qualifies, then show the committed binary is the program the minimum selects.

Code

The Lean project lives in proof/. The gnaf-* commands of xtask read it by path.

The README forbids editing its status paragraph while the proof is open, and the project rule is: if you cannot prove it, omit it. No unproved statement is stubbed or assumed.

How it connects to this repository

The root repository's xtask tool has gnaf-* subcommands (xtask/src/gnaf_*.rs, six files on main) that read this tree, and about 26 documents mention it. Those files move together with the project. The repository's manually dispatched workflow formal_verification.yml (not scheduled) runs the Kani model checker over a different crate, uor-r4-proof-model, not this Lean tree, and no CI step builds the Lean project (folder audit, docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/folders.json). Do not read a green CI run as a check on these proofs.

Where the originals are

This project is already tracked in git, so it has no Hugging Face tar. It is not part of the 19 October backup of the untracked research/ folder. The source is preserved by origin/main itself.

Source files brought into this folder

All 141 files move with their history by git mv, together with the matching xtask/src/gnaf_*.rs subcommands and the xtask entries that reference the old path. No file is dropped.
